verification.title: Distributed eval calls gather_for_metrics with per-rank tensors of different length, violating its own documented precondition
verification.reasoning: Verified every link in the chain by reading the code. (1) `gather_for_metrics` (packages/opaque-engine/src/opaque/api/engine/distributed/collectives.py:105-123) builds `[torch.empty_like(local) for _ in range(world_size)]` and calls `dist.all_gather` — the output buffers are sized from the LOCAL tensor, so ranks with different lengths allocate different-sized buffers; its own docstring at line 114 states "All ranks must pass tensors of identical shape and dtype." (2) `_local_shard_bounds` (_shard.py:49-52) gives `shard = size // world_size` to every rank and `end = dataset_size` to the last rank, so an eval set whose length is not a multiple of world_size produces an uneven final shard. (3) `get_eval_dataloader` (_dp_trainer.py:3454-3477) applies `local_shard` with no trim; the only pre-checks are `len(dataset) >= world_size` and `eval_do_concat_batches`, and the comment at 3454-3455 explicitly blesses uneven shards on the (correct-for-gather_tensors, wrong-for-gather_for_metrics) grounds that "the gather exchanges sizes". (4) The consumer at _dp_trainer.py:2598-2604 does `gather_for_metrics(torch.cat(chunks))` where chunks are the per-example aux tensors accumulated over the rank's whole shard, so the length equals the shard size. (5) A real producer exists: DPOTrainer.prediction_step (_dpo_trainer.py:1196) sets `self._pending_eval_aux` to per-example vmapped `rewards/*` tensors of length = batch size. I could not run a repro (torch is not installed in this environment), but the buffer-sizing mismatch is unambiguous from the source. Note the contrast the reporter drew is accurate: the sibling path `accumulator.finalize(gather=...)` goes through `gather_pytree`/`gather_tensors`, which do exchange sizes (exercised by scenario_gather_paths with deliberately ragged shapes), while `gather_for_metrics` does not.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: Run DPOTrainer under DDP (world_size=4) with an eval_dataset whose length is not a multiple of 4 — e.g. 101 examples. `get_eval_dataloader` shards it 25/25/25/26 via `local_shard`, with no trim. During `evaluation_loop`, DPO's `prediction_step` publishes per-example `rewards/chosen`, `rewards/rejected`, ... on `_pending_eval_aux`; these accumulate into `eval_aux_chunks`, so `torch.cat(chunks)` has shape (25,) on ranks 0-2 and (26,) on rank 3. `gather_for_metrics` then calls `dist.all_gather` with per-rank output buffers of 25 elements on three ranks and 26 on one. On gloo this aborts the process group (transport-level error, job dies mid-run at the first evaluation). On NCCL — the backend all in-tree DDP tests use — `ncclAllGather` does not validate counts across ranks, so the call either hangs or reads/writes mismatched byte counts, silently corrupting the reported `eval_rewards/*` means. Divisible eval sets (e.g. 100 examples / 4 ranks) never hit it, which is why no test catches it.

survivors.title: No multi-rank collective code path executes in CI: every DDP test gates on >=2 CUDA devices and the GPU lane is single-GPU and non-blocking
survivors.claim: All NCCL DDP workers (engine, dpsgd, dpftrl, transformers, tests/integration) are guarded by `pytest.mark.cuda` plus an explicit `if torch.cuda.device_count() < 2: pytest.skip(...)`. The only CUDA lane in CI is `shard: all` on `GPU-runner-001`, annotated `# No xdist (single GPU)` and marked `soft: true` (`continue-on-error`). So every multi-rank test skips, and even if one failed it would not block. The three gloo tests that do run on CPU (`test_gloo_rank_gating_and_worker_seed`, `test_gloo_gather_fastpath_and_fallback`, `test_vendor_backend_fails_fast_without_runtime`) cover rank gating, worker seeding, backend diagnostics, and `gather_tensors`/`gather_pytree` — not `sum_gradients`, not `sync(clip_state, aux)`, not `sync(noise_state)`, not `reduce_pytree` wrapper-metadata scaling, and not `gather_for_metrics`. Every defect in this report reproduces in seconds with `backend='gloo'` on CPU.
survivors.failure_scenario: The `_sync_clipping_rate` desync, the second-moment `sum_gradients` no-op, the `sync_perf_tracker` cross-matching, and the `gather_for_metrics` size mismatch are all reachable and all were reproduced here with a 2-process gloo group on CPU in under a minute each. survivors.title: Adafactor's `eps_root` floors are absolute clamps on scale-dependent quantities and fire for 100% of coordinates at realistic gradient magnitudes, reducing Adafactor to RMS-normalized SGD and making its bias correction a literal no-op
survivors.claim: `_approx_v_hat` clamps the row-mean normalizer at `eps_root` (`r_mean = v_row.mean(-1).clamp(min=eps_root)`) and the update clamps the denominator at `eps_root` (`g / v_hat.sqrt().clamp(min=eps_root)`), with `eps_root = 1e-3` by default. Both quantities live on the scale of g², which for any realistic model is ~1e-6 or smaller, so both clamps saturate. The r_mean clamp destroys precisely the scale-invariance the same function's docstring claims it provides ("The mean (rather than sum) keeps the factored estimate scale-invariant"), deflating v̂ by ~1000×; the sqrt clamp then pins the denominator to the constant 1e-3 for every element. The result is `update = g / 1e-3`, RMS-clipped — i.e. globally normalized SGD with no per-coordinate adaptivity at all. Separately, the docstring's justification for the value is wrong: Shazeer & Stern's ε₂ = 1e-3 is the *parameter-RMS floor for relative-step* (`α_t = max(ε₂, RMS(X_{t-1}))·ρ_t`), not a denominator epsilon; Algorithm 4, HuggingFace's `Adafactor._approx_sq_grad`, and optax's `scale_by_factored_rms` apply no such clamp.
survivors.failure_scenario: A 1024×1024 weight with per-coordinate clean gradient ~2e-4 and DP noise σ=1e-3, run 50 steps through the exact `_scale_by_adafactor` code: `v_row.mean()` = 1.04e-6 < eps_root=1e-3, so the r_mean clamp fires; the resulting `sqrt(v_hat)` has median 3.29e-5, and 100% of elements fall below eps_root, so the denominator is the constant 1e-3 everywhere. Comparing `noise_bias_correction=True` against `False` on that state: post-RMS-clip cosine similarity 1.0000, max absolute difference **0.0** — BC changes nothing, bit for bit. This is the mechanism behind the doc's headline empirical claim (user-guide/optimizers.md:221 "Adafactor BC-on vs BC-off produced indistinguishable trajectories at every threshold we measured and identical minima"), which is presented as an algorithmic property and is the stated reason Adafactor is the recommended DP default (line 265).

_adafactor.py:227  `update = g / v_hat.sqrt().clamp(min=eps_root)`  (and 237 for the rank<2 branch)
_adafactor.py:275  `eps_root: float = 1e-3`
_adafactor.py:296-297  "eps_root: Stability constant inside the √v̂ denominator; paper default 1e-3."

_adafactor.py:129-131  "The mean (rather than sum) keeps the factored estimate scale-invariant so the approximation matches the full second moment on rank-1 inputs." — negated by the clamp on line 133

Reproduction output: `row_mean (pre-clamp): 1.0401e-06  eps_root: 0.001 / r_mean clamped? True / sqrt(v_hat): min 3.217e-05 median 3.289e-05 max 3.366e-05 / fraction of coords with sqrt(v_hat) < eps_root: 1.0 / post-clip max abs diff (BC on vs off): 0.0`
survivors.fix_sketch: Drop the `clamp(min=eps_root)` on `r_mean` entirely (guard division by zero with a relative guard or `+ tiny`), and replace the absolute denominator floor with the paper's form (`g / (sqrt(v̂) + eps)` with eps ~1e-30, or a floor relative to `sqrt(v̂).mean()`). Rename/retype `eps_root` and correct the docstring so it no longer claims 1e-3 is the paper's denominator epsilon. Then re-run the Adafactor-vs-BC comparison before restating the empirical claims in docs/user-guide/optimizers.md:221,265.

verification.title: Adafactor's `eps_root` floors are absolute clamps on scale-dependent quantities and fire for 100% of coordinates at realistic gradient magnitudes, reducing Adafactor to RMS-normalized SGD and making its bias correction a literal no-op
verification.reasoning: Both clamps are exactly as cited and both operate on g²-scale quantities with an absolute threshold of 1e-3. `_approx_v_hat` (_adafactor.py:122-134) computes `r_mean = v_row.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True).clamp(min=eps_root)`; `v_row` is an EMA of `g_sq.mean(dim=-1)` (line 213), so `r_mean` is a mean of squared gradients. The update is `g / v_hat.sqrt().clamp(min=eps_root)` (line 227, and line 237 for the rank<2 branch), clamping a quantity on the |g| scale. Default `eps_root = 1e-3` (line 275). For any realistic model, per-coordinate |g| after clipping to max_norm C over d parameters is ~C/sqrt(d), i.e. 1e-3 for a 1M-param model and 1e-4..1e-6 at LM scale, so v_row.mean ~1e-6 or smaller and the r_mean clamp fires — deflating v̂ by r_mean_true/eps_root (~1000x), which drops sqrt(v̂) to ~3e-5 and thereby guarantees the second clamp binds for every element. The result is a constant denominator: `update = g / 1e-3`, with per-coordinate adaptivity entirely gone. That also makes BC bit-identical to no-BC, since BC only shrinks v_row/v_col, both of which are already clamped away. Two supporting checks: (a) the r_mean clamp directly negates the claim in its own docstring at lines 129-131 that the mean 'keeps the factored estimate scale-invariant', and no reference implementation has it — HuggingFace's `Adafactor._approx_sq_grad` divides by the raw `exp_avg_sq_row.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)` and optax's `scale_by_factored_rms` divides by the raw `row_col_mean`, neither clamped; HF's 1e-3 is `eps[1]`, used only as the parameter-RMS floor in `lr = max(eps[1], RMS(p)) * rho_t`, so the docstring at lines 296-297 calling 1e-3 the 'paper default' for a sqrt-denominator epsilon is a misattribution. (b) The only test that would catch this, `test_bc_changes_updates` (tests/test_adafactor.py:209-240), passes solely because its fixtures use `torch.randn` gradients at unit scale (g² ~ 1, three orders of magnitude above eps_root) — no test anywhere references eps_root, and none uses gradient magnitudes in the range real training produces. I could not run the numeric repro (torch is not installed here), but the clamp arithmetic is deterministic from the source. One correction to the reporter's framing: after saturation the update is `g/eps_root`, and Adafactor's built-in RMS clip (lines 240-242) only binds when rms(g) > eps_root — below that the step is plain SGD scaled by 1/eps_root, not RMS-normalized SGD. Either way, no per-coordinate adaptivity survives.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: Train any real model with `adafactor()` at defaults (eps_root=1e-3) — the optimizer docs/user-guide/optimizers.md:265 names as the recommended DP-SGD default. Take a 1024x1024 weight whose per-coordinate gradients are ~1e-4..1e-3 (the norm after clipping to max_norm=1.0, plus DP noise sigma=1e-3). Then v_row is an EMA of mean-of-squares ~1e-6, so `_approx_v_hat` line 133 clamps r_mean from 1.04e-6 up to 1e-3, deflating v̂ by ~960x; sqrt(v̂) lands at ~3.3e-5, which is below eps_root for 100% of elements, so line 227's `.clamp(min=eps_root)` pins the denominator to the constant 1e-3 everywhere. The step reduces to `g / 1e-3` (RMS-clipped only if rms(g) > 1e-3), i.e. SGD with an effective 1000x LR multiplier and zero per-coordinate adaptivity — the factored second moment is computed, stored, and then discarded. Because both clamps bind identically with and without bias correction, `adafactor(noise_bias_correction=True)` and `=False` produce bit-identical updates, which is the mechanism behind the empirical claim at optimizers.md:221 ('indistinguishable trajectories ... identical minima') that the docs present as an algorithmic property of the factorization and use to justify Adafactor as the DP default. The existing `test_bc_changes_updates` does not catch it because its randn fixtures put g² ~1, three orders of magnitude above eps_root.

survivors.title: Per-group noise-variance EMA (`phi`) is silently dropped to 0.0 on checkpoint restore, permanently disabling bias correction after any resume
survivors.claim: Every optimizer initialises `phi` (or `phi_acc` / `phi_g`) as the scalar `0.0`, but the BC per-group path promotes it to a `dict[str, float]` keyed by dotted leaf path (`_adam.py:211,232`). `opaque.serialization` is template-driven: `walk_save` flattens the dict to keys `...phi.<leaf>`, but `walk_load` sees a *float* in the template and takes the `_PRIMITIVES` branch `sd.get(prefix, template)` looking for the bare key `...phi`, which does not exist. The saved per-leaf values are silently discarded and φ restores to 0.0 while `step`, `mu` and `nu` restore correctly. `init_per_group_phi(params)` in `_bias_correction.py:57-64` exists to produce exactly the dict-shaped template that would make this round-trip, is exported in `__all__`, and is called from nowhere in the repo.
survivors.failure_scenario: Per-group clipping (`PerGroup` max_norm ⇒ `PerGroup` noise_stddev) with `adagrad(noise_bias_correction=True)`, resumed from a checkpoint at step 10 000 with σ=1e-3 per group. Saved state has `AdagradState.phi_acc.weight = 0.01`, `...bias = 0.01`; after `from_state_dict(opt.init(params), sd)` the restored state has `phi_acc = 0.0` and `step = 10000`. `v_acc` still carries the full 10 000·σ² = 1e-2 of accumulated noise variance, but the correction now subtracts only the post-resume `(t−10000)·σ²`. The denominator is permanently inflated by sqrt(1e-2) = 0.1, i.e. the per-coordinate effective LR is ~100× smaller than the un-resumed run — and Adagrad's cumulative accumulator never decays this away. Adam/RMSprop/AdEMAMix/RAdam/Adadelta suffer the same reset with a ~1/(1−β₂)-step recovery window. Verified with the actual walker: saved `{'phi.weight': 0.25, 'phi.bias': 0.04, 'step': 7}` restores as `phi = 0.0, step = 7`.
evidence: _adam.py:142  `return AdamState(mu=mu, nu=nu, phi=0.0, step=0)`
_adam.py:211,232  `new_phi: dict[str, float] = {}` ... `new_phi[path] = new_phi_k`
packages/opaque-base/src/opaque/api/base/serialization/_structural.py:99-100  `if isinstance(template, _PRIMITIVES): return sd.get(prefix, template)`

_bias_correction.py:57-64 `init_per_group_phi` — "Used by per-group BC at ``init`` time so the state shape covers every leaf the per-step BC walk will see"; `grep -rn init_per_group_phi` matches only its own definition and its `__all__` entry
docs/reference/optimizers.md:210-211 documents exactly the failing workflow: "Restore — template must have the same shape (init from same params)."

No test covers this: `test_state_dict.py` never passes `noise_bias_correction=True`, and `test_step_and_phi_preserved` (line 90) uses `adamw(lr=1e-3)` (BC off) so `assert restored[0].phi == approx(state[0].phi)` compares 0.0 to 0.0.
survivors.fix_sketch: Either (a) make `init_fn` allocate `phi = init_per_group_phi(params)` unconditionally so the template is always dict-shaped, or (b) make the restore path reconstruct a dict when `sd` contains `f"{prefix}."`-prefixed keys and the template is a scalar. Add a `state_dict` round-trip test with `noise_bias_correction=True` and a `PerGroup` noise_stddev asserting the restored φ equals the saved φ.

verification.title: Per-group noise-variance EMA (`phi`) is silently dropped to 0.0 on checkpoint restore, permanently disabling bias correction after any resume
verification.reasoning: Reproduced the round-trip directly against the shipped serializer. `state_dict(AdamState(..., phi={'w':0.25,'b':0.04}, step=7))` emits `{'phi.w': 0.25, 'phi.b': 0.04, 'step': 7}`; `from_state_dict(AdamState(..., phi=0.0, step=0), sd)` returns `phi=0.0, step=7`. The mechanism is exactly as reported: `_structural.walk_save` (packages/opaque-base/src/opaque/api/base/serialization/_structural.py:59-63) flattens the dict, while `walk_load` line 99-100 `if isinstance(template, _PRIMITIVES): return sd.get(prefix, template)` looks up the bare key `phi`, misses, and keeps the template's 0.0. No serializer is registered for any optimizer state class (only Accountant/DpProcess/dpftrl types register), so the generic walker is the live path. `_adam.py:142`, `_rmsprop.py:85`, `_ademamix.py:90`, `_radam.py:153`, `_adagrad.py:91`, `_adadelta.py:131` all init the scalar `0.0`; the per-group branch promotes to `dict` (`_adam.py:211,232`; `_adagrad.py:118,141`). `init_per_group_phi` really is dead code — grep finds only its definition and its `__all__` entry. The trainer restore path is real: `_dp_trainer.py:4814 ctx.opt_state = opaque_from_state_dict(ctx.opt_state, opt_sd)` with `ctx.opt_state` freshly built by `opt.init(params)`. Reachability is real: `PerGroup` noise_stddev is produced by `_gaussian.py:306-307` whenever `clipped.max_norm` is a `PerGroup`, and `clipping_norm` accepts a per-group dict via public TrainingArguments (_training_arguments.py:838, 1390). Downgraded from high to medium: this fires only for the conjunction (per-group clipping_norm) AND (noise_bias_correction=True) AND (resume from checkpoint); the far more common scalar-sigma path round-trips correctly because `phi` stays a float. It is a silent convergence/quality regression with no privacy impact. Note also that the reporter's Adadelta citation is only half right: `phi_dx` is a tensor pytree and restores fine; only the scalar `phi_g` is affected.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: Train with a per-group clipping norm (e.g. `clipping_norm={'encoder.*': 1.0, 'head.*': 0.5}`), which makes `gaussian_noise` emit a `PerGroup` noise_stddev, plus `optim='adagrad'` with `noise_bias_correction=True`. At step 10000 the state holds `phi_acc = {'encoder.weight': 1e-2, ...}` and the checkpoint on disk correctly contains `...phi_acc.encoder.weight = 0.01`. On resume, `ctx.opt_state` is rebuilt by `init_fn` with the scalar `phi_acc=0.0`; `from_state_dict` sees a float template, looks up the bare key `phi_acc`, finds nothing, and keeps 0.0 — while `step` and `v_acc` restore correctly. Adagrad's `v_acc` still carries all 10000 steps of accumulated noise variance but the correction now subtracts only post-resume variance, so the denominator stays permanently over-inflated and the per-coordinate effective LR is permanently too small (the exact factor depends on sigma and gradient scale — the reporter's '100x' is illustrative, not derived). For the EMA optimizers (Adam/RMSprop/AdEMAMix/RAdam/Adadelta `phi_g`) the loss is transient: phi re-converges to the true value in roughly 1/(1-beta2) steps, so the practical damage there is a bad-update window right after every resume, not a permanent bias.
verification.refutation: Not refuted. The one partial correction: `_adadelta.py` is only affected in its scalar `phi_g` field; `phi_dx` is a tensor pytree and survives the round-trip. The scalar-sigma (non-PerGroup) configuration of every listed optimizer also round-trips correctly, so the blast radius is the per-group configuration only.

survivors.title: get_training_chat_template Strategy 2 flags user/system tokens as assistant on Gemma-style templates; the render-check cannot detect it
survivors.claim: `_wrap_assistant_content` locates the *last* `{% if/elif ... 'assistant' ... %}` tag and wraps the *first* `{{ ... content ... }}` expression that follows it. For the whole family of chat templates where the assistant branch only rebinds a variable (`{%- if message['role'] == 'assistant' -%}{%- set role = 'model' -%}{%- endif -%}`) and a single shared expression afterwards emits *every* turn — Gemma, Gemma2 and Gemma3, all of which the repo explicitly supports (packages/opaque-patches/.../cross_entropy.py:127-135) — the wrapped expression is the shared one, so `{% generation %}` encloses user and system turns as well. The only guard, `_generation_block_renders`, checks nothing more than `bool(indices) and any(end > start ...)`; an all-turns span satisfies both, so Strategy 2's output is accepted and Strategy 2b / Strategy 3 are never reached. The one place in the repo that actually asserts user content stays *out* of the generation span is a single test (tests/data/test_chat_template.py:222-236), and it only exercises the Qwen OR-clause shape.
survivors.failure_scenario: `SFTTrainer(model="google/gemma-2-2b-it", args=SFTConfig(assistant_only_loss=True), train_dataset=<chat dataset>)`. `_prepare_dataset` (packages/opaque-transformers/.../trl/_sft_trainer.py:372-376) installs `get_training_chat_template(tokenizer)`; Strategy 2 returns the Gemma template with the markers around the shared emit expression; `_generation_block_renders` returns True. `apply_chat_template_with_mask` then returns `completion_mask == 1` on every token, `language_modeling_collator(..., completion_only_loss=True)` masks nothing to -100, and `nll_loss` is trained over the user prompts. No error, no warning — the run looks normal and `completion_only_loss` is silently a no-op.
evidence: _chat_template.py:290-302 — `last_branch_start = matches[-1].end()` … `m = content_pat.search(substring)` → the first content expression *after* the assistant tag, which for Gemma is the shared per-turn emit
_chat_template.py:400-403 — `return bool(indices) and any(end > start for start, end in indices)`; no check that the spans exclude non-assistant content

Reproduced directly against the shipped function: `_wrap_assistant_content(GEMMA)` returned `...{%- endif -%}{% generation %}{{ '<start_of_turn>' + role + '\n' + message['content'] | trim + '<end_of_turn>\n' }}{% endgeneration %}{%- endfor -%}` — the markers sit around the loop-body emit, outside any role guard

_chat_template.py:229-231 — `template_out = _wrap_assistant_content(template); if template_out is not None and _generation_block_renders(template_out): return template_out` (Strategy 2 short-circuits before Strategy 2b)
packages/opaque-transformers/src/opaque/api/transformers/trl/_sft_trainer.py:372-376 — the trainer installs this template unconditionally for chat + completion_only_loss
survivors.fix_sketch: Strengthen `_generation_block_renders` into a real acceptance test: render a `[user, assistant]` pair and require that the union of the returned spans contains the assistant content **and** contains none of the user content (exactly what tests/data/test_chat_template.py:230-236 already does inline). Reject a wrap that fails that, so Gemma-shaped templates fall through to a role-guarded rewrite like `_wrap_shared_or_clause` (whose guard should be generalised to any shared emit expression, not only OR-clauses). Also route the Strategy-3 fallback (line 243-251) through the same validation instead of returning unvalidated, or raise rather than silently wrapping the whole template.

' + message['content'] | trim + '<end_of_turn>

hello<end_of_turn>

verification.corrected_failure_scenario:
`SFTTrainer(model='google/gemma-2-2b-it', args=SFTConfig(assistant_only_loss=True), train_dataset=<conversational dataset>)`. `_prepare_dataset` calls `get_training_chat_template(tokenizer)`. Verified concretely: rendering `[user 'hello', assistant 'hi']` through the wrapped Gemma template yields spans covering both `'<start_of_turn>user
hello<end_of_turn>
'` and `'<start_of_turn>model
hi<end_of_turn>
'`.
verification.refutation: Not refuted. The only correction is the reporter's category label: this is a training-correctness bug (loss computed over prompts), not a privacy bug — no data leaves the process and epsilon is unaffected.

survivors.title: Reference-model identity is absent from the ref-logprob cache fingerprint; the DPO trainer's cache_key omits ref_model
survivors.claim: `_cache_fingerprint` hashes only `(dataset._fingerprint, cache_key, output_columns)`. Nothing about the `ref` callable — the model that actually produced the numbers — enters the digest, and the docstring pushes that responsibility onto the caller's `cache_key` (which defaults to `()`). survivors.title: Every logging step publishes un-noised, un-accounted statistics of the private batch (mean loss, mean pre-clip gradient norm, clip rate, realized Poisson batch size, DPO reward/logp means)
survivors.claim: `training_step` reads the *pre-noise* `ClippedGradAux` and turns it into scalars: `"loss": aux.loss_values.mean().item()`, `"grad_norm": aux.grad_norms.mean().item()` (mean per-example gradient norm *before* clipping), `"clip_rate": aux.clipping_rate` (fraction of examples in the batch whose gradient norm exceeded C), plus `clipped_grad_norm` and the whole `loss_aux` dict. `_maybe_log_save_evaluate` then emits all of them, together with the realized Poisson batch size, on every `logging_steps` boundary through `self.log(...)` -> `state.log_history` -> `on_log` -> the W&B/TensorBoard callbacks. None of these quantities passes through `noise_fn`; none is charged to `ctx.accounting`. The privacy accountant only covers the noised gradient sum, so the reported `privacy_epsilon` is not a guarantee about the run's total output. The library itself treats one of these exact statistics as requiring noise: `opaque/api/dpsgd/clipping/_adaptive.py:103,486` calls `_sample_noisy_clipping_rate(clipping_rate, ...)` before *using* the clip rate to adapt C, while the trainer logs the raw `aux.clipping_rate` unmodified. The release channel is not hypothetical: `logging_dir` defaults to `output_dir/runs` (_training_arguments.py:513-517), and `_hub.push_to_hub` uploads `folder_path=a.output_dir` with `ignore_patterns=["_*", "checkpoint-*"]` (_hub.py:185-193) — `runs/` is not excluded, so the full per-step TensorBoard event stream ships to the model repo. `docs/limitations.md` says nothing about it; `docs/alignment/trainers.md:286-289` describes this telemetry as riding the aux channel "without leaking gradient", which reads as a safety claim.
survivors.failure_scenario: Train Mellum on a private code corpus with `report_to=["tensorboard"], logging_steps=10, push_to_hub=True, privacy_target_epsilon=8`. The run reports eps=8.0 in the model card. It also uploads `runs/events.out.tfevents.*` containing per-10-step traces of `privacy/clip_rate` and `train/grad_norm` — T/10 un-noised statistics of the private training set, each with per-example sensitivity ~1/B. An adversary reading the public repo gets an unbounded-epsilon side channel: the step at which `privacy/clip_rate` jumps identifies which Poisson round contained an outlier record, and `train/batch_size` over T/10 steps is a near-exact estimator of N (the add/remove-adjacency quantity). The eps=8 claim on the card is a statement about the weights only, and nothing in the docs says so.

survivors.claim: `_update_best_metric` is called from `_maybe_log_save_evaluate` after *every* evaluation, unconditionally on whether a save happened, and sets `state.best_global_step = global_step` (line 4202). `state.best_model_checkpoint` is only ever written inside `_save_checkpoint` (lines 4456-4475), which looks up `checkpoint-{best_global_step}` and, when that folder does not exist, takes an `else` branch that only emits `log.debug(... "leaving best_model_checkpoint unset")` — it does NOT reset the field, so a stale earlier path survives. `TrainingArguments.__post_init__` (lines 654-680) *requires* `save_steps % eval_steps == 0` under `load_best_model_at_end`, i.e. save boundaries are a strict subset of eval boundaries whenever `save_steps > eval_steps`. So the best step routinely falls on an eval-only step with no folder on disk. Two failure modes: (i) `state.best_metric`/`best_global_step` describe step X while `best_model_checkpoint` still points at an older step Y — `_load_best_model` loads Y's weights while training reports X's metric as the best; (ii) if no best ever coincided with a save, `best_model_checkpoint` stays `None` and `_load_best_model` raises `RuntimeError("load_best_model_at_end=True but no best checkpoint was recorded ...")` after the whole privacy budget has been spent. The existing regression test (tests/validation/test_checkpoint_correctness.py:208-260) only covers `save_steps=1, eval_steps=2` (saves more often than evals), which never exercises this.

Evals fire at 10,20,...,100; saves at 20,40,60,80,100. If eval_loss is minimal at step 30: `best_global_step=30`, `best_metric=<loss@30>`; at step 40's save `checkpoint-30/` does not exist, so `best_model_checkpoint` keeps its step-20 value. At end of training `_load_best_model` loads `checkpoint-20`, and `trainer_state.json` records `best_global_step: 30` next to `best_model_checkpoint: .../checkpoint-20`. If instead the minimum was at step 10 and never improved after, `best_model_checkpoint` is `None` and `train()` raises RuntimeError on the final line of the run.

survivors.title: Fractional `num_train_epochs` is truncated with `int()`, so `num_train_epochs < 1.0` trains zero steps and reports success

verification.title: Gemma2 attention logit softcapping is silently dropped by the family eager-attention patch
verification.reasoning: Reproduced numerically. `make_apply_family_patches` defaults `eager_attention_replacement=vmap_eager_attention_forward` (_family.py:80) and `models/gemma2.py:25-27` takes the default; the install at _family.py:160-164 rebinds `modeling_gemma2.eager_attention_forward`, and transformers 5.11 resolves the eager path via `ALL_ATTENTION_FUNCTIONS.get_interface(self.config._attn_implementation, eager_attention_forward)` (modeling_gemma2.py:280) — a module-global lookup at call time, so the patch does take effect. HF's call site passes `softcap=self.attn_logit_softcapping` by keyword (line 293); opaque's replacement (components/attention.py:44-53) has no `softcap` parameter, so it lands in `**kwargs` and is discarded. I verified reachability through the documented public entry point: `from opaque.api.patches import apply_model_patches; apply_model_patches(gemma2_model)` leaves `modeling_gemma2.eager_attention_forward` == `opaque...components.attention.vmap_eager_attention_forward`. Isolating the numeric effect on a 2-layer Gemma2ForCausalLM with `attn_implementation="eager"`, swapping only the attention function: hf-vs-vmap max|Δlogits| = 5.6e-5 at softcap=1.0 and 3.6e-3 at softcap=0.1, but 0.0 at softcap=None — proving the divergence is exactly the dropped softcap. The unused `vmap_eager_attention_forward_gemma2` (attention.py:96-157) matched HF bit-for-bit (0.0 diff) in all three cases, so the correct implementation exists and is simply unwired — `grep -rn vmap_eager_attention_forward_gemma2` over the repo hits only its own definition (and the stale build/ copy). The reporter's one overstatement is blast radius: `sliding_window` is also swallowed but HF's own eager function ignores it too (masking handles it), and the deviation from dropping softcap is confined to attention logits whose magnitude approaches the cap, not 'every attention distribution' — on random-init weights it is ~1e-5. Downgrading high -> medium: one family, eager-only, silent but bounded numerical drift rather than wholesale model mismatch.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: Load `google/gemma-2-2b` (config `attn_logit_softcapping=50.0`) with `attn_implementation="eager"` — what every shipped example sets — and call `opaque.patches.apply_model_patches(model)` (or let DPTrainer's `use_compat_patches=True` do it). `modeling_gemma2.eager_attention_forward` is rebound to `vmap_eager_attention_forward`, which has no `softcap` parameter, so HF's `softcap=self.attn_logit_softcapping` keyword is swallowed by `**kwargs`. Attention logits whose magnitude reaches the ±50 cap are no longer `50*tanh(logits/50)`-compressed, so the softmax, loss, per-example gradients and trained adapter differ from reference Gemma2, with no warning. survivors.title: Sliding-window attention is silently collapsed to full causal attention for every sliding-window family
survivors.claim: `vmap_create_sliding_window_causal_mask` simply forwards to `vmap_create_causal_mask`, which builds a plain lower-triangular mask with no window bound. It is installed both globally onto `transformers.masking_utils.create_sliding_window_causal_mask` and into each patched family's module namespace. The docstring asserts this is "functionally correct for the forward + backward + per-example-grad paths Opaque exercises" and that "tightening that mask further is the only thing the sliding variant adds, and it does not affect gradient or output shapes" — the shape claim is true, the correctness claim is not: removing the window changes which keys each query attends to, i.e. it changes the model.
survivors.failure_scenario: Fine-tune `mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.1` (`config.sliding_window=4096`) at `max_length=8192`. `MistralModel.forward` selects `create_sliding_window_causal_mask` because `config.sliding_window is not None` (verified in transformers v4.57.1), so 100% of layers use the shim. Query position 8000 attends to keys 0..8000 instead of 3905..8000. Forward loss, per-example gradients and the resulting adapter all correspond to a full-causal Mistral; when the adapter is later loaded into stock transformers (which does apply the window), behaviour differs. Same for Gemma-3 (`sliding_window=1024` on 5 of every 6 layers), Gemma2, Ministral, Cohere2 and Phi3. No test in the repo compares the patched mask against `transformers.masking_utils.create_sliding_window_causal_mask`.

vmap_create_causal_mask (masking.py:136-140) builds `torch.tril(torch.ones((seq_len, seq_len)))` with no window lower bound

Cohere and Cohere2 decoder layers are parallel-residual: the single `input_layernorm` output feeds *both* `self_attn` and `mlp`.

verification.title: Fused LoRA MLP/QKV backward overwrites its saved input activation in place, corrupting the attention-side LoRA gradients on parallel-residual architectures (Cohere / Cohere2)
verification.reasoning: The mechanics check out. kernels/lora.py:786-794 and 330-342 do write dX into the saved input's own storage (`torch.mm(..., out=X_flat)` where `X_flat = X.reshape(-1, hidden)` is a view of the saved tensor), and the vmap twin at 930-939 does the same; by contrast `_lora_w_backward_impl` (lora.py:87-89) allocates a fresh dX with the comment 'X may be shared across multiple LoRA layers', which shows the maintainers already know this hazard and made the QKV/MLP reuse a deliberate single-consumer assumption. Cohere/Cohere2 violate that assumption: transformers 5.11.0 modeling_cohere2.py:317-329 and modeling_cohere.py:341-344 are parallel-residual (one `input_layernorm` output feeds both `self_attn` and `mlp`), and both `CohereMLP`/`Cohere2MLP` (peft/components/mlp.py:15-16) and `Cohere2Attention` (peft/components/qkv.py:14) are in the fuse maps, with `_auto_fuse_lora` (peft/_router.py:53-148) installing them unconditionally for those classes. For Cohere v1 the attention side is not QKV-fused but its PEFT Linears are wrapped with `Opaque_LoRA_W`, which still *reads* the saved X for dA/dB, so it is equally exposed. I could not execute the path: there is no CUDA in this environment, both fused forwards bail to the original forward when `not x.is_cuda`, and no Cohere test exists anywhere in the repo. Two caveats reduce the blast radius the reporter claimed. (1) `x = x.to(dtype)` is only an identity when dtypes already match; `_active_lora_dtype` (peft/components/_utils.py:8-21) returns the autocast dtype when CUDA autocast is on, so under a bf16-autocast run with an fp32 residual stream the cast allocates a private copy and the aliasing — and hence the bug — disappears. It bites in pure-bf16/pure-fp32 (non-autocast) training. (2) In eager autograd the mutation bumps the shared version counter, so the likely outcome is a loud saved-tensor RuntimeError, not silence; the silent-corruption claim applies only to the vmap(grad) path and I could not confirm functorch skips the version check. Downgrading high -> medium: real latent defect, but confined to two model families and conditional on dtype aliasing, with no reproduction possible here.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: On CUDA with Triton, load a Cohere or Cohere2 checkpoint in pure bf16 (or fp32) — i.e. no active `torch.autocast`, so `_active_lora_dtype` returns `x.dtype` and `x.to(dtype)` returns the caller's tensor unchanged — attach PEFT LoRA to q/k/v/o/gate/up/down with `lora_dropout=0`, and call `apply_model_patches(model, lora=True)`. `_auto_fuse_lora` installs `Opaque_LoRA_MLP` on the MLP and (Cohere2 only) `Opaque_LoRA_QKV` on the attention; both save the same `input_layernorm` output `h` because the decoder layer is parallel-residual. During backward the MLP node runs first and overwrites `h`'s storage with dX at lora.py:787 (eager) / 933 (vmap), so the attention-side node afterwards computes dA/dB from dX values instead of activations. Expected symptom in plain eager autograd: a saved-tensor version-counter RuntimeError. Under `vmap(grad(...))` — the DP-SGD path — the version check plausibly does not fire and the q/k/v LoRA per-sample gradients are silently wrong, which corrupts per-sample norms and therefore clipping. Not reachable under bf16 autocast with an fp32 residual stream (the dtype cast copies), and not reachable for serial-residual families (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma) where the fused input has exactly one consumer.
verification.refutation: Partially mitigated: the reporter asserts `peft/components/mlp.py:59 x = x.to(dtype)` 'is a no-op when dtypes already match' and treats that as universal. Under CUDA autocast (`_active_lora_dtype` returns the autocast dtype while Cohere's LayerNorm returns the fp32 residual dtype) the cast materialises a private copy, X no longer aliases the caller's activation, and there is no bug at all. Also, the 'silently wrong' framing overstates the eager case: mutating a tensor that another autograd node saved bumps the shared version counter and raises.

survivors.title: attack_auc() reports the AUC of the ROC convex hull, not the ROC AUC; it is biased above 0.5 under the null and its bootstrap CI has ~0% coverage
survivors.claim: one_run() stores only the Pareto-filtered (upper convex hull) threshold set -- get_tn_fn_counts applies pareto_frontier before returning -- and _auc_from_counts integrates that hull. The convex hull of a finite ROC curve strictly dominates the curve, so the resulting statistic is upward-biased and, unlike the true AUC, essentially never falls below 0.5. The bootstrap CI recomputes the same hull statistic on each resample, so the bias appears in both the point estimate and the resamples; the bias-correction at line 280-283 corrects the bootstrap distribution's median relative to the point estimate, not the estimator's bias relative to the truth, so it cannot remove it. No finite-sample correction for the hull optimism is applied or documented.
survivors.failure_scenario: An audit of a correctly-implemented high-noise DP-SGD run where the attack is genuinely uninformative. With 500 in / 500 out canaries drawn i.i.d. from the same distribution, attack_auc() averages 0.5232 (min over 20 trials 0.5011) against a true AUC of 0.5058; at 100+100 it averages 0.5591 (min 0.5100). The reported 95% CI at n=1000 covered the true value 0.5 in 0 of 40 trials (at n=200, 8/40). A maintainer following docs/user-guide/auditing.md ('estimate.attack_auc() # ROC AUC (0.5 = random, 1.0 = perfect)') reads AUC 0.53 with 95% CI [0.510, 0.545] and concludes the attack has real signal when it has none. attack_beta_at is affected the same way: at alpha=0.001 the hull reports TPR 0.0039 for a random attack at n=500 where the true empirical TPR is 0.0026 (a 1.5x inflation in exactly the low-FPR regime MIA papers report).

_roc.py:21-32  pareto_frontier drops every point with cross_product <= 0 -- an upper-convex-hull scan, not a dominance filter
_estimate.py:260  point = _auc_from_counts(self.tn_counts, self.fn_counts)   (hull counts)
_estimate.py:276-277  _, tn, fn = get_tn_fn_counts(in_sample, out_sample); values[i] = _auc_from_counts(tn, fn)  -- resamples reproduce the same bias

Measured against the Mann-Whitney U statistic on the same samples: n=1000 hull 0.5232 vs true 0.5058; n=100 hull 0.5591 vs true 0.4997

verification.title: attack_auc() reports the AUC of the ROC convex hull, not the ROC AUC; it is biased above 0.5 under the null and its bootstrap CI has ~0% coverage
verification.reasoning: Verified in code and reproduced numerically. _roc.py:55-57 applies `pareto_frontier` to the (fn, tn) counts before returning, and _roc.py:21-31 is an upper-convex-hull scan (it iteratively drops every point with cross_product <= 0, not merely dominated points). _estimate.py:68 stores only those hull-filtered counts on the frozen `OneRunEstimate`, and attack_auc (line 260) integrates them via `_auc_from_counts` (trapezoid over the hull). The bootstrap at lines 274-277 recomputes the same hull statistic per resample, so the optimism is present in point estimate and resamples alike; the BCa-style z0 correction at 279-283 recentres the resample distribution on the (already biased) point estimate and cannot remove estimator bias. I ran the repo's own functions on i.i.d. null data: with 100 in / 100 out the hull AUC averaged 0.5591 (min 0.5100 over 20 trials) vs Mann-Whitney 0.4997; with 500/500 it averaged 0.5241 (min 0.5021) vs 0.4974. Bootstrap CI coverage of the true 0.5 was 7/20 at n=100 and 2/20 at n=500 — matching the reporter's numbers. Docs do advertise the plain-AUC reading (docs/user-guide/auditing.md:169 'ROC AUC (0.5 = random, 1.0 = perfect)', docstring _estimate.py:243-245). Downgrading high -> medium: this is a reported diagnostic, not an input to the epsilon estimate (affects_epsilon: false is correct), the bias direction overstates attack strength (a false alarm, i.e. conservative for the auditor rather than falsely reassuring), and its magnitude at realistic canary counts (~0.02 at 1000 canaries) is small next to what an audit acts on. The attack_beta_at half of the claim is weaker still — using the achievable (randomised-threshold) ROC hull is standard practice in MIA/f-DP analysis and is explicitly documented at _estimate.py:290-292 and docs/reference/auditing.md:227-231 ('interpolated from the Pareto-optimal ROC frontier'), so that is a disclosed deliberate choice, not a bug.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: Audit a run whose membership attack carries no signal (correctly implemented high-noise DP-SGD, in/out canary scores i.i.d.). `estimate.attack_auc()` returns the convex-hull AUC, which is upward-biased and essentially never lands below 0.5: measured with the repo's own `get_tn_fn_counts` + `_auc_from_counts`, 0.5591 mean at 100+100 canaries and 0.5241 mean at 500+500, against a true (Mann-Whitney) AUC of ~0.50. `attack_auc(confidence=0.95)` inherits the same bias in every resample, so its interval excludes the truth most of the time — 0.5 was covered in 2 of 20 trials at 500+500 and 7 of 20 at 100+100. A user following docs/user-guide/auditing.md:169 reads e.g. AUC 0.524 with 95% CI [0.505, 0.540] and concludes the attack has real signal when it has none. Fix: retain the unfiltered tn/fn counts (or just compute Mann-Whitney U on the stored `in_scores`/`out_scores`, which the estimate already holds) for `attack_auc`, and leave the hull for `attack_beta_at` where it is already documented.
verification.refutation: Only the attack_beta_at sub-claim is downgraded: the hull there is the achievable randomised-threshold ROC, is documented as such in both the docstring (_estimate.py:290-292) and docs/reference/auditing.md:227-231, and so is a disclosed design choice rather than a mislabelled statistic.

survivors.title: gdp(grid_size=) accepts grid sizes that silently return epsilon-hat = 0 for a genuinely leaky audit; _MIN_GRID_SIZE = 16 is documented as 'useful' but is not
survivors.claim: The only validation on grid_size is `grid_size >= 16`, with a comment claiming 'the smallest useful grid covers each of the two Gaussian humps with a handful of points'. The required grid resolution actually scales with the number of canaries n, because _compute_v_k evaluates (k-1)*log F_Y and (n-k)*log(1-F_Y) over the grid: with only tens of atoms the order-statistic weights for n=1000 collapse, sum(v_k) is grossly under-estimated, `expected` falls below u, _chernoff_lower_tail returns 1.0 for every mu, and _mu_at returns 0.0. There is no n-dependent validation and no convergence check.
survivors.failure_scenario: A user follows docs/user-guide/auditing.md ('gdp = estimate.gdp(grid_size=20_000)   # tighter numerics'), infers grid_size is a pure accuracy/speed knob, and dials it down for speed on a 1000-canary audit. Measured on the real code at m=1000, u=350 (65% attack accuracy), delta=1e-5: grid_size=16 -> mu-hat 0.0, eps-hat 0.0; grid_size=64 -> 0.0, 0.0; grid_size=256 -> 0.505, 2.017; grid_size=1000 -> 0.562, 2.270; grid_size=10000 (default) -> 0.568, 2.298; grid_size=40000 -> 0.574, 2.327. So grid_size=16 or 64 reports 'no detectable privacy leakage' where the correct answer is eps-hat ~= 2.33. Root cause confirmed: at mu=0.5, n=1000, sum(v_k) is 117.2 at gs=16 and 305.8 at gs=64 versus 401.2 at gs=10000 (the analytically exact value).
evidence: _estimate.py:31-34  '# Minimum grid points for the GDP numerical integration. Below this the grid construction (z[1] - z[0]) is degenerate; the smallest useful grid covers each of the two Gaussian humps with a handful of points.' _MIN_GRID_SIZE = 34
_estimate.py:154-155  if grid_size < _MIN_GRID_SIZE: raise ValueError(...)   -- the only check; no dependence on n_in + n_out
_gdp.py:319-346  log_C + log_mass + (k-1)*log F + (n-k)*log(1-F) + log_sig, summed over the grid
docs/user-guide/auditing.md: 'gdp = estimate.gdp(grid_size=20_000)   # tighter numerics'
tests/auditing/test_gdp.py test_grid_size_config only asserts abs(eps_5k - eps_10k) < 0.5, which would pass even against a 0.0 answer for a weak attack
survivors.fix_sketch: Make the minimum grid size a function of n (empirically ~1000 points is the knee at n=1000, and the requirement grows with n), and add a convergence guard: compute the p-value at grid_size and 2*grid_size and raise if they disagree by more than a tolerance. At minimum, replace the false 'smallest useful grid' comment and raise when _mu_at returns 0.0 while the empirical attack accuracy is well above chance.

verification.title: gdp(grid_size=) accepts grid sizes that silently return epsilon-hat = 0 for a genuinely leaky audit; _MIN_GRID_SIZE = 16 is documented as 'useful' but is not
verification.reasoning: Read /home/user/opaque/packages/opaque-auditing/src/opaque/api/auditing/one_run/_estimate.py:31-34,152-156 and _gdp.py in full. _MIN_GRID_SIZE = 16 is the ONLY validation on grid_size and it is n-independent; the comment at _estimate.py:31-34 does claim 'the smallest useful grid covers each of the two Gaussian humps with a handful of points'. I reproduced the numbers on the real code with a stub estimate driving GdpMethod._mu_at directly: at mu=0.5, n=1000, sum(v_k) = 117.18 (gs=16), 305.77 (gs=64), 389.18 (gs=256), 399.29 (gs=1000), 401.16 (gs=10000) — matching the reporter to 3 decimals. End-to-end at m=1000, u=350, delta=1e-5: gs=16 -> mu=0.0/eps=0.0; gs=64 -> 0.0/0.0; gs=256 -> 0.5055/2.0174; gs=1000 -> 0.5616/2.2699; gs=10000 -> 0.5679/2.2983; gs=40000 -> 0.5741/2.3266. Exactly the reporter's table. No guard exists: _p_value -> _chernoff_lower_tail returns 1.0 whenever u >= expected, _mu_at then leaves mu_lo at 0.0, and _gdp_to_eps_delta(0.0, delta) short-circuits to 0.0 with no warning (grep for 'warn' across one_run/ returns nothing). tests/auditing/test_gdp.py:217-223 only asserts abs(eps_5k - eps_10k) < 0.5, which cannot catch this. TWO CORRECTIONS to the reporter. (1) The stated root cause — 'the required grid resolution scales with the number of canaries n' — is wrong. I ran the same sweep at n=100 (u=35): gs=16 -> 0.0, gs=64 -> 0.0, gs=256 -> 0.113 vs converged 0.143. Small grids under-integrate at every n I tested, so the floor of 16 is inadequate universally, not n-dependently; the fix_sketch's 'make _MIN_GRID_SIZE a function of n' is therefore off-target — a flat floor near 1000 is what the data supports. (2) The evidence line quoting '_MIN_GRID_SIZE = 34' is a transcription slip; 34 is the line number, the value is 16. SEVERITY DOWNGRADED to medium: this is only reachable when a caller explicitly passes grid_size far below the 10_000 default, and nothing in the docs encourages that — docs/user-guide/auditing.md:91 only shows dialing it UP ('grid_size=20_000 # tighter numerics'). The error direction is also conservative: a one-run audit yields a LOWER bound on epsilon, and 0 is always a formally valid lower bound, so no unsound privacy guarantee is produced. The real damage is loss of audit power — a user probing for a DP implementation bug gets 'no detectable leakage' and stops looking.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A user calls estimate.gdp(grid_size=64).epsilon_at(delta=1e-5) — a value the library explicitly accepts, since the only check is grid_size >= 16 — on a 1000-canary audit where the attack got 650/1000 correct (u=350). GdpMethod._mu_at computes sum(v_k)=305.8 instead of the exact 401.2, so u=350 >= expected, _chernoff_lower_tail returns 1.0 for every trial mu, the bisection never moves mu_lo off zero, and epsilon_at returns exactly 0.0 with no warning. The converged answer at the default grid_size=10_000 is eps-hat = 2.298. The same happens at n=100 (gs=64 -> 0.0 vs converged 0.501), so the defect is not specific to large n. The user concludes their DP-SGD implementation leaks nothing.
verification.refutation: Not refuted. Partial correction only: the reporter's mechanism ('order-statistic weights collapse for n=1000') and the n-dependent fix are wrong — the failure reproduces identically at n=100 — and severity is downgraded because it requires an explicit far-below-default grid_size and yields a valid-but-trivial lower bound rather than an unsound privacy claim.

survivors.title: The documented `pip install` command resolves to an unrelated `opaque` project on PyPI, not this library
survivors.claim: Both the README and the installation guide tell users to run `pip install opaque --extra-index-url https://europe-west4-python.pkg.dev/jetbrains-ml4se-fed/jbr-fed-python/simple/`. `--extra-index-url` does not scope a package to that index: pip collects candidate links from PyPI *and* the extra index and picks the highest version overall. The name `opaque` is already taken on PyPI by an unrelated project ('python libopaque wrapper') at version 1.0.0, while this project publishes 0.x versions (git tags are `v0.*`; ci.yml/pr.yml compute `0.X.Y.devN`). The highest candidate is therefore always PyPI's 1.0.0.
survivors.failure_scenario: A user follows docs/getting-started/installation.md verbatim. pip queries PyPI (opaque 1.0.0, a libopaque PAKE binding) and the JetBrains registry (opaque 0.2.x). It selects 1.0.0 from PyPI, installs a completely different C-extension package, and `import opaque.dpsgd` fails with ModuleNotFoundError. The `uv add opaque --index ...` variant on the next line is fine (uv defaults to first-index strategy), so the two documented commands do different things.

docs/getting-started/installation.md:12-15 same command
`curl https://pypi.org/pypi/opaque/json` -> `opaque 1.0.0`, summary 'python libopaque wrapper', releases ['0.2.0','1.0.0']
git tags/versioning: .github/workflows/ci.yml:243-252 computes `v0.0.1`-style next tags; .github/scripts/set_build_versions.sh normalizes `vX.Y.Z`
survivors.fix_sketch: Use `--index-url` (not `--extra-index-url`) so the JetBrains registry is authoritative, or `pip install --index-url <jb> --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple` plus an explicit version floor; better, rename the distribution to something unclaimed (e.g. `opaque-dp`) since `opaque` on PyPI can never be reclaimed.

verification.title: The documented `pip install` command resolves to an unrelated `opaque` project on PyPI, not this library
verification.reasoning: Verified both call sites: README.md:57-59 and docs/getting-started/installation.md:12-15 both use `pip install opaque --extra-index-url https://europe-west4-python.pkg.dev/.../simple/`. So the documented pip command selects PyPI's 1.0.0. The reporter is also right that the `uv add opaque --index <jb>` line two lines below behaves differently (uv defaults to first-index strategy, so the JetBrains index wins for any name it serves) — the two documented commands genuinely do different things. verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A new user copies the command from docs/getting-started/installation.md:12-15 verbatim. pip pools candidates from PyPI (opaque 1.0.0, a libopaque PAKE C-extension wrapper) and the JetBrains registry (opaque 0.x), picks 1.0.0 as the highest version, and either fails to build it (no libopaque headers on the host) or installs it successfully. verification.refutation: Not refuted — the fact pattern checks out against live PyPI and pip's documented resolution semantics. Severity reduced to medium: loud, immediately-diagnosed failure fixed by a docs edit (--index-url instead of --extra-index-url), and no security consequence on its own.

survivors.title: `opaque` metapackage ships completely unpinned sub-package requirements; the preflight script that claims to pin them is a no-op
survivors.claim: The root `opaque` distribution declares its sub-packages with no version specifier at all (`"opaque-engine"`, `"opaque-accounting"`, …). `set_build_versions.sh` documents itself as rewriting `opaque-*==0.0.0.dev0` / `opaque-*>=0.0.0.dev0` pins into `opaque-*==<version>` — but the string `0.0.0.dev0` never appears in the root pyproject.toml, so all four sed expressions match nothing. The published `opaque` wheel therefore carries bare `Requires-Dist: opaque-engine`, contradicting both the manifest comment ('it pins the curated sub-package bundle so `pip install opaque` resolves consistently') and the script header.

Any symbol moved between those releases (e.g. an `opaque.api.engine.types` rename) raises ImportError at `import opaque.dpsgd`, or worse silently changes a mechanism's behavior with no version signal.
