verification.refutation: Not refuted — the sed no-op reproduces exactly (zero diff on the real file). Severity lowered to medium because unpinned latest-of-everything is self-consistent for the default `pip install opaque`; the breakage is confined to version-pinned reproductions and dev/preview wheels.

survivors.title: Dependency confusion: five `opaque-*` distribution names are unregistered on PyPI while the documented install adds PyPI as a candidate index
survivors.claim: `opaque-engine`, `opaque-base`, `opaque-accounting`, `opaque-dpsgd`, `opaque-alignment` all return HTTP 404 from the PyPI JSON API — the names are unclaimed. Combined with the `--extra-index-url` install path (which makes pip consider PyPI for every name) and the unpinned `Requires-Dist` entries in the `opaque` metapackage (previous finding), any third party can register these names on PyPI and win resolution by version number.
survivors.failure_scenario: An attacker uploads `opaque-engine==99.0.0` to PyPI containing a `setup.py`/import-time payload. Every user or CI job running the documented `pip install opaque --extra-index-url <jetbrains>` gets the attacker's `opaque-engine` (99.0.0 > any real 0.x from the private registry) and executes attacker code inside the environment that holds the training data. `opaque-accounting` is the highest-value target: it is a compiled extension that computes the epsilon reported to users.
evidence: `curl -o /dev/null -w %{http_code} https://pypi.org/pypi/<name>/json` -> opaque-engine 404, opaque-base 404, opaque-accounting 404, opaque-dpsgd 404, opaque-alignment 404 (opaque itself: 200)
docs/getting-started/installation.md:12-15 and README.md:57-59 use `--extra-index-url`
pyproject.toml:33-40 unpinned sub-package requirements
survivors.fix_sketch: Defensively register all `opaque-*` names on PyPI (even as empty placeholder projects pointing at the real index), and switch the documented command to `--index-url` so PyPI is not consulted for these names at all.

verification.title: Dependency confusion: five `opaque-*` distribution names are unregistered on PyPI while the documented install adds PyPI as a candidate index
verification.reasoning: Facts verified live: curl against the PyPI JSON API returns 404 for opaque-engine, opaque-base, opaque-accounting, opaque-dpsgd, opaque-alignment, and I additionally checked opaque-auditing, opaque-patches, opaque-optimizers — all 404. Only `opaque` itself returns 200. docs/getting-started/installation.md:12-15 and README.md:57-59 do use --extra-index-url, which pools PyPI with the private registry and resolves by highest version, and pyproject.toml:33-39 leaves the sub-package requirements unpinned. So the exposure is real. But the stated failure scenario is factually wrong as written and I have to correct it: 'Every user or CI job running the documented `pip install opaque --extra-index-url <jetbrains>` gets the attacker's opaque-engine' does not hold today, because that exact command resolves `opaque` itself to PyPI's unrelated 1.0.0 (the previous finding), and 1.0.0 declares no opaque-* dependencies — the transitive names are never requested. Reachability is also narrower than claimed on the other paths I checked: dev and CI installs go through [tool.uv.sources] with workspace = true (pyproject.toml:97-108) so they never query any index for opaque-*, and the documented `uv add opaque --index <jb>` uses uv's default first-index strategy, which pins each name to the JetBrains index. Note too that pinning (the previous finding's fix) does NOT close this — an attacker who publishes the same version number still competes. SEVERITY DOWNGRADED from high to medium: genuine latent dependency-confusion exposure with severe consequence if exploited, but it requires an attacker to act, the mainline documented commands do not currently reach it, and the single-line --index-url fix closes it for good.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: An attacker registers the unclaimed name `opaque-engine` on PyPI and uploads version 99.0.0 with an import-time or build-time payload. A user who works around the broken metapackage resolution — e.g. `pip install opaque==0.2.4 --extra-index-url <jetbrains>` to skip PyPI's unrelated opaque 1.0.0, or `pip install "opaque[auditing]"`, or installs a sub-package by name — has pip pool both indexes for `opaque-engine`; 99.0.0 beats the private registry's 0.2.4 on version, and the attacker's code executes in the environment holding the training data. The same vector applies to opaque-accounting, which ships the compiled Rust extension that computes the reported epsilon. Developer and CI installs are not exposed: pyproject.toml's [tool.uv.sources] resolves all ten opaque-* names from the local workspace.
verification.refutation: Not refuted, but the failure scenario as written is wrong: the documented `pip install opaque --extra-index-url ...` never requests the opaque-* names, because it resolves `opaque` to PyPI's dependency-free 1.0.0. Exposure is confined to version-pinned installs, extras, and direct sub-package installs over the --extra-index-url path; uv and workspace/CI installs are immune. Severity reduced to medium accordingly.

survivors.title: Self-hosted GPU runner executes untrusted fork PR code with no same-repository guard
survivors.claim: `pr.yml` triggers on `pull_request: branches: [main]` and its `python-tests` matrix includes a leg with `os: GPU-runner-001` — a self-hosted runner. The job runs `uv sync --group dev --all-packages --extra all` (which executes the PR's own build backends) and then `uv run pytest` (which executes the PR's own test code) on that persistent machine. There is no `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` condition and no `environment:` approval gate on the job.
survivors.failure_scenario: Anyone opens a PR from a fork adding `packages/opaque-engine/tests/test_x.py` containing `os.system(...)`. GitHub schedules the CUDA leg onto GPU-runner-001 and runs it. Because self-hosted runners are not ephemeral by default, the attacker gets code execution on a persistent JetBrains-controlled GPU host, can read `~/.cache/uv`, the runner's `.credentials` token file, and any state left by previous jobs, and can poison the toolchain/cargo caches used by subsequent runs of the same runner.
evidence: .github/workflows/pr.yml:2-4 `on:\n  pull_request:\n    branches: [ main ]`
.github/workflows/pr.yml:148-155 `uv sync --group dev --all-packages --extra all` then `uv run pytest ...`
.github/WORKFLOWS.md:~'Workflows follow security best practices: ✅ Minimal permissions' — the self-hosted exposure is not mentioned
survivors.fix_sketch: Add `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` to the GPU leg (or gate the whole job behind a manually-approved `environment:`), and make the runner ephemeral (actions-runner-controller / `--ephemeral`).

verification.title: Self-hosted GPU runner executes untrusted fork PR code with no same-repository guard
verification.reasoning: The workflow facts check out exactly as reported. `.github/workflows/pr.yml:3-5` is `on: pull_request: branches: [main]`; the `python-tests` job at :82-130 carries an `include` leg with `os: GPU-runner-001` (:125), a self-hosted label. Steps :147-157 run `uv sync --group dev --all-packages --extra all` (executes the PR's build backends, including the Rust `opaque-accounting` build via `dtolnay/rust-toolchain` at :137) and then `uv run pytest packages tests -m "cuda and not slow"` (executes the PR's test code). There is no `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` anywhere in the file, no `environment:` on the job, and no top-level `permissions:` block (only `conventional-title` sets one, at :21-22). `enable-cache: true` on setup-uv (:141) plus the fact that a self-hosted runner's `~/.cache/uv` and cargo/rustup dirs live on persistent disk means cross-run cache poisoning is a genuine vector — GH Actions cache scoping does not isolate on-disk tool caches. So the missing guard is real and the exposure mechanism is real. What the reporter got wrong is the population of attackers. `gh api repos/JetBrains-Research/opaque` returns `"private": true`, `"visibility": "internal"`, `"forks_count": 0`, `"allow_forking": true`. An internal repo is not forkable by the public — only by members of the JetBrains GitHub Enterprise. So the attacker must be an authenticated, employed enterprise member, not an anonymous internet user, and GitHub's fork-PR approval policy (which for private/internal repos defaults to requiring approval for non-collaborator fork PRs) sits in front of the first run. That is an insider-risk / lateral-movement finding, not a drive-by RCE finding, which is roughly a one-severity-step difference. Note the finding becomes genuinely high the moment the repo flips public — and `.github/WORKFLOWS.md` (GitHub Pages at jetbrains-research.github.io/opaque, public badge URLs, Codecov) reads as though public release is planned, so the fix is still worth doing before that flip rather than after.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: The repo is `internal` to the JetBrains GitHub Enterprise with `allow_forking: true`. Any enterprise member (not the general public) forks the repo and opens a PR to `main` adding e.g. `packages/opaque-engine/tests/test_pwn.py` with module-level `os.system(...)`, or a malicious `build-system` hook in a package `pyproject.toml`. Once the fork-PR workflow is approved (first-timers) or automatically (anyone with a prior merged PR), GitHub schedules the CUDA `include` leg onto the self-hosted `GPU-runner-001`. `uv sync` and `uv run pytest` both execute the attacker's code as the runner user on a persistent machine. Because the runner is not ephemeral, the attacker can read the runner's `.credentials` registration token, the persistent `~/.cache/uv`, `~/.cargo`, and `~/.rustup` directories, and any state left by prior jobs, and can plant a poisoned wheel or cargo artifact that subsequent trusted runs of the same runner (including main-branch runs of ci.yml, which uses the same label at ci.yml:77) will silently consume. No secrets leak directly from this job — the fork PR token is read-only and codecov-action@v4 is invoked tokenless — so the impact is runner-host compromise and supply-chain cache poisoning rather than credential theft. If the repository is later made public, the same path opens to anonymous internet users and the severity becomes high.
verification.refutation: Not refuted — the missing guard is exactly as described. Severity downgraded from high to medium because the reporter's scenario opens with "Anyone opens a PR from a fork," which is false: `gh api repos/JetBrains-Research/opaque` reports `"visibility": "internal"` / `"private": true`, so forking is restricted to JetBrains enterprise members and GitHub's fork-PR approval gate applies. Also note no secrets are exposed by this job (fork PR GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only; the only secret-bearing jobs, `publish-dev-wheels` / `publish`, live in ci.yml and release.yml and never run on pull_request).

survivors.title: Release and dev-wheel publishing do not depend on any test job — wheels ship from a red tree
survivors.claim: `release.yml` contains no test job at all: `publish` needs `merge-wheels` needs the three `build-*` jobs need `tag-guard` (which only checks that the tag is an ancestor of origin/main). Nothing runs pytest or `cargo test`. The same holds in `ci.yml`: `publish-dev-wheels` needs only `merge-wheels`, which needs only the build jobs — neither `rust-tests` nor `python-tests` is in any `needs` chain. Wheels are published to the GCP Artifact Registry and attached as GitHub Release assets regardless of test status.
survivors.failure_scenario: A PR merges to main that the PR gate did not cover (e.g. anything under a `slow` marker, which the PR gate excludes via `not slow`). `ci.yml`'s `python-tests` job goes red on the slow suite, but `build-python-wheels` → `merge-wheels` → `publish-dev-wheels` proceed in parallel and push a broken dev wheel to the registry. A maintainer then publishes the draft Release; `release.yml` builds and publishes the same tree with zero tests executed. Users install a release wheel whose slow accounting/parity tests were never green.
evidence: .github/workflows/release.yml job graph: `tag-guard` -> `build-python-wheel`/`build-opaque-wheel`/`build-opaque-accounting` -> `merge-wheels` -> `publish` (no test job exists in the file)
.github/workflows/ci.yml:154 `merge-wheels: needs: [build-python-wheels, build-opaque-wheel, build-accounting-wheels]`
.github/workflows/ci.yml:164 `publish-dev-wheels: needs: [merge-wheels]`
.github/workflows/ci.yml:12-16 comment claims this lane 'catches regressions that the PR gate's fast suite missed' — but nothing consumes that result
survivors.fix_sketch: Add `rust-tests` and `python-tests` (or a reusable-workflow call to them) to `needs:` for `publish-dev-wheels` in ci.yml, and add a test job to release.yml gating `publish`.

verification.title: Release and dev-wheel publishing do not depend on any test job — wheels ship from a red tree
verification.reasoning: The job graphs are exactly as reported. `.github/workflows/release.yml` contains six jobs — `tag-guard`, `build-python-wheel`, `build-opaque-wheel`, `build-opaque-accounting`, `merge-wheels`, `publish` — and I read all 213 lines: there is no pytest or `cargo test` invocation anywhere in the file. `publish` (:165-167) needs only `merge-wheels`, which needs only the three build jobs (:153-155), which need only `tag-guard` (:36, :80, :109). `tag-guard` (:17-32) does nothing but `git merge-base --is-ancestor "$GITHUB_SHA" origin/main`. In ci.yml, `merge-wheels: needs: [build-python-wheels, build-opaque-wheel, build-accounting-wheels]` (:234) and `publish-dev-wheels: needs: [merge-wheels]` (:246); `rust-tests` (:18) and `python-tests` (:38) appear in no `needs:` list in the file. The comment at ci.yml:13-17 does claim this lane 'catches regressions that the PR gate's fast suite missed', and indeed nothing consumes that result. All verified. Where the reporter overstates: the tree is not untested. pr.yml's `python-tests-gate` (:171-181) is a required-check aggregator over the CPU and MPS legs of a 4-shard x 2-device matrix running the full non-slow suite, plus `rust-tests` (cargo test with doctests), `smoke-imports`, and `docs` — all of which must pass before a commit reaches main. So the actual uncovered surface is narrower than 'zero tests': it is (a) `slow`-marked tests, (b) `cuda`-marked tests (which never gate anyway — see the DDP finding), and (c) main-only breakage such as a semantic conflict between two PRs each green on a stale base. Blast radius is further bounded by the fact that both publish jobs carry `environment: release` (ci.yml:248, release.yml:169) — GitHub environments can carry required reviewers and branch restrictions, which I cannot inspect from the repo but which the maintainer may already have configured on the release environment; and by the repo being internal, so the GCP Artifact Registry audience is internal rather than the public PyPI.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: Two PRs merge to main in quick succession; each was green against its own base, but together they break an interaction that only the `slow`-marked accounting parity suite exercises (the PR gate excludes it via `-m "... and not slow"` at pr.yml:110/115). On the main push, ci.yml's `python-tests` CPU leg — which does run slow tests (`marker: "not cuda and not mps"`, ci.yml:63) — goes red. In parallel and entirely independently, `build-python-wheels` / `build-opaque-wheel` / `build-accounting-wheels` succeed, `merge-wheels` succeeds, and `publish-dev-wheels` pushes the broken dev wheels to the GCP Artifact Registry, because no test job appears in any `needs:` chain leading to it. Internal consumers pulling dev wheels get the regression. A maintainer, seeing the draft Release that `upsert-draft` refreshed on the same push, publishes it; release.yml then rebuilds and publishes the identical tree with zero tests executed anywhere in its job graph — `tag-guard` only proves the tag is an ancestor of origin/main, not that origin/main is green. Users installing the release wheel and its GitHub Release assets get a build whose slow accounting/parity suite was last known red.
verification.refutation: Not refuted — the `needs:` chains are exactly as claimed and neither file contains a test job feeding a publish job. Severity downgraded from high to medium because 'wheels ship from a red tree' overstates it: every commit on main has already passed the required `python-tests-gate` (full non-slow CPU+MPS matrix), `rust-tests`, `smoke-imports`, and `docs` at PR time, so the genuinely ungated surface is the `slow` and `cuda` markers plus cross-PR merge interactions — not the whole test suite. Both publish jobs also sit behind `environment: release`, which may already carry a manual-approval reviewer rule that is invisible from the repo.

survivors.title: The entire distributed/DDP correctness surface can never fail a build
survivors.claim: Every DDP test is reachable only from a `continue-on-error: true` leg. (a) Wheel-local suites `packages/{opaque-engine,opaque-dpsgd,opaque-dpftrl}/tests/ddp/` are marked `cuda` — they match the PR gate's GPU leg marker `cuda and not slow`, but that leg carries `soft: true` -> `continue-on-error`, and `python-tests-gate` explicitly reads `needs.python-tests.result`, which continue-on-error masks to success. (b) The cross-wheel DDP suites `tests/integration/ddp/*` and `tests/integration/transformers/test_ddp_pipeline.py` are `pytest.mark.slow + pytest.mark.cuda`, so the PR gate's `cuda and not slow` filter excludes them entirely; they only ever run on ci.yml's GPU leg, which is also soft.
survivors.failure_scenario: A change to `packages/opaque-engine/src/opaque/api/engine/distributed/gradients.py` breaks multi-rank noise calibration (exactly the class of bug in the already-known sqrt(W) / equal-seed issue). `packages/opaque-dpsgd/tests/ddp/test_gaussian_noise.py` and `tests/integration/ddp/test_dpsgd_sampler_short_run_parity.py` would catch it. On the PR the first never gates (soft leg) and the second never runs (`not slow`); the `Python tests` required check goes green and the PR merges. On main the ci.yml GPU leg goes red but is `continue-on-error`, so nothing blocks the dev-wheel publish either.
evidence: .github/workflows/pr.yml:85 `continue-on-error: ${{ matrix.soft == true }}`; :126 `marker: "cuda and not slow"`; :130 `soft: true`

.github/workflows/pr.yml:166-179 `python-tests-gate` -> `test "$result" = "success"` on `needs.python-tests.result`; comment at :167-169 concedes 'the GPU leg's `continue-on-error` masks its result to success, so this gate reflects CPU + MPS only'

tests/integration/ddp/test_dpsgd_sampler_short_run_parity.py:40 `pytestmark = [pytest.mark.slow, pytest.mark.cuda]`; same at tests/integration/ddp/test_dpftrl_sampler_short_run_parity.py:40 and tests/integration/transformers/test_ddp_pipeline.py:48

packages/opaque-dpsgd/tests/ddp/test_clipped_grad.py:25 `pytestmark = pytest.mark.cuda`; packages/opaque-engine/tests/ddp/test_collectives.py:17 same; packages/opaque-dpftrl/tests/ddp/test_band_mf_noise.py:25 same
survivors.fix_sketch: Split the GPU leg into a soft 'exploratory' leg and a required 'ddp-correctness' leg (`-m "cuda"` over `packages/*/tests/ddp tests/integration/ddp`) that is not continue-on-error; alternatively make the DDP suites gloo/CPU-runnable so they gate on ubuntu.

verification.title: The entire distributed/DDP correctness surface can never fail a build
verification.reasoning: The mechanism is real and I confirmed every link in the chain. pr.yml:85 `continue-on-error: ${{ matrix.soft == true }}` — only the GPU `include` leg sets `soft: true` (:130), so only that leg is soft; the CPU/MPS legs have `matrix.soft` undefined, `null == true` is false, so they gate normally. GitHub's documented semantics are that a job whose `continue-on-error` is true and which fails reports `conclusion: success`, so the matrix aggregate `needs.python-tests.result` read at pr.yml:179-181 stays `success` — and the workflow's own comment at :166-169 concedes this explicitly. Marker arithmetic checks out: the PR gate's GPU leg is `-m "cuda and not slow"` (:126), so `tests/integration/ddp/test_dpsgd_sampler_short_run_parity.py:40` and `test_dpftrl_sampler_short_run_parity.py:40` and `tests/integration/transformers/test_ddp_pipeline.py:48`, all `pytestmark = [pytest.mark.slow, pytest.mark.cuda]`, are excluded from the PR gate entirely and run only on ci.yml's GPU leg (`marker: "cuda"`, :78), which is also `soft: true` (:81) — and ci.yml's `python-tests` feeds no downstream job at all. I verified the wheel-local markers directly: `packages/opaque-engine/tests/ddp/test_collectives.py:17`, `test_profiler_sync.py:11`, `packages/opaque-dpsgd/tests/ddp/test_adaptive_clipping.py:17`, `test_clipped_grad.py:25`, `packages/opaque-dpftrl/tests/ddp/test_auto_clipped.py:11`, `test_band_mf_noise.py:25`, `test_clipped_grad.py:26`, `test_mf_gaussian_noise.py:15` all carry module-level `pytestmark = pytest.mark.cuda`, and all three `*_ddp_helpers.py` hardcode `dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl")` — so every genuine multi-rank test is NCCL/CUDA-only and lands exclusively on soft legs. `conftest.py:19-20` auto-skips `cuda` tests when `torch.cuda.is_available()` is false, so they are also a no-op on the CPU/MPS legs. Net: no multi-rank collective, multi-rank noise, or multi-rank clipping test can ever fail a required check. Two corrections to the reporter. First, the specific file cited in the failure scenario is wrong: `packages/opaque-dpsgd/tests/ddp/test_gaussian_noise.py` has NO module-level `pytestmark`; only `TestDistributedGaussianNoiseSpawn` at line 211 is `@pytest.mark.cuda`. Its other ~14 tests (including `test_rank_fold_in_produces_distinct_streams` and `test_distributed_preserves_stddev`) are plain CPU tests that DO run and DO gate on the required check. Same for `packages/opaque-engine/tests/ddp/test_core_utilities.py` and `test_local_shard.py`, which carry no cuda marks at all. So the claim '(a) Wheel-local suites packages/*/tests/ddp/ are marked cuda' is true of most files but not all, and single-process rank-folding logic is in fact gated. Second, this is a documented deliberate tradeoff: pr.yml:77-81 spells out the soft-GPU rationale and says 'Drop `soft` once the GPU runner reliably runs CUDA.' The reporter's added insight — that the tradeoff silently leaves the entire distributed privacy path with zero gating signal — is legitimate and not documented, but the maintainer already knows the GPU leg is non-blocking. One point in the reporter's favor that they did not make: the comment's claim that the soft leg 'turns the overall run red' is wrong — GitHub renders a continue-on-error failure as a neutral/warning icon and the workflow run conclusion is success, so the visible signal the maintainer is relying on is weaker than they believe.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A change to `packages/opaque-engine/src/opaque/api/engine/distributed/gradients.py` breaks multi-rank noise calibration — e.g. every rank draws from the same seed so the summed noise scales as W instead of sqrt(W), inflating the effective epsilon by sqrt(W) in DDP training. The tests that would catch it are all NCCL-spawn tests: `TestDistributedGaussianNoiseSpawn` (packages/opaque-dpsgd/tests/ddp/test_gaussian_noise.py:211, `@pytest.mark.cuda`), `packages/opaque-dpftrl/tests/ddp/test_band_mf_noise.py` and `test_mf_gaussian_noise.py` (module-level `pytest.mark.cuda`), `packages/opaque-engine/tests/ddp/test_collectives.py` (same), and `tests/integration/ddp/test_dpsgd_sampler_short_run_parity.py` (`[slow, cuda]`). On the PR: the parity test never runs (the GPU leg filters `cuda and not slow`), and the cuda-marked spawn tests run only on the `GPU-runner-001` leg, which is `soft: true` so its failure is masked to `success` in `needs.python-tests.result`; the required `Python tests` check goes green and the PR merges. Note the single-process CPU tests in the same files (rank fold-in, stddev preservation) still gate, so a purely local seeding regression would be caught — only the genuine multi-rank collective path is blind. On main, ci.yml's GPU leg runs the full `cuda` marker including the slow parity tests and goes red, but it is `continue-on-error` (ci.yml:41/81), so it does not even show as a failed run, and no publish job lists `python-tests` in `needs:` anyway. The sqrt(W) epsilon regression reaches the dev-wheel registry with every CI surface green.
verification.refutation: Not refuted — the soft-leg masking, the marker arithmetic, and the NCCL-only nature of every multi-rank test all check out. Severity downgraded from high to medium for three reasons: (1) the specific file the reporter cited as the would-catch test, `packages/opaque-dpsgd/tests/ddp/test_gaussian_noise.py`, is only partly cuda-marked — 14 of its 15 tests run and gate on the CPU leg, so the claim that the whole wheel-local `tests/ddp/` surface is ungated is overstated (`test_core_utilities.py` and `test_local_shard.py` carry no cuda marks either); (2) the arrangement is an explicitly documented, explicitly temporary tradeoff (pr.yml:77-81, 'Drop `soft` once the GPU runner reliably runs CUDA'), not an oversight; (3) the failure mode is 'a regression could slip through', not an extant defect. It stays at medium rather than lower because `affects_epsilon` is correct — nothing in CI can currently fail on a multi-rank noise-calibration bug — and because the maintainer's stated mitigation ('the GPU leg still turns the overall run red') does not actually hold under GitHub's continue-on-error rendering.

survivors.title: BLT mechanism doc: two reference titles are swapped onto the wrong arXiv IDs and all three first authors are wrong
survivors.claim: All three matrix-factorization references in the BLT page are defective. (1) arXiv:2404.16706 is titled "Efficient and Near-Optimal Noise Generation for Streaming Differential Privacy" by Dvijotham, McMahan, Pillutla, Steinke, Thakurta — the doc gives it the title "Optimal Matrix-Factorization Mechanisms with Applications to Group Privacy" (no such paper) and attributes it to "Choquette-Choo et al.". (2) arXiv:2408.08868 is "A Hassle-free Algorithm for Private Learning in Practice: Don't Use Tree Aggregation, Use BLTs" by McMahan, Xu, Zhang — the doc gives it the title "Multi-Epoch Matrix Factorization Mechanisms for Private Machine Learning", which is the real title of arXiv:2211.06530, and again attributes it to "Choquette-Choo et al.". (3) arXiv:2405.13763 is "Banded Square Root Matrix Factorization for Differentially Private Model Training" by Kalinin & Lampert — the doc gives it the title "Efficient and Near-Optimal Noise Generation for Streaming Differential Privacy" (which belongs to 2404.16706) attributed to "Dvijotham et al.", then adds the contradictory gloss "BSR paper with Toeplitz min-sep sensitivity theorem". So (1) and (3) have their titles literally swapped.
survivors.failure_scenario: A reviewer or user reading docs/mechanisms/dp-ftrl/blt.md wants the multi-epoch sensitivity analysis referenced at line 212-213. They open arXiv:2408.08868 and find a federated-learning systems paper with a different title, no section matching "Multi-Epoch Matrix Factorization Mechanisms". Searching for the stated title lands them on arXiv:2211.06530, a different mechanism family. The doc gives no way to reach the paper that actually backs the code's `blt_strategy(..., max_participations=...)` sensitivity path.

verification.title: BLT mechanism doc: two reference titles are swapped onto the wrong arXiv IDs and all three first authors are wrong
verification.reasoning: Every factual claim verified. `docs/mechanisms/dp-ftrl/blt.md:210-215` reads exactly as quoted. I independently fetched all three arXiv abstract pages: 2404.16706 is 'Efficient and Near-Optimal Noise Generation for Streaming Differential Privacy' by Dvijotham, McMahan, Pillutla, Steinke, Thakurta; 2408.08868 is 'A Hassle-free Algorithm for Private Learning in Practice: Don't Use Tree Aggregation, Use BLTs' by McMahan, Xu, Zhang; 2405.13763 is 'Banded Square Root Matrix Factorization for Differentially Private Model Training' by Kalinin, Lampert. So all three titles in the doc are wrong, the 2404.16706 title has literally been moved onto the 2405.13763 entry, and none of the three 'et al.' attributions names an actual first author. The reporter is right on the facts. But the failure scenario's conclusion is wrong and the severity is inflated. The URLs are all correct for what the doc is trying to cite, and so are the one-line glosses: 2404.16706 genuinely is the BLT paper ('BLT mechanism with buffered linear Toeplitz optimization' — correct), 2408.08868 genuinely is the multi-epoch BLT paper ('Multi-epoch sensitivity analysis for BLT' — correct), and 2405.13763 genuinely is the BSR paper with the Toeplitz min-sep theorem ('BSR paper with Toeplitz min-sep sensitivity theorem' — correct). So the reporter's closing sentence, 'The doc gives no way to reach the paper that actually backs the code's blt_strategy(..., max_participations=...) sensitivity path,' is false: clicking the link at :212 lands the reader on precisely that paper. The code's own citations are sound — `packages/opaque-dpftrl/src/opaque/api/dpftrl/noise/_blt_math.py:98,113` cite Algorithms 2 and 3 of 2408.08868 for the multi-epoch path and :198/:498/:542/:930 cite Prop 4.5 / Lemmas 5.2-5.4 of 2404.16706, all consistent with the real papers. Worth flagging as scope the reporter missed: the wrong-author problem is repo-wide, not confined to blt.md. `packages/opaque-accounting/src/matrix_factorization/mf_gaussian.rs:19` and `mod.rs:38` both say '- BLT: Choquette-Choo et al. (2024) <https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16706>' (should be Dvijotham et al.), and `docs/user-guide/noise.md:584` attributes 2408.08868 to 'Choquette-Choo et al.' (should be McMahan et al.). Conversely `docs/mechanisms/dp-ftrl/bsr.md:7,89` gets 2405.13763 exactly right — title and 'Kalinin, Lampert (2024)' — which is a ready-made template for the fix and confirms this is sloppy copy-paste in one block rather than a systematic misunderstanding. `sensitivity.rs:10,258` correctly pairs 'Choquette-Choo et al. (2022)' with 2211.06530, so the name is not wrong everywhere.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A reviewer auditing the multi-epoch sensitivity path opens docs/mechanisms/dp-ftrl/blt.md, reads the References block, and follows the link at line 212 for 'Multi-Epoch Matrix Factorization Mechanisms for Private Machine Learning'. arXiv:2408.08868 loads as 'A Hassle-free Algorithm for Private Learning in Practice: Don't Use Tree Aggregation, Use BLTs' by McMahan, Xu, Zhang — which IS the correct paper backing `blt_strategy(..., max_participations=...)` (the code cites its Algorithms 2 and 3 at packages/opaque-dpftrl/src/opaque/api/dpftrl/noise/_blt_math.py:98,113), but under a title that appears nowhere in it. The reviewer now cannot tell whether the link or the title is the error; searching the stated title lands them on the unrelated arXiv:2211.06530 (Choquette-Choo et al., a different mechanism family). Line 210 is worse: the title 'Optimal Matrix-Factorization Mechanisms with Applications to Group Privacy' matches no paper at all, so a reader who trusts titles over links is chasing a citation that does not exist. Line 214 compounds it by printing 2404.16706's real title over the BSR paper's URL, while the same repo cites that URL correctly at docs/mechanisms/dp-ftrl/bsr.md:7. Net effect: wasted reviewer time and a credibility hit on a privacy library's bibliography — no user-facing breakage, no effect on computed epsilon, and no broken links.
verification.refutation: Not refuted on the facts — I fetched all three arXiv pages and every title and author attribution in blt.md:210-215 is wrong exactly as described. Severity downgraded from high to low because the reporter's stated harm does not hold: all three arXiv links resolve, and each resolves to the correct paper for the accompanying gloss, so the doc does give the reader a way to reach the multi-epoch sensitivity paper — contradicting the finding's own closing sentence. The defect is bibliographic (wrong titles, wrong 'et al.' names) with no correctness, epsilon, or link-rot impact. It is trivially fixable and should be fixed, and the fix should extend beyond blt.md to packages/opaque-accounting/src/matrix_factorization/mf_gaussian.rs:19, .../mod.rs:38, and docs/user-guide/noise.md:584, which carry the same Choquette-Choo misattribution the reporter did not catch.

survivors.title: DPTrainer and three example scripts invert `target_clipping_rate` when wiring adaptive clipping
survivors.claim: `adaptive_clipped_grad`'s `target_quantile` is the target fraction of gradients that ARE clipped: `_adaptive_clipping_norm_update` computes `C * exp(eta * (noisy_clipping_rate - target_quantile))` where `noisy_clipping_rate` is derived from `num_clipped = (grad_norms > threshold).sum() / batch_size`, so the fixed point is clipped_fraction == target_quantile, and the docstring says 'target_quantile: Target fraction of clipped gradients.' DPTrainer passes `target_quantile=1.0 - target_clip_rate`, applying an Andrew-et-al.-style 'quantile = fraction *below* threshold' convention that this implementation does not use. The same inversion is copied verbatim into examples/train_sft.py:1744, examples/train_dpsgd.py:1414 and examples/train_dpo.py:2197. The bug is invisible at the default (`target_clipping_rate=0.5` is a fixed point of x -> 1-x), which is why it survives the test suite (tests/opaque_transformers/test_config.py only ever uses 0.5).
survivors.failure_scenario: `TrainingArguments(clipping_mode='adaptive', clipping_kwargs={'target_clipping_rate': 0.9})` — user asks for aggressive clipping, 90% of per-example gradients clipped. DPTrainer passes `target_quantile=0.1`, the geometric update drives C upward until only ~10% of gradients exceed it, and the run ends with a clip norm roughly an order of magnitude larger than requested (bounded by `norm_max=10.0`). Symmetrically, `target_clipping_rate=0.1` produces ~90% clipping. Noise is calibrated to whatever C the tracker lands on, so the privacy guarantee holds but the utility knob is inverted and silent.

survivors.title: Nothing in the docs states that the DP noise is drawn from a deterministic, seed-derived PRNG whose seed is user-chosen, printed, and checkpointed — the guarantee is void against anyone who learns the seed
survivors.claim: Noise is generated from `RngKey(seed: int, impl='opaque_threefry_like')` via `generator_from_key`, and `GaussianNoiseState` stores `_rng_key` so it survives serialization/checkpointing. Every doc example uses a literal `key(42)`; the distributed guidance *requires* the same key on every rank; docs/user-guide/rng-key.md:288-300 tells users to `torch.save` the noise state. An adversary who knows the seed can regenerate the exact noise for every step and subtract it, recovering the un-noised clipped gradient sum — the (eps, delta) guarantee collapses to eps=inf. A repo-wide grep for 'secure', 'csprng', 'cryptograph', 'Mironov' across docs/ and packages/*/src returns nothing but one unrelated hit. There is no `secure_mode`-style option and no warning that the seed must be secret and must not be logged or shipped with a checkpoint, while the shipped examples take `--seed` (default 42) and log the full arg set.
survivors.failure_scenario: A team trains with `examples/train_dpsgd.py --seed 42 --target-epsilon 3` and publishes the run: checkpoint (containing `GaussianNoiseState._rng_key`), the W&B config with `seed=42`, and the exact command line. Anyone with the two consecutive checkpoints and the seed recomputes `fold_in(key(42), t)`, regenerates the per-step noise tensor exactly, subtracts it from the parameter delta, and recovers the noiseless clipped gradient sum for every step — a quantity with no privacy protection at all. Nothing in docs/limitations.md, docs/user-guide/rng-key.md, or docs/reference/rng.md warns against this.

verification.title: Nothing in the docs states that the DP noise is drawn from a deterministic, seed-derived PRNG whose seed is user-chosen, printed, and checkpointed — the guarantee is void against anyone who learns the seed
verification.reasoning: Every technical claim checks out. packages/opaque-engine/src/opaque/api/engine/random/_engine.py:36-102 defines RngKey(seed:int) and generator_from_key() as `torch.Generator().manual_seed(rng_key.seed % (2**63-1))`; fold_in mixes with blake2b — deterministic, reproducible on any machine, not a CSPRNG. packages/opaque-dpsgd/src/opaque/api/dpsgd/noise/_gaussian.py:68-81 stores _rng_key on GaussianNoiseState, and the sampling path is `generator_from_key(rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, st._step_counter))` (lines ~380-400), so the whole noise trajectory is a pure function of the integer seed. docs/user-guide/rng-key.md:288-300 does tell users to torch.save the noise state; docs/user-guide/distributed.md:26-29 does require the same key on every rank; examples/train_dpsgd.py:514 defaults --seed 42 and line 975 passes `config=vars(args)` to wandb.init, so the seed is logged verbatim. My own repo-wide grep for secure|csprng|cryptograph|urandom|threat model over docs/ and packages/*/src returns only the unrelated 'cryptographically small' at docs/user-guide/dp-concepts.md:25 — there is no secure-mode option and no statement anywhere that the seed must stay secret. So the omission is real. I downgrade from high to medium for three reasons: (1) it is a documentation gap, not a code defect — no shipped code path leaks the seed to an untrusted party by itself, and the DP guarantee holds against the standard adversary who sees only the mechanism output; (2) the same pseudorandom-noise caveat applies to essentially every DP framework except Opacus's opt-in secure_mode, i.e. this is a known-caveat-to-document rather than a miscalibration; (3) the exploit requires the operator to voluntarily publish both the checkpointed noise state and the seed. The reporter's 'eps=inf' framing is correct only conditional on that disclosure.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: An operator runs examples/train_dpsgd.py --seed 42 --target-epsilon 3 with wandb enabled (default). The seed lands in the public W&B config via `wandb.init(config=vars(args))` (examples/train_dpsgd.py:975), and any checkpoint that includes GaussianNoiseState (the pattern docs/user-guide/rng-key.md:288-296 teaches) embeds _rng_key.seed. 1. The clamp is not the root cause and cannot simply be removed. `torch.rand` fp32 emits 0 with probability 2^-24, and `erfinv(2*0-1) = -inf`; some clamp is mandatory. The fp32 lattice alone caps the sampler at `sqrt(2)*erfinv(2*(1-2^-24)-1) = 5.2947σ`. So the clamp costs 5.29σ -> 5.17σ, moving the per-step non-overlap probability at nm=1 from 8.7e-6 to 1.5e-5 — a factor of 1.8, not the whole effect the title attributes to it.

2. Finite-support noise is a property of every float-based DP sampler, including the `torch.randn` path the report itself cites (~5.57σ empirical) and the samplers in Opacus/TF-Privacy. This is a known finite-precision limitation of the field, not a defect unique to this code.

The library already, explicitly and deliberately, accounts truncated noise as a standard Gaussian on the `bound=` path: the module docstring (_gaussian.py:23-31) says 'bounding only modifies the noise distribution' and the accounting stays '(ε, δ)-Gaussian' — and `bound=3.0` truncates at 3σ, far more aggressively than 5.17σ. survivors.failure_scenario: An adversary mounts membership inference on a canary record engineered so that its per-example gradient overflows fp16 at the current loss scale (any activation gradient above 65504/S). I reproduced the no-op through the public Python API with the installed extension: gaussian(1.1).pld(pessimistic_estimate=True/False).epsilon_at(1e-5) = 3.921250256423968 in both cases, and (poisson(gaussian(0.8),0.01)*1000).epsilon_at(1e-5) = 3.1410183214958485 in both cases with `a == b` evaluating True. The docs do promise otherwise: discretization.py:73-75 ('If False, round downward (optimistic estimate...)'), config.rs:47-53 ('false: Discards truncated mass, providing a tighter but potentially underestimating bound'), and README.md:138. One imprecision in the report: coarsen IS in principle reachable on the analytic path when max_grid_size is exceeded post-composition, not only 'off the analytic path'. I probed that too (discretization=1e-2 with max_grid_size=2000/20000/200000 on poisson(gaussian(0.8),0.01)*200) and got 1.8112360570801809 identically for both flag values, so in practice the flag is inert there as well — the claim is if anything understated on that sub-point. Severity downgraded from medium to low: the failure mode is fail-safe (the result is always the pessimistic/upper bound, so no guarantee is ever weakened), affects_epsilon is correctly false, and the harm is confined to a documentation promise plus a dead knob. It is a genuine unimplemented-but-documented feature, not a correctness or privacy defect.

survivors.title: Unbounded Gaussian path hard-truncates at ±5.16σ and piles the excess tail into point masses, while claiming float32 sampling satisfies the standard Gaussian analysis
survivors.claim: The unbounded path builds noise as `center + std*√2*erfinv(2u-1)` from `u = torch.rand(..., dtype=torch.float32)` clamped to `[eps, 1-eps]` with `eps = finfo(float32).eps = 1.19e-7`. Two consequences the accountant does not model: (a) the released noise is hard-truncated at ±std·√2·erfinv(1-2.4e-7) ≈ ±5.16σ — it is not a Gaussian; (b) the clamp does not discard the excess tail, it maps it onto a *point mass* at exactly ±5.16σ of total probability ≈2.4e-7 per coordinate (torch.rand in float32 emits k·2^-24, so u ∈ {0, 5.96e-8, 1.19e-7} all clamp to the same value, as does u = 1-2^-24 at the top). The docstring justifies `compute_dtype=torch.float32` by asserting that "the Gaussian-mechanism privacy guarantee requires sampling from a true Gaussian — sampling uniforms in torch.bfloat16 produces a coarsely-discretized lattice that does not satisfy the standard analysis." float32 inverse-CDF sampling is also a coarse lattice (2^-24) and also does not satisfy the standard analysis; the repo contains no discrete Gaussian (Canonne–Kamath–Steinke) or secure-noise implementation. `dpsgd_acc.gaussian(nm)` computes the PLD of an untruncated, continuous N(0, σ²).
survivors.failure_scenario: Train a d = 1e8-parameter model with `gaussian_noise(noise_multiplier=1.0, key=...)`. Per step, the expected number of coordinates landing on a clamp atom is d·2.4e-7 ≈ 24, so it happens on every step. For neighbouring datasets the atoms sit at μ_j ± 5.16σ vs μ'_j ± 5.16σ — different locations for every coordinate the record touches — so those outputs have a likelihood ratio dominated by an atom-vs-lattice-density comparison that the continuous Gaussian PLD never sees. The reported ε from `poisson(gaussian(1.0), q) * T` is the ε of a mechanism that was not run.

verification.title: Unbounded Gaussian path hard-truncates at ±5.16σ and piles the excess tail into point masses, while claiming float32 sampling satisfies the standard Gaussian analysis
verification.reasoning: The mechanical claims are all accurate and I measured them. _gaussian.py:270-274 does `eps = torch.finfo(compute_dtype).eps` (1.1920928955078125e-07 for float32), `u = torch.clamp(u, min=eps, max=1.0-eps)`, `sample = center_c + std*_SQRT2*torch.erfinv(2.0*u-1.0)`. Over 4e8 float32 torch.rand draws I measured P(u < eps) = 1.15e-07 (theory 2·2^-24 = 1.19e-07) and P(u > 1-eps) = 5.0e-08 (theory 2^-24 = 5.96e-08), and the resulting support is hard-capped at exactly ±5.16657829284668·σ (closed-form ±5.1665781197). So yes: clamp (not rejection) maps the outer tail onto two atoms of combined mass ~2.3e-07 per coordinate, the released noise is not Gaussian beyond ±5.17σ, and gaussian.rs models a continuous untruncated N(0,σ²). What I could not establish, and what keeps this at PLAUSIBLE rather than CONFIRMED, is the reporter's headline conclusion that 'the reported ε is the ε of a mechanism that was not run' in any way specific to this code. Every floating-point Gaussian sampler has this property — this is the well-known Mironov-class floating-point/lattice gap. torch.normal's own float32 Box-Muller path truncates at sqrt(2·24·ln2) ≈ ±5.77σ from the same 2^-24 uniform lattice, so the alternative implementations used by Opacus/TF-Privacy are in the same regime, and the reporter's own fix (float64 uniforms) only moves the cut to ~±8.15σ without removing the lattice. The reporter's dimensional arithmetic is right (d=1e8 → ~24 clamped coordinates per step), but they do not carry it through to an actual δ increment, and a naive per-coordinate union bound is far too loose to support 'affects_epsilon: true' as stated. The docstring at lines 189-196 is a genuine but soft overclaim: read literally it only asserts that bf16 uniforms are a coarse lattice that fails the standard analysis — true — while implying by contrast that float32 does satisfy it, which is not strictly so. Severity downgraded from medium to low: the substance reduces to (a) a docstring that should not imply exactness and (b) an unacknowledged, industry-standard float-sampling caveat; I found no note anywhere in the repo (grep for Mironov/floating point/secure noise/discrete Gaussian) acknowledging it, so a documentation fix is warranted, but there is no demonstrated epsilon error against a realistic threat model.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: With `gaussian_noise(noise_multiplier=1.0, key=...)` (unbounded path, default compute_dtype=torch.float32), each noise coordinate is drawn as center + σ·√2·erfinv(2u−1) with u a float32 uniform on the 2^-24 lattice clamped to [1.192e-07, 1−1.192e-07]. Measured over 4e8 draws: the clamp fires on ~1.15e-07 of draws at the bottom and ~5.0e-08 at the top, and the released noise never exceeds ±5.16657829·σ. So the released mechanism is a lattice-supported, hard-truncated distribution with two point masses at ±5.1666σ (combined mass ~2.3e-07 per coordinate), while dpsgd_acc.gaussian(nm) accounts for a continuous, untruncated N(0,σ²). For a d=1e8 model roughly 23 coordinates per step land on a clamp atom. The gap between the accounted and released distributions is real but is the generic floating-point-DP gap shared with torch.normal (which truncates at ~±5.77σ off the same 2^-24 lattice) and with Opacus/TF-Privacy; no concrete δ inflation is established here. The concrete defect that is fully established is documentation: _gaussian.py:189-196 implies float32 uniform inverse-CDF sampling 'satisfies the standard analysis' while bf16 does not, and neither the clamp comment (lines 266-269) nor anywhere else in the repo acknowledges the truncation, the atoms, or the lattice.
verification.refutation: Not refuted, but the blast radius is overstated. The clamp is not the dominant deviation — the 2^-24 uniform lattice is, and it is inherent to any float32 sampler including the torch.normal path that mainstream DP libraries use (Box-Muller from the same lattice truncates at ~±5.77σ, barely wider than the ±5.17σ here). The reporter's proposed float64 fix only shifts the cut to ~±8.15σ and does not remove the lattice, so it does not restore the 'standard analysis' either. No quantified δ increment is provided, so 'affects_epsilon: true' is asserted rather than demonstrated.

survivors.title: Microbatched clipping accumulates across microbatches in the input dtype, contradicting the documented `compute_dtype` contract
survivors.claim: `_microbatch_accumulate` calls `_sum_clipped_tensor(x, dim=0, output_dtype=dtype, compute_dtype=compute_dtype)` per microbatch, and `_sum_clipped_tensor` casts its result back to `output_dtype if output_dtype is not None else tensor.dtype` before returning. The cross-microbatch running sum `acc + new` therefore happens in the *input* dtype, not in `compute_dtype`. For bf16/fp16 gradients with `dtype=None` this means every microbatch boundary rounds to 8 mantissa bits and the entire across-microbatch accumulation is bf16 — exactly the case the auto-promotion exists to prevent. The `clipped_fun` docstring explicitly promises the opposite: "``compute_dtype=fp32`` with ``dtype=None`` accumulates in fp32 internally and casts back to input dtype at the boundary." The non-microbatch path does the right thing (one fp32 sum, one cast), so the two paths disagree numerically. The existing test only asserts the output *dtype*, never accuracy.
survivors.failure_scenario: `clipped_grad(loss_fn, clipping_norm=1.0, normalize_by=1024, microbatch_size=8, compute_dtype=torch.float32)` on a model held in bf16 with a logical batch of 1024. Each of the 128 microbatch sums is computed in fp32 and then downcast to bf16 before being added to a bf16 accumulator, so the final clipped sum accrues ~128 bf16 rounding steps (relative error of order 128·2^-8 worst case, ~2% typical) instead of the single rounding the fp32 path would produce. The Gaussian noise added afterwards is calibrated to the exact sum, so the rounding shows up as an un-modelled, non-zero-mean perturbation of the private gradient — and the same code with `microbatch_size=None` produces a materially different answer.

verification.title: Microbatched clipping accumulates across microbatches in the input dtype, contradicting the documented `compute_dtype` contract
verification.reasoning: Confirmed by code reading and by direct measurement. _clipped_fun.py:236-247 calls `_sum_clipped_tensor(x, dim=0, output_dtype=dtype, compute_dtype=compute_dtype)` per microbatch, and _sum_clipped_tensor (lines 98-104) computes `target = output_dtype if output_dtype is not None else tensor.dtype` and casts the fp32 result down to that target before returning — so with dtype=None on a bf16 tensor every microbatch partial sum is rounded to bf16, and the cross-microbatch `acc + new` at line 246 then runs entirely in bf16. The non-microbatch path (lines 517-522) does the single fp32 sum + one cast, so the two paths genuinely disagree. The docstring at lines 145-153 states the opposite explicitly: 'compute_dtype: Optional internal accumulation dtype for the across-microbatch sum' and 'compute_dtype=fp32 with dtype=None accumulates in fp32 internally and casts back to input dtype at the boundary.' Measured on B=1024 bf16 inputs with microbatch_size=8, taking the fp32 non-microbatch result as reference: microbatch path relative L2 error 1.66e-02, non-microbatch bf16 path 2.36e-03 — a ~7x degradation, matching the reporter's '~2% typical' estimate. The decisive point, which the reporter states but does not measure: passing compute_dtype=torch.float32 explicitly changes nothing — I got a bit-identical 1.66e-02. So the documented escape hatch is inert on this path, and the default (compute_dtype=None) is affected too, since _resolve_compute_dtype's bf16→fp32 auto-promotion is undone by the immediate downcast. The cited test at tests/clipping/test_compute_dtype.py:197-217 does indeed assert only `result.dtype == torch.bfloat16` with no accuracy check, so nothing catches this. Reachability is high, not exotic: microbatch_size is a first-class parameter on clipped_fun, clipped_grad, the AUTO-S path (_auto.py), and is plumbed all the way to the HF trainer (_training_arguments.py, _dp_trainer.py), and bf16 model dtype is the norm for LLM fine-tuning. Severity held at medium: affects_epsilon is correctly false (this is a utility/accuracy defect, not a sensitivity or privacy defect — the clipping bound and the noise calibration are untouched), but it silently defeats a documented numerical-stability guarantee under the default configuration and cannot be worked around with the parameter that exists for exactly this purpose.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: Call `clipped_fun`/`clipped_grad` with `microbatch_size` set on a model whose gradients are bf16 (or fp16) and `dtype=None` — the default, and the configuration the HF DP trainer exposes via microbatch_size. Each microbatch is summed in fp32 (correct) but `_sum_clipped_tensor` casts the partial sum back to bf16 before returning, so the running `acc + new` at line 246 accumulates in bf16 across all B/microbatch_size boundaries. Measured with B=1024 bf16 inputs and microbatch_size=8 (128 boundaries), against the fp32 reference: microbatch relative L2 error 1.66e-02 vs 2.36e-03 for the same call with microbatch_size=None — a ~7x accuracy loss, and the two paths return materially different clipped sums for identical inputs. Critically, `compute_dtype=torch.float32` does not help: the result is bit-identical at 1.66e-02, so the documented contract ('compute_dtype=fp32 with dtype=None accumulates in fp32 internally and casts back to input dtype at the boundary', lines 145-153) is violated with no available workaround short of setting dtype=torch.float32 and casting manually. Privacy is unaffected — the clipping bound and noise calibration are unchanged — but the private gradient carries an extra ~2% un-modelled perturbation, and test_clipped_fun_microbatch_honors_compute_dtype (test_compute_dtype.py:197-217) passes anyway because it only asserts the output dtype.

survivors.title: No test in opaque-dpsgd connects the deployed noise mechanism to the accountant that charges for it
survivors.claim: The dpsgd test suite splits cleanly into mechanism tests (which never touch accounting) and accounting tests (which never run a mechanism). `test_adaptive_quantile_noise.py` has seven tests covering reproducibility, key propagation and step counting, but none checks the *scale* of the injected quantile noise against anything, nor that the released statistic has the sensitivity `adaclip()` assumes; nothing anywhere asserts that the `fraction_noise_std` used by `adaptive_clipped_grad` and the one passed to `adaclip()` agree (the trainer reads `clipping_kwargs` for `target_clipping_rate`, `norm_max` and `gamma` but never for `fraction_noise_std`, so a user override would silently desync the two). `test_bounded_gaussian.py`'s 30 tests all run with σ comparable to the bound and never enter the regime where `alpha`/`beta` saturate, so the critical finding above is invisible to CI. This is the structural reason the privacy-correctness findings above can coexist with a green suite.
survivors.failure_scenario: Any of the above defects — the bounded-Gaussian saturation, the realised-batch-size quantile denominator, or a `fraction_noise_std` override that reaches the mechanism but not the accountant — passes the entire opaque-dpsgd suite unchanged, because no test ever evaluates a released quantity against the PLD that is supposed to describe it.

survivors.title: `lr_schedule` is excluded from strategy equality/hash while the PLD workers are `lru_cache`d on `self` — two different BLT mechanisms share one cached ε
survivors.claim: `BltStrategy.lr_schedule` and `BandMfStrategy.lr_schedule` are declared `field(default=None, compare=False)`. Two accountants that differ only in `lr_schedule` therefore hash and compare equal and collide in the cache — but BLT's coefficients genuinely depend on the schedule (`_blt_optimize_cached` is keyed on `lr_key`, and the BnB Gram is built from those coefficients), so they are different mechanisms with different ε.

survivors.title: Paired second-moment MF allocation splits the budget with single-participation sensitivities while the accountant charges the multi-participation sensitivity
survivors.claim: `make_second_moment_mf_noise` computes `c1 = first_strategy.sensitivity(n_steps=n_steps, min_sep=n_steps, max_participations=1)` and `c2` likewise — deliberately forcing single participation — then calls `paired_noise_stddevs(noise_multiplier / c1, first=max_norm*c1, second=squared_max_norm*c2)`. The accountant (`MfGaussian.pld`) instead uses `strategy.sensitivity(n_steps, min_sep, max_participations)` at the real participation context. Writing r1 = S1/c1 and r2 = S2/c2 for the two streams' participation-amplification ratios, the deployed joint Mahalanobis budget evaluates to (c1²/(nm²·S))·[max_norm·r1²·c1 + sq·r2²·c2] with S = max_norm·c1 + sq·c2. That equals the accountant's (S1/nm)² only when r1 == r2; when r2 > r1 the joint release is under-noised relative to the reported ε. Separately, for `BltStrategy` the `min_sep=n_steps, max_participations=1` query triggers a *different* L-BFGS run (`_blt_optimize_cached(n_steps, n_steps, 1, ...)`) than the one that produced the deployed streaming matrix, so `c1` is not the max column norm of the C that actually generates the noise — contradicting the module docstring's "``c1`` is the first strategy's max column norm".
survivors.failure_scenario: `mf_gaussian_noise(template, identity_strategy(), n_steps=1000, min_sep=100, max_participations=10, noise_multiplier=nm, key=k, second_moment_strategy=lambda_cgd_strategy(lambda_=0.9))`. Stream 1 (identity) has r1 = sqrt(10) ≈ 3.162; stream 2 (normalized λ-CGD, λ=0.9) has r2 > sqrt(10) because its columns are positively correlated at separation 100. With r2 > r1 the true joint Mahalanobis distance exceeds the (c1/nm)² the allocation targets, so the effective joint noise multiplier falls below `nm / S1` and the ε reported by `MfGaussian(nm, identity_strategy()).pld()` understates the true privacy loss of the paired release. With BLT as the first strategy the mismatch fires even for matched streams, because c1 comes from a BLT optimised at a participation context the run never uses.

It is real but is only (a) a redundant L-BFGS run per call and (b) a docstring inaccuracy in _second_moment.py:74 ('c1 is the first strategy's max column norm'). The failure requires r1 != r2, i.e. mismatched participation-amplification behaviour between the two strategies. survivors.title: The dense-matrix MF engine path redraws the base Gaussians every step, producing temporally independent noise instead of correlated MF noise
survivors.claim: `_tensor_mf_noise.noise_fn` derives a fresh generator per step (`step_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, st._step_counter); g = generator_from_key(step_key)`) and hands it to `_gaussian_linear_combination`, which draws a brand-new `torch.randn` for *every* column index of the row. The MF mechanism requires a single base sequence z_0…z_{n−1} shared across all steps, with the noise at step t equal to Σ_j C^{-1}[t,j]·z_j. Here z_j at step t is independent of z_j at step t′, so Cov(noise_t, noise_t′) = 0. Only the per-step marginal variance (σ²·‖row_t‖²) is right; the correlation structure — the entire point of MF and the basis of its sensitivity reduction — is absent. `_engine.py`'s module docstring advertises `_matrix_factorization_noise` as "the engine that all strategy modules call", and the dense branch has its own test class — but every shipped strategy returns a `StreamingMatrix`, so today only the streaming branch is reachable from `mf_gaussian_noise`.
survivors.failure_scenario: `noise_fn, state = _matrix_factorization_noise(grad_template, C_inv_dense, key=key(0))` with any dense `C^{-1}` (e.g. the inverse of the prefix-sum matrix, or a future dense strategy). The released stream is no longer a post-processing of `C·g + z`, so the MF sensitivity reduction the accountant applies does not hold for it at all; empirically the accumulated prefix-sum error grows like O(√n) (independent noise) instead of the O(polylog n) the mechanism is paid for. Secondary: the dense path issues one full-parameter-shape `randn` per non-zero column, i.e. O(t) draws at step t and O(n²) over the run.

            result = result + coef * noise`

verification.title: The dense-matrix MF engine path redraws the base Gaussians every step, producing temporally independent noise instead of correlated MF noise
verification.reasoning: The math claim is correct and I measured it. _engine.py:242-243 derives a fresh generator per step from fold_in(rng_key, step_counter), and _gaussian_linear_combination (165-176) draws a new torch.randn for every non-zero column index, so the z_j at step t are independent of the z_j at step t'. Empirical check with C^{-1} = tril(ones(4,4)) over 4000 independent keys: Var(n_0) = 0.985, Var(n_1) = 2.037 (correct marginals, as claimed), but corr(n_0, n_1) = 0.014 where correct MF noise would give 1/sqrt(2) = 0.707. So the dense branch produces the right per-step variance with no cross-step correlation. However the reachability is nil: _make_raw_mf_noise (_mf_gaussian_noise.py:238-248) always calls strategy.streaming_matrix(...), and every shipped strategy returns a StreamingMatrix (identity() for IdentityStrategy, inverse_as_streaming_matrix(...) for BandMF/BSR/BiSR, _blt_inverse_as_streaming_matrix for BLT); LambdaCgdStrategy raises NotImplementedError there and is special-cased to the PRNG-replay path. The only callers of the dense branch are the private _matrix_factorization_noise and the tests. affects_epsilon should be false in practice: no shipped mechanism releases this noise, so no reported epsilon is currently wrong. This is a latent trap in dead code, not a live privacy defect — medium overstates it.

survivors.title: `row_norms_squared` is O(bands·n²) and runs eagerly at noise-function construction; the in-code claim says it is sub-second at n=10⁴
survivors.claim: For every non-Identity, non-λ-CGD strategy the factory eagerly evaluates `streaming.row_norms_squared(n_steps)`. `StreamingMatrix.row_norms_squared` runs n iterations of `multiply_next` on length-n unit-vector probes. For a banded Toeplitz C^{-1} each `multiply_next` does a `tensordot(coef[1:], state)` over a `(bands-1, n)` state plus a full `torch.roll` of that state — O(bands·n) work and a fresh (bands−1)×n allocation per iteration, i.e. O(bands·n²) total, not the O(n²) the comment claims, and nowhere near sub-second.
survivors.failure_scenario: `mf_gaussian_noise(template, band_mf_strategy(bands=64), n_steps=10_000, noise_multiplier=1.0, key=key(0))` performs 10⁴ iterations, each a 63×10⁴ float64 tensordot plus a 5 MB roll — ~5 GFLOP and ~50 GB of allocation/copy traffic. A pure-numpy reproduction of exactly this recurrence (no torch dispatch, no per-iteration allocation overhead) takes 5.87 s on this machine; the torch path allocating a new (bands−1, n) tensor per step will be slower. At bands=256 the same horizon is ~25 s+. This is pure startup latency in the noise-function constructor, paid solely to populate `NoisedPytree.noise_stddev` for Adam bias correction — a value most optimizer configurations never read.
