survivors.title: Streaming MF noise has no horizon guard: calls past `n_steps` keep producing noise the whole-run accountant does not cover
survivors.claim: `_streaming_mf_noise.noise_fn` never compares `st._step_counter` against the `n_steps` the strategy/streaming matrix was built for — `n_steps` is not even captured in the closure. Every DP-FTRL accountant in this package is a *whole-run* process defined only on `[1, n_steps]` (`DpFtrlProcess._pld_at_horizon` raises for `n_steps > self.n_steps`, and `PerStep.repeated_pld` raises for `count > self.proc.n_steps`), so any release beyond step `n_steps − 1` is outside the reported guarantee. The dense-tensor sibling does guard, and `row_l2_at` clamps its index — so the over-run is invisible: the published `noise_stddev` freezes at the last row's value and training continues.
survivors.failure_scenario: A BandMF run is configured with `n_steps=1000` and its ε reported from `poisson(mf_gaussian(nm, band_mf_strategy(bands=32)), sample_rate=q, n_steps=1000)`. The operator then bumps the epoch count or resumes and the loop makes 1200 `noise_fn` calls. The streaming Toeplitz C^{-1} happily extends to row 1199, the accountant object is never re-queried (and `per_step(proc)*1200` would have raised `count (1200) exceeds n_steps (1000)`), and the run reports the 1000-step ε for a 1200-step release. Nothing in the noise path raises or warns.
evidence: _engine.py:319-341  `def noise_fn(clipped_grads, st, *, stddev): step_key = rng_fold_in(...); ... corr_noise, new_streaming_state = noising.multiply_next(iid_noise, s_state)` — no bound on `st._step_counter`

_engine.py:245-249  the dense path's guard: `if index >= max_steps: raise ValueError(f"Step {index} exceeds noising matrix size {max_steps}. The noising matrix must have at least as many rows as steps.")`
_mf_gaussian_noise.py:265-267  `def row_l2_at(step): idx = min(step, row_norms.shape[0] - 1); return float(row_norms[idx])` — silently clamps rather than flagging the over-run

packages/opaque-dpftrl/src/opaque/api/accounting/dpftrl/_base.py:64-67 (`Raises: ValueError: If ``n_steps`` is outside ``[1, self.n_steps]``.`) and composition/_per_step.py:78-83 (`if count > self.proc.n_steps: raise ValueError(...)`) — the accountant side is strict, the noise side is not
survivors.fix_sketch: Thread `n_steps` into `_matrix_factorization_noise` / `_make_raw_mf_noise` and raise from all three `noise_fn` implementations (streaming, dense, λ-CGD) when `st._step_counter >= n_steps`, reusing the dense path's message.

verification.title: Streaming MF noise has no horizon guard: calls past `n_steps` keep producing noise the whole-run accountant does not cover
verification.reasoning:
Every element of the claim checks out, and the real behaviour is worse than reported.

Code: `_engine.py:319-341` (`_streaming_mf_noise.noise_fn`) does not receive or capture `n_steps` and never bounds `st._step_counter`. The dense sibling `_tensor_mf_noise` does guard, at `_engine.py:245-249`. `_mf_gaussian_noise.py:265-267` clamps `idx = min(step, row_norms.shape[0]-1)`, so the published σ silently freezes. Accountant side is strict as claimed: `composition/_per_step.py:78-83` raises `count (N) exceeds n_steps (M); ... undefined beyond its declared horizon`, and `_base.py:64-67` documents `_pld_at_horizon` as raising outside `[1, self.n_steps]`. I grepped for any step-budget enforcement in the noise/engine path; the only such check in the repo is the dense-path one.

I reproduced both paths through the public API.

Streaming (BandMF, bands=3, n_steps=5), 8 calls: no error, noise keeps being produced past step 4, published `noise_stddev` frozen at 1.2547 from step 4 onward. Exactly the silent over-run described.

λ-CGD is worse than the reporter realized, and their own fix sketch names that path. `_lambda_cgd.py:230` applies `d_t = _column_norm(lambda_, n_steps, step)` with the UNCLAMPED step (unlike `_lambda_cgd_row_l2`, which does clamp via `min(step, n_steps-1)`). At `step == n_steps`, `remaining = 0` so `lambda2r = 1` and `_column_norm` returns exactly 0.0. Verified end-to-end: `mf_gaussian_noise(..., lambda_cgd_strategy(lambda_=0.5), n_steps=3)` called 5 times returns, at call index 3, `pytree['w'] == [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]` for a zero input — the clipped gradient sum is released with EXACTLY ZERO noise, while `noise_stddev` still reports 1.118. Call index 4 then dies with `ValueError: math domain error` (`sqrt` of a negative). So an off-by-one loop bound on a λ-CGD run leaks one completely un-noised gradient release.

Reachability does require the operator to run past the declared horizon (resume, epoch bump, `range(n_steps+1)`), so this is not spontaneous. But nothing in the library prevents it, the dense path proves the maintainers consider the guard necessary, and the consequence in the λ-CGD case is a raw release rather than merely an unaccounted one. That is an upgrade to high, not medium.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: Streaming path (BandMF/BLT): configure `mf_gaussian_noise(..., band_mf_strategy(bands=3), n_steps=5, ...)` and call the returned `noise_fn` 8 times. Verified: no error is raised; correlated noise continues to be drawn from rows 5-7 of C^{-1}, and `NoisedPytree.noise_stddev` freezes at the row-4 value (1.2547) because `row_l2_at` clamps its index. Meanwhile `per_step(proc).repeated_pld(8)` would raise `count (8) exceeds n_steps (5)`, so the run reports a 5-step ε for an 8-step release stream. λ-CGD path (same `mf_gaussian_noise` entry point, `_lambda_cgd.py:230` uses the unclamped step in `_column_norm`): with `lambda_cgd_strategy(lambda_=0.5), n_steps=3`, the 4th call (step index 3 == n_steps) computes `d_t = _column_norm(0.5, 3, 3) = 0.0` and returns the clipped gradient sum with exactly zero noise added — verified output `[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]` for a zero input — while still publishing `noise_stddev = 1.118`. The 5th call raises `ValueError: math domain error`. An off-by-one loop bound therefore leaks one entirely un-noised release before crashing.

survivors.title: Tensor deserialisation accepts a shape-mismatched checkpoint value silently, while the ndarray handler rejects it
survivors.claim: `_tensor_load` validates only that the saved value is a `torch.Tensor` and then returns `saved.to(dtype=template.dtype, device=template.device)` — no shape check. The sibling `_ndarray_load` (lines 43-55) explicitly raises `ValueError` on a shape mismatch. So the same wrong checkpoint is caught for numpy leaves and waved through for torch leaves.
survivors.failure_scenario: Load a DP-FTRL `MFNoiseState` (whose `_inner_state` is the streaming-matrix buffer pytree, shaped like the gradient tree) from a checkpoint taken against a different model or a different `n_steps`. `from_state_dict` returns the saved buffers at the WRONG shape with no error. Verified minimal case: `from_state_dict(S(t=torch.zeros(3)), {'t': torch.arange(10.)})` returns `t = tensor([0..9])` — shape (10,) where the template says (3,). Downstream `grad + noise` then either raises an opaque broadcast error many steps later, or (when the shapes happen to broadcast, e.g. (1,N) against (N,)) silently applies correlated noise with the wrong per-coordinate variance while the accountant reports the intended sigma.
evidence: _structural.py:28-36 `_tensor_load(...): saved = sd.get(''); if saved is None: return template; if not isinstance(saved, torch.Tensor): raise TypeError(...); return saved.to(dtype=template.dtype, device=template.device)` — no `saved.shape != template.shape` branch
_structural.py:47-52 `_ndarray_load`: `if arr.shape != template.shape: raise ValueError(f"state_dict ndarray has shape {arr.shape}; template expects {template.shape}")`
survivors.fix_sketch: Mirror the ndarray handler: `if saved.shape != template.shape: raise ValueError(...)` in `_tensor_load` before the dtype/device cast.

verification.title: Tensor deserialisation accepts a shape-mismatched checkpoint value silently, while the ndarray handler rejects it
verification.reasoning:
The asymmetry is exactly as stated and I reproduced it. `_structural.py:28-36` `_tensor_load` checks only `isinstance(saved, torch.Tensor)` and returns `saved.to(dtype=..., device=...)`; `_ndarray_load` at 47-52 raises on shape mismatch. Running it: `from_state_dict(S(t=torch.zeros(3)), {'t': torch.arange(10.)})` returns `S(t=tensor([0..9]))` with no error, while the identical numpy case raises `ValueError: state_dict ndarray has shape (10,); template expects (3,)`. The dispatcher (`_dispatch.py:64-68`) routes by exact type with no shape checking of its own, so nothing upstream catches it. There is even a test asserting the numpy behaviour (`packages/opaque-engine/tests/serialization/test_pergroup_numpy.py:46 test_numpy_leaf_wrong_shape_errors`) with no torch counterpart, which confirms shape validation is the intended contract rather than a deliberate omission.

Where I disagree is blast radius. The reporter's headline harm — 'silently applies correlated noise with the wrong per-coordinate variance' — requires the wrong shape to be broadcast-compatible with the right one, and for the MF state that is hard to arrange. `_streaming_mf_noise` builds `_inner_state` from `inverse_as_streaming_matrix`'s `init`, giving per-leaf state of shape `(bands-1, *param.shape)`. A checkpoint from a different `bands` gives a leading dim that then hits `torch.tensordot(coef[1:], state)` with a mismatched contraction dim and raises; a checkpoint from a different model gives per-parameter shapes that almost never broadcast. The realistic outcome is a delayed, opaque RuntimeError one step later — annoying and hard to diagnose, but loud. There is no evidence of a realistic silent-wrong-variance path, so this is a validation/consistency gap worth a one-line fix, not a medium numerical-correctness bug.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: Load a checkpoint whose torch leaves have different shapes than the template (e.g. an `MFNoiseState` saved from a run with a different model or a different `bands`). `from_state_dict` returns the saved tensors at the wrong shape with no error — verified: `from_state_dict(S(t=torch.zeros(3)), {'t': torch.arange(10.)})` returns `t = tensor([0.,...,9.])`, shape (10,) against a (3,) template — whereas the identical numpy case raises `ValueError` from `_ndarray_load`. The failure then surfaces one or more steps later as an opaque broadcast/contraction RuntimeError inside `torch.tensordot(coef[1:], state)` or `grad + noise`, far from the `from_state_dict` call that caused it. Silent numerical corruption requires the wrong shape to be broadcast-compatible with the template, which the MF state layout `(bands-1, *param.shape)` makes unlikely in practice.
verification.refutation: Not refuted — the missing check is real and inconsistent with the sibling handler. Downgraded to low because the claimed silent-wrong-variance outcome is not demonstrably reachable: the MF streaming state's `(bands-1, *param.shape)` layout means a mismatched checkpoint hits a contraction-dim error in `_toeplitz._next`'s `tensordot` rather than broadcasting, so the practical harm is a delayed confusing exception, not corrupted noise.

survivors.title: distributed sync() cannot dispatch AUTO-S clipping state or aux — exact-type registry misses every documented ClippedGradAux subclass except the one DP-SGD registers by hand
survivors.claim: `sync()`'s `_sync_one` resolves `state_type = type(single)` and requires an exact key in `_SYNC_REGISTRY`. `_distributed.py` registers only `FixedClipState`, `ClippedFunAux`, `ClippedGradAux`; `opaque-dpsgd` hand-registers `AdaptiveClipState`/`AdaptiveClippedGradAux`. Nothing registers `AutoClipState`, `AutoClippedFunAux`, or `AutoClippedGradAux`, so the documented `sync()` path fails for AUTO-S even though `sync_clipped_grad_aux`'s own docstring claims it 'Handles any subclass of ClippedGradAux' and `sync_aux()` (isinstance-based) does.
survivors.failure_scenario: DDP run using `auto_clipped_grad(..., return_aux=True)` (a first-class documented entry point, clipping/__init__.py:7-8) then calling `opaque.distributed.sync(aux)` per the module docstring at clipping/__init__.py:22-23. Verified: raises `TypeError: No sync function registered for AutoClippedGradAux. Registered types: ['FixedClipState', 'ClippedFunAux', 'ClippedGradAux', 'PerfState', 'PerfTracker']`. The same happens for `sync(AutoClipState())`. Per-example gradient-norm diagnostics used to tune R are therefore never gathered across ranks in an AUTO-S DDP run, or the run crashes at the sync call.
evidence: _state.py:266-276 `state_type = type(single)` ... `if state_type in _SYNC_REGISTRY: return _SYNC_REGISTRY[state_type](single)` ... `raise TypeError(f"No sync function registered for {state_type.__name__}...")`
clipping/_distributed.py:131-133 registers only the three base types
clipping/_auto.py:46-82 defines `AutoClippedFunAux(ClippedFunAux)`, `AutoClippedGradAux(ClippedGradAux)`, `AutoClipState(ClipState)` with no registration call

clipping/_distributed.py:99-105 `sync_clipped_grad_aux` docstring: 'Handles any subclass of ClippedGradAux ... the constructor of type(aux) is used to rebuild the synced instance' — true of the function, not of the dispatcher that routes to it
clipping/__init__.py:22-23 'Use :func:`opaque.distributed.sync` to synchronize clipping state or aux objects across ranks.'
survivors.fix_sketch: Make `_sync_one` walk `type(single).__mro__` against `_SYNC_REGISTRY` after the exact-type miss (matching the isinstance semantics `sync_aux` already uses), and register `AutoClipState` in `clipping/_auto.py` or `_distributed.py`.

verification.title: distributed sync() cannot dispatch AUTO-S clipping state or aux — exact-type registry misses every documented ClippedGradAux subclass except the one DP-SGD registers by hand
verification.reasoning:
Reproduced exactly. `_state.py:268-278` `_sync_one` does `state_type = type(single)` and requires an exact registry key, falling back only to `_ensure_builtin_sync_types_loaded()` (which imports the same three registrations) before raising. `clipping/_distributed.py:131-133` registers only `FixedClipState`, `ClippedFunAux`, `ClippedGradAux`; `opaque-dpsgd/.../clipping/_distributed.py:134-135` hand-registers `AdaptiveClipState`/`AdaptiveClippedGradAux`. A full grep for `register_sync_type` across all packages confirms nothing registers any AUTO-S type. Running it:
  sync(AutoClipState())      -> TypeError: No sync function registered for AutoClipState. Registered types: ['FixedClipState', 'ClippedFunAux', 'ClippedGradAux', 'PerfState', 'PerfTracker']
  sync(AutoClippedGradAux()) -> same TypeError
  sync(AutoClippedFunAux())  -> same TypeError
`auto_clipped_grad` returns `AutoClipState()` unconditionally (`_auto.py:317`) and `AutoClippedGradAux` when `return_aux=True` (`_auto.py:329`), and both are exported (`_auto.py:346,348`); `auto_clipped_grad` is a first-class public entry point (`clipping/__init__.py:7`). `sync_aux` is isinstance-based and would work, but it is not exported on the `opaque.distributed` façade (I enumerated it: only `sync` is public), so `sync` is the only public route. `FixedClipState` being registered as a marker passthrough while the equally-marker `AutoClipState` is not is plainly an oversight, and `sync_clipped_grad_aux`'s docstring at `_distributed.py:99-105` explicitly promises subclass support that the dispatcher's exact-type lookup defeats.

One caveat against the reporter: `docs/reference/clipping.md:67-69` enumerates the supported `sync()` inputs and does NOT list AUTO-S, so the reference doc is narrower than the module docstring's generic 'synchronize clipping state or aux objects' and `docs/reference/index.md:80`'s 'Auto-dispatch sync for any state/aux type'. And the failure is a loud, self-describing TypeError that lists the registered types — not a silent skip, so the reporter's 'diagnostics are never gathered across ranks' alternative outcome does not happen. Medium stands: it hard-breaks a documented public path in DDP with a trivial fix, but it is visible and has no privacy or numerical impact.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: In a DDP run using `auto_clipped_grad(..., return_aux=True)`, calling `opaque.distributed.sync(clip_state)` or `sync(aux)` — the only public sync entry point, per `clipping/__init__.py:22-23` — raises immediately, on every rank, single-process included: `TypeError: No sync function registered for AutoClipState. Registered types: ['FixedClipState', 'ClippedFunAux', 'ClippedGradAux', 'PerfState', 'PerfTracker']` (same for `AutoClippedGradAux` and `AutoClippedFunAux`). The run crashes at the sync call; it does not silently skip the gather. The equivalent fixed-clipping and DP-SGD adaptive-clipping runs work because those exact types are registered, and `sync_clipped_grad_aux` would in fact handle the AUTO-S subclass correctly if the dispatcher ever routed to it — the defect is purely the exact-type lookup in `_sync_one` plus the missing `register_sync_type(AutoClipState, ...)`.

survivors.title: _split_aux_fields classifies aux fields by runtime value, so an optional field that is None on one rank changes that rank's all_gather count
survivors.claim: `_split_aux_fields` routes a field to `tensor_fields` (which costs one `all_gather_object` inside `gather_pytree`) or to `scalar_fields` (zero collectives) based on `value is None or isinstance(value, (int, float))` — i.e. on the *value* this rank happens to hold, not on the dataclass schema. `ClippedGradAux.group_norms`, `loss_aux`, `loss_values`, and `clipped_grad_norms` are all `X | None`. When any of them is None on one rank and populated on another, that rank issues fewer gathers than its peers, misaligning the process group in the same way as the `_sync_clipping_rate` branch. This is a second, independent trigger with a different fix: it fires even when both ranks have non-empty batches.
survivors.failure_scenario: world_size=2 with per-group clipping (`clipping_norm=PerGroup(...)`) and one rank drawing an empty Poisson batch. The empty-batch aux constructed at `_clipped_grad.py:216-223` leaves `group_norms` at its `None` default and `loss_aux=None`, while the non-empty rank carries `group_norms={g: Tensor}`. Verified under gloo, world_size=2: rank 0 reports tensor fields `['clipped_grad_norms', 'grad_norms', 'group_norms']` and rank 1 reports `['clipped_grad_norms', 'grad_norms']` — rank 0 issues one extra `all_gather_object` that rank 1 never matches.
evidence: _distributed.py:49-54 — `if value is None or isinstance(value, (int, float)): scalar_fields[f.name] = value else: tensor_fields[f.name] = value`
_state.py:130-144 — `gather_pytree` maps over the dict, issuing one `gather_tensors` (i.e. one `all_gather_object`) per tensor leaf
_clipped_grad.py:46-52 — `loss_aux: Any | None = None`, `group_norms: dict[str, torch.Tensor] | None = None`
_clipped_grad.py:216-223 — the empty-batch aux leaves `group_norms` and `loss_aux` at None
gloo repro: `RANK 0 tensor fields -> ['clipped_grad_norms', 'grad_norms', 'group_norms']` / `RANK 1 tensor fields -> ['clipped_grad_norms', 'grad_norms']`
survivors.fix_sketch: Split on the dataclass *schema* rather than the value: derive the tensor-field name list once from `dataclasses.fields(type(aux))` (or all-gather and intersect the name lists), and have every rank contribute a zero-length placeholder tensor for a field it holds as None so the gather count is identical on all ranks.

verification.title: _split_aux_fields classifies aux fields by runtime value, so an optional field that is None on one rank changes that rank's all_gather count
verification.reasoning: `_split_aux_fields` (_distributed.py:49-54) routes on the runtime value, and `gather_pytree`/`gather_tensors` (_state.py:130-144, 116-127) issue exactly one `all_gather_object` per tensor leaf, so the number of collectives equals the number of tensor leaves this rank happens to hold. `ClippedGradAux.group_norms` defaults to None (_clipped_grad.py:52) and the empty-batch short-circuit `_empty_batch_response` (_clipped_grad.py:214-224) omits it entirely, while the non-empty per-group path fills it from `aux.group_norms` (_clipped_grad.py:279, 303; also propagated verbatim by `AutoClippedGradAux` at _auto.py:328-336 and by `sync_adaptive_clipped_grad_aux`, which just delegates). The path is live: `_dp_trainer.py:1898` calls `sync(clip_state, aux)` on every DDP step, and empty Poisson rounds are an explicitly supported case there (`empty_collate`, comment at _dp_trainer.py:1821-1827); `examples/train_dpsgd.py:1767` does the same under `--per-group-clipping` with parallel Poisson sampling (per-rank independent draws, line 1222). Note the gather at line 110 runs *before* `_sync_clipping_rate` at 112, so under per-group clipping this is the first mismatch to fire, not a downstream duplicate. No DDP test covers per-group clipping at all (`grep per_group packages/*/tests/ddp/*.py` is empty). The same codebase elsewhere treats exactly this pattern as a deadlock bug worth a hard error (_dp_trainer.py:3445-3470). Severity stays medium: it is a hang, requires per-group clipping plus an empty local batch, and the trainer's `_sync_clipping_rate` path already desyncs on an empty batch under any clipping config.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: world_size=2 under DDP with `clipping_norm=per_group(params, ...)` (G groups) and Poisson sampling. Rank 1 draws an empty batch, so `clipped_grad`'s `_empty_batch_response` returns `ClippedGradAux(loss_values=empty, grad_norms=empty, clipped_grad_norms=empty, group_norms=None)`; rank 0 returns the same three tensors plus `group_norms={g_1: Tensor, ... g_G: Tensor}`. At `_dp_trainer.py:1898` -> `sync_clipped_grad_aux` -> `gather_pytree`, rank 0 issues 3+G `all_gather_object` calls and rank 1 issues 3. The process group desynchronizes on the 4th collective and the run hangs (or, with a timeout set, dies with an NCCL/gloo timeout on all ranks).
verification.refutation: Not refuted. One overstatement corrected: the claim that this "fires even when both ranks have non-empty batches" is not supported. `group_norms` is None-vs-dict only because of the empty-batch short-circuit; under SPMD both ranks run the same `clipping_norm` config, so with non-empty batches both hold a dict. The only non-empty-batch variant would be `loss_aux` differing (needs `has_aux=True` and a loss whose aux is None on one rank only), which is contrived.

survivors.title: sync_object silently skips non-numeric fields and builds its default field map from per-rank values, making its collective count data-dependent
survivors.claim: `sync_object` is a documented public API (listed in docs/user-guide/distributed.md's API table). With `field_ops=None` it constructs the reduction map by scanning `getattr(state, f.name)` on the local rank and keeping only fields whose *current value* is a non-bool `int`/`float`. With an explicit `field_ops` it still does `if not isinstance(value, (float, int)): continue`. In both cases the number of `reduce_scalar` calls depends on the runtime values a rank happens to hold, so a field that is `None` on one rank and a float on another produces mismatched collective counts and a permanently desynchronized group. The silent `continue` also means an `"assert_equal"` request on a non-scalar field (e.g. `MFNoiseState._first_max_norm` when it is a `PerGroup`) performs no check at all while appearing to.
survivors.failure_scenario: A user follows the documented pattern `sync_object(my_state)` on a state dataclass with an optional metric field `last_clip_norm: float | None`, populated only on steps where clipping fired. On a step where rank 0's batch triggered clipping and rank 1's did not, rank 0 issues one more `all_reduce` than rank 1; every subsequent collective in the run is off by one and returns values from the wrong call site, with no exception. Separately, `sync(MFNoiseState)` with `PerGroup` clipping requests `"_first_max_norm": "assert_equal"` (dpftrl/noise/_distributed.py:72) and the check is silently skipped because `PerGroup` is not an int/float — leaving only the 64-bit fingerprint, which is itself weakened by the float32 issue reported separately.
evidence: _state.py:174-179 — `for f in fields(state): val = getattr(state, f.name); if isinstance(val, (float, int)) and not isinstance(val, bool): field_ops[f.name] = "mean"`
_state.py:201-202 — `if not isinstance(value, (float, int)): continue`
_state.py:189 — `for field_name, field_op in field_ops.items():` — one `reduce_scalar` (or two, for `assert_equal`) per surviving field
dpftrl/noise/_distributed.py:70-74 — `"_first_max_norm": "assert_equal"` on a field typed `float | PerGroup`
docs/user-guide/distributed.md API table lists `sync_object(state, field_ops)` as a supported public entry point
survivors.fix_sketch: Derive the field set from the dataclass schema, not from values, and issue the same collective for every listed field on every rank (reducing a sentinel for a locally-`None` field, then asserting the None-ness itself is consistent). Raise instead of `continue` when an explicitly requested `field_op` cannot be applied to the field's value.

verification.title: sync_object silently skips non-numeric fields and builds its default field map from per-rank values, making its collective count data-dependent
verification.reasoning: The mechanical claim about the code is accurate: with `field_ops=None` the map is built from local values (_state.py:174-179) and with explicit ops non-numeric values are silently skipped (_state.py:201-202), so `reduce_scalar` counts are value-dependent. But every in-repo caller passes explicit, always-numeric ops that cannot diverge in lockstep training: `_MF_NOISE_STATE_FIELD_OPS` (dpftrl/noise/_distributed.py:70-74), `_NOISE_STATE_FIELD_OPS` (dpsgd/noise/_distributed.py:39), and `{_num_clipped: sum, _batch_size: sum}` (dpsgd/clipping/_distributed.py:85-91). Nothing in the repo calls `sync_object` with `field_ops=None`, so the default-map branch has no library trigger; the failure needs user code whose optional numeric field is populated on some ranks only. The second half of the claim is materially wrong. `_first_max_norm` is `float | PerGroup | None`: in the scalar case `assert_equal` does run; in the PerGroup case it is skipped, but that is not "no check at all" — `_first_max_norm_sync_fingerprint` is set in the very same `replace()` as `_first_max_norm` (_mf_gaussian_noise.py:185-195 and _second_moment.py:158-186), is an `int`, and therefore *does* get `assert_equal`'d. `fingerprint_per_group_max_norm` hashes `sorted(pg.groups.items())` + `sorted(pg.values.items())`, which is precisely the designed PerGroup equality check (see its docstring: "avoids re-hashing the full param->group map on the hot path"). Also note the collective count for `_first_max_norm` is consistent across ranks either way, since the scalar-vs-PerGroup choice is configuration, identical under SPMD. Downgraded to low: a robustness wart in a public helper, no reachable in-repo failure.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A user writes their own dataclass with an optional metric field (`last_clip_norm: float | None`) and calls the documented `sync_object(state)` (docs/user-guide/distributed.md:279) each step. On a step where rank 0 populated the field and rank 1 left it None, rank 0's default field map contains one extra entry, so it issues one more `all_reduce` than rank 1; from that point on every collective is paired with the wrong call site and the run silently produces wrong reduced values (or hangs at the next unpaired collective). No in-repo state hits this — the effect requires a user-defined state whose numeric fields are conditionally populated.
verification.refutation: The `_first_max_norm` half is refuted: the PerGroup equality check is not lost, it is carried by `_first_max_norm_sync_fingerprint` (an int, so `assert_equal` applies), which is written atomically with `_first_max_norm` at _mf_gaussian_noise.py:194-195 and _second_moment.py:180-186. The desync half stands but has no library-side trigger, hence the downgrade.

survivors.title: compute_ref_logprobs_for_dataset never shards the forward pass; its cross-rank gather makes the result unusable under world_size > 1
survivors.claim: The module docstring claims "Per-column shards are concatenated across ranks with gather_for_metrics." There is no sharding: `DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=batch_size, collate_fn=collator)` has no sampler and no `local_shard`, so every rank runs the reference forward over the *entire* `dataset` (W× redundant compute) and `local` has length `len(dataset)` on every rank. `gather_for_metrics` then concatenates to `W * len(dataset)`, and `result.add_column(name, values)` is handed `W * len(dataset)` values for a `len(dataset)`-row dataset. The local variable is even named `shards`, but it holds per-*batch* chunks, not per-rank shards. There is no code path that produces a correct result for world_size > 1.
survivors.failure_scenario: world_size=2, DPO reference precompute over a 10,000-example preference dataset on a cache miss. Both ranks compute all 10,000 reference logprobs; `gather_for_metrics` returns a 20,000-element tensor; `Dataset.add_column('ref_chosen_logps', <20000 floats>)` raises a length-mismatch error against the 10,000-row dataset. On a cache *hit* the function returns correctly, so the failure only appears the first time the cache is cold — i.e. on the first real DDP run.
evidence: _precompute.py:219 `loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=batch_size, collate_fn=collator)` — no sampler, no `local_shard`
_precompute.py:231-239 — `local = torch.cat(shards[name], dim=0) ...; gathered[name] = gather_for_metrics(local)`
_precompute.py:251-255 — `values = gathered[name].detach().cpu().float().tolist(); result = result.add_column(name, values)`
_precompute.py:35-39 module docstring: "Per-column shards are concatenated across ranks with gather_for_metrics; only is_main_process writes the cache"
`compute_ref_logprobs_for_dataset` is exported (`__all__` at :62, re-exported at alignment/dpo/reference/__init__.py:23-30) and has no in-repo caller, so the path has never been exercised
survivors.fix_sketch: Iterate a `local_shard(dataset, rank, world_size)` (or a DistributedSampler) inside the loop, keep the gather so every rank ends up with the full column, and add an assertion that `len(gathered[name]) == len(dataset)` before `add_column`.

verification.title: compute_ref_logprobs_for_dataset never shards the forward pass; its cross-rank gather makes the result unusable under world_size > 1
verification.reasoning: Verified line by line. `_precompute.py:220` builds `DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=..., collate_fn=collator)` with no sampler and no `local_shard`, so every rank iterates the full dataset; `shards` holds per-batch chunks, not per-rank shards. `gather_for_metrics` (collectives.py:105-124) is a plain `dist.all_gather` + `torch.cat` with `torch.empty_like` buffers — it requires identical shapes, which is satisfied here precisely *because* nothing is sharded, so the gather succeeds and returns `world_size * len(dataset)` elements. That is then passed to `Dataset.add_column` at line 255 against a `len(dataset)`-row table, which raises. The module docstring at lines 35-39 claims per-rank shards, so the gather is clearly vestigial intent, not a deliberate choice. The trainer shards *training* data separately and later (`local_shard` at _dp_trainer.py:3353-3359), so precompute is correctly meant to run over the full dataset — the gather is simply wrong. Reachability: `_dpo_trainer.py:544` calls this from `__init__` after `args.device` (line 283) has already initialized the process group under torchrun, so `is_distributed()` is True. Severity medium: loud crash, not silent corruption, and only on a cold cache.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: world_size=2 DPO run under torchrun with a cold reference cache and a 10,000-row preference dataset. `DPOTrainer.__init__` -> `_precompute_ref_logps` -> `compute_ref_logprobs_for_dataset`: both ranks run the full 10,000-example reference forward (2x redundant compute), `gather_for_metrics` all-gathers the identically-shaped (10000,) tensors into (20000,), and `result.add_column('ref_chosen_logps', <20000 floats>)` raises a length/row-count error on every rank before training starts. A warm cache takes the early-return at line 210-217 and works, so the failure appears only on the first distributed run.
verification.refutation: Not refuted. One evidence bullet is wrong and should be corrected before filing: the function does have in-repo callers — `packages/opaque-transformers/src/opaque/api/transformers/trl/_dpo_trainer.py:544` and `:597`, plus `examples/train_dpo.py:1436` — and unit tests at `packages/opaque-alignment/tests/dpo/reference/test_precompute.py`. What is true is that all of them are single-process; there is no DDP test for DPO (`packages/opaque-transformers/tests/distributed/` has none), which is why the path has never been exercised under world_size>1.

survivors.title: The private-second-moment stream and the squared-noisy-gradient branch are on different scales (Σᵢgᵢ² vs (Σᵢgᵢ)²), so swapping between them changes the effective learning rate by ~√B despite being documented as interchangeable
survivors.claim: `SecondMomentClippingOutput.squared_grads` is `Σᵢ gᵢ² / normalize_by` — the *per-example* second moment, correctly documented as such in the engine (`_clipped_fun.py:353`, `types.py:405-408`). The standard branch builds `nu` from `(Σᵢ gᵢ / normalize_by)²`, the square of the *aggregate*. These are different statistics: `E[Σgᵢ²] = Σgᵢ² ≈ B·E[g²]` while `(Σgᵢ)² ≈ B²·ḡ²`; they differ by a factor of order B (the within-batch gradient variance) even in the noiseless limit σ→0. The optimizer docstring and user guide present them as two answers to the *same* bias, differing only in privacy cost: "Modes (3) and (4) target the same source of bias — that E[(g+noise)²] is not E[g²] — by different means. They are alternatives... pick one per training run." Nothing rescales the SM stream, and nothing warns the LR must be retuned.
survivors.failure_scenario: A user follows the docs table (user-guide/optimizers.md:270-271) and switches from `adamw(lr=1.5e-4, noise_bias_correction=True)` to `adamw(lr=1.5e-4) + SecondMomentNoiseOutput` to spend the extra ~22% budget on private second moments. With B=256 per-example clipped gradients (C=1, d=4096, mild shared signal), the steady-state update RMS is 1.00 for the squared-aggregate branch and 10.35 for the private-g² branch — a 10× effective-LR jump at the identical nominal lr. The factor tracks √B and the within-batch alignment, so it is invisible at the toy batch sizes used in `test_adam.py::TestSecondMomentMode` (which only asserts finiteness and state shape, never scale).
evidence: _adam.py:169-173  `new_nu = tree_map(lambda v, g2: b2 * v + (1 - b2) * g2, state.nu, noisy_squared_grads)` — g2 substituted directly, no rescaling

_adam.py:29-33  "Modes (3) and (4) target the same source of bias — that ``E[(g+noise)²]`` is not ``E[g²]`` — by different means.  They are alternatives, not stack on top of each other; pick one per training run."

packages/opaque-engine/.../clipping/_clipped_fun.py:353  "per-example squared clipped values, i.e. ``Σᵢ gᵢ²``"; _clipped_grad.py:196 `output_squared_max_norm = (clipping_norm * clipping_norm) / normalize_by`
packages/opaque-engine/.../clipping/_clipped_fun.py:249-261 — `microbatch_squared_sum` is a plain sum over the example axis of per-example squares
Measured: `RMS(update) standard v=(sum g)^2 : 1.000 / RMS(update) SM v= sum g^2 : 10.348` at B=256, d=4096, C=1
Same substitution without rescaling in _rmsprop.py:104-120, _ademamix.py:117-138, _adadelta.py:151-163
survivors.fix_sketch: Either divide the incoming `noisy_squared_grads` by the effective batch size so `nu` estimates the aggregate's second moment, or state explicitly in the docstring and user guide that the SM branch preconditions by the empirical per-example Fisher and requires an independent LR sweep. Add a test asserting the two branches give comparable update RMS on a noiseless batch of identical examples (where Σgᵢ² and (Σgᵢ)²/B coincide).

verification.title: The private-second-moment stream and the squared-noisy-gradient branch are on different scales (Σᵢgᵢ² vs (Σᵢgᵢ)²), so swapping between them changes the effective learning rate by ~√B despite being documented as interchangeable
verification.reasoning: I traced the whole path. `_clipped_fun.py:397-399` sets `output_max_norm = C/normalize_by` and `output_squared_max_norm = C²/normalize_by`; lines 548-551 divide BOTH the summed gradient stream and the summed-squared stream by the same `normalize_by`. `microbatch_squared_sum` (lines 249-261) is a plain per-example-axis sum of per-example squares, so with the documented `normalize_by=batch_size` the two streams are ḡ = (1/B)Σgᵢ and (1/B)Σgᵢ² — the aggregate mean and the per-example second moment. In `_adam.py:169-173` the second stream is substituted verbatim into the ν EMA (`b2*v + (1-b2)*g2`) with no rescaling, while `_adam.py:192` builds ν from `g*g` on the aggregate. `_second_moment.py` (dpftrl) only calibrates noise; it applies no batch-size factor either. Nothing in the docs warns about a scale change: user-guide/optimizers.md:270-271 lists the two as adjacent rows of a 'when to use which' table, and _adam.py:29-33 calls them 'alternatives... pick one per training run'. `examples/train_dp_ftrl.py` uses the same `--learning-rate` with and without `--second-moment`. `test_adam.py::TestSecondMomentMode` feeds `sq_grads = grads**2` (a B=1 stand-in), so it structurally cannot catch the scale difference. Same unrescaled substitution appears in _rmsprop.py, _ademamix.py and _adadelta.py:151-163.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A user follows the docs table and switches from `adamw(lr=1.5e-4, noise_bias_correction=True)` to `adamw(lr=1.5e-4)` fed by `clipped_grad(..., normalize_by=batch_size, second_moment=True)` + `mf_gaussian_noise(..., second_moment_strategy=...)`. The ν EMA now tracks (1/B)Σgᵢ² ≈ E[g²] instead of ḡ², and since E[g²]/ḡ² grows with the within-batch gradient variance (up to B), the Adam denominator √ν grows by up to √B and the effective step shrinks accordingly. Simulated at B=256, d=4096, C=1 with the documented normalize_by=B: RMS(update) is 1.000 for the squared-aggregate branch versus 0.061 (weak shared signal), 0.27 (moderate) and 0.59 (strong) for the private-g² branch — i.e. up to a 16× effective-LR *drop*, so the run silently under-trains rather than diverging. The user sees a worse loss curve and attributes it to the extra privacy budget spent on the second stream rather than to an untuned LR.
verification.refutation: Not refuted, but the reporter's direction and number are wrong for the documented configuration. Their measured '10.35× larger update' reproduces only with normalize_by=1 (raw sums) plus a strong shared signal; I measured ratio 9.39 in exactly that setting. With the flow the docs actually prescribe (`normalize_by=batch_size`, reference/optimizers.md:145-150), the SM branch makes updates ~1/√B *smaller*, not √B larger. The magnitude (~√B) and the root cause (no rescaling between a per-example and an aggregate second moment, presented as interchangeable) both hold; only the sign of the effect and the failure mode (under-training vs divergence) needed correcting.

verification.title: Adafactor's module docstring states `noise_bias_correction` "defaults to True", the signature defaults to False, and the argument doc justifies that default by citing `relative_step` — a feature the same file says is not implemented
verification.reasoning: All three quoted strings are verbatim in the file. _adafactor.py:30-31 says 'defaults to ``True`` so BC is on by default'; line 280 is `noise_bias_correction: bool = False`; lines 306-307 justify the False default with 'Adafactor's relative-step per-tensor normalization'; lines 41-42 list `relative_step` under 'Skipped', and lines 286-287 in the `lr` argument doc say outright 'we don't ship ``relative_step`` yet, so set an explicit LR'. There is no relative-step code in the file — `lr` goes straight into `make_optimizer_chain` at 339-345. The four doc references also check out (user-guide:67, 221, 265; reference:50). So the drift is exactly as described. Partial mitigation on the substance: Adafactor does ship a genuine self-normalizing mechanism (`update_rms_clip=1.0` baked into the moment scaler, _adafactor.py:277 and the 'do not stack' note at 340-342), so the *idea* that Adafactor per-tensor-normalizes is not fabricated — only the attribution to relative-step is.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A developer reading `_adafactor.py` (the module docstring is what you see opening the source; note `help(adafactor)` shows the *function* docstring, which states the correct `False` default) concludes BC is on by default, ships a DP run with `adafactor(...)` and `NoisedPytree` updates, and gets no bias correction at all — φ stays 0.0 for the entire run because `bc_active = noise_bias_correction and noise_stddev is not None` (line 195) is False. A second reader accepts 'relative-step normalization makes BC a no-op' (user-guide:265) as the reason Adafactor is the recommended DP default and never ablates BC, on the strength of a feature the same file says is unimplemented.
verification.refutation: Not refuted — the contradiction is real and verbatim. Downgraded from medium to low: there is zero runtime or privacy consequence, the *public* surface (`help(adafactor)`, the argument docstring, and user-guide/optimizers.md's 'BC default is off' text at line 252) all state the correct default, and the misleading sentence lives in a private module's module-level docstring. The reporter also overstated reachability by claiming it is 'help(adafactor)'s first paragraph' — it is not; help() renders the function docstring, which is correct.

survivors.title: Adadelta allocates `phi_dx` unconditionally (3× params of state even with BC off) and its memory claim relative to Adam is backwards
survivors.claim: `init_fn` allocates three full param-shaped pytrees (`v_g`, `v_dx`, `phi_dx`) regardless of `noise_bias_correction`. The module docstring claims "Total: roughly 1.5× vanilla Adadelta's footprint — still less than Adam's ``m + v + φ``" (repeated verbatim at docs/user-guide/optimizers.md:400). Adam's `init_fn` (_adam.py:140-142) allocates exactly two param-shaped pytrees (`mu`, `nu`) plus a scalar `phi`. 3× params is strictly more than 2× params, not less. The non-DP user pays a 50% optimizer-state overhead for an EMA that is never advanced.
survivors.failure_scenario: A user picks `adadelta(...)` over `adamw(...)` on the docstring's memory argument for a 7B-parameter model in fp32: Adadelta reserves 84 GB of optimizer state (3 × 28 GB) versus AdamW's 56 GB (2 × 28 GB) — an extra 28 GB, and with `noise_bias_correction=False` the third buffer stays all-zeros for the entire run.
evidence: _adadelta.py:127-131  `v_g = tree_map(torch.zeros_like, params)` / `v_dx = tree_map(torch.zeros_like, params)` / `phi_dx = tree_map(torch.zeros_like, params)` — no `noise_bias_correction` guard

_adadelta.py:33-36  "Memory cost: ``2 · |params|`` tensors for the second moments (same as vanilla) plus one scalar/dict ``φ_g`` and one tensor ``φ_dx`` per leaf when BC is active.  Total: roughly 1.5× vanilla Adadelta's footprint — still less than Adam's ``m + v + φ``."
_adam.py:140-142  `mu = tree_map(torch.zeros_like, params); nu = tree_map(torch.zeros_like, params); return AdamState(mu=mu, nu=nu, phi=0.0, step=0)`
docs/user-guide/optimizers.md:400 repeats the claim
survivors.fix_sketch: Allocate `phi_dx = None` when `noise_bias_correction=False` (the walker already skips it in that branch), and correct both docstring and user guide: 3×|params| with BC on, 2×|params| with BC off, i.e. more than Adam's 2×|params| + O(1) when BC is on.

verification.title: Adadelta allocates `phi_dx` unconditionally (3× params of state even with BC off) and its memory claim relative to Adam is backwards
verification.reasoning: Both factual halves check out. _adadelta.py:127-131 allocates `v_g`, `v_dx` and `phi_dx` as three full param-shaped pytrees with no `noise_bias_correction` guard, while _adam.py:140-142 allocates `mu`, `nu` plus a scalar `phi=0.0`. So Adadelta is 3×|params| and Adam is 2×|params| + O(1), making the docstring's 'still less than Adam's ``m + v + φ``' (_adadelta.py:35-36, echoed at user-guide/optimizers.md:400) inverted. The '1.5× vanilla Adadelta' half of the same sentence is correct. BUT the unconditional allocation is a deliberate, documented design decision, not an oversight: the `AdadeltaState` docstring (lines 79-83) says explicitly 'Carries both noise-variance EMAs (``phi_g``, ``phi_dx``) regardless of whether BC is active so the state shape is stable across calls and checkpoints don't depend on call history' — the identical rationale given for `AdamState.phi` at _adam.py:88-91. The reporter's fix sketch is also wrong on the code: `_walk_compute` (lines 199-220) recurses through `phi_dx_node[k]` at every dict level unconditionally, so `phi_dx=None` would raise, not 'already be skipped'.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A reader comparing optimizer memory footprints takes _adadelta.py:35-36 / user-guide:400 at face value and picks `adadelta` over `adamw` to save optimizer state. In fact Adadelta's `init_fn` reserves 3×|params| (v_g, v_dx, phi_dx) against AdamW's 2×|params| + one scalar — 50% more, not less. With `noise_bias_correction=False` the third buffer is provably dead weight: every write site for `phi_dx_new_t` is gated on `noise_bias_correction and noisy_squared_grads is None` (lines 277-289), so it stays all-zeros for the whole run and is still serialised into every checkpoint.
verification.refutation: Half-refuted. The 'allocates unconditionally' half is not a defect — it is an explicitly documented invariant (AdadeltaState docstring lines 79-83, matching AdamState's), so a maintainer would close that half as working-as-intended. What survives is a one-sentence docs error (the Adam comparison is backwards) plus a defensible-but-costly design tradeoff. Downgraded medium→low accordingly; the 7B/84GB framing is also unrealistic since Adadelta is a legacy, first-moment-free optimizer nobody runs at that scale, and the arithmetic there merely restates 3× vs 2×.

survivors.title: Schedule-free's claimed √n noise reduction is wrong by an order of magnitude: the averaged iterates are a cumulative sum, not independent
survivors.claim: Both docs assert "under DP, the per-step iterate noise is approximately independent (the gradient samples are independent), so Var[x_n] ≈ Var[z]/n" and "The published checkpoint has √n× less noise than the final iterate at the same privacy budget." The premise is false for the quantity being averaged. `z` is defined by `new_z = z + inner_update` (_schedule_free.py:162) — a running sum, so `z_1..z_n` are maximally correlated, not independent. For a driftless random walk, Var[x_n] = (1/n²)Σ_s (n−s+1)²σ² ≈ nσ²/3 = Var[z_n]/3, a constant-factor reduction independent of n.
survivors.failure_scenario: A practitioner budgets ε on the strength of this claim: at n = 500 steps the docs promise √500 ≈ 22× lower checkpoint noise. Monte-Carlo over 4000 trials of the exact averaging rule gives Var[x_n]/Var[z_n] = 0.335 (√ratio 1.73×), versus the claimed 1/n = 0.002. The claim overstates the utility win by ~13× in standard deviation.
evidence: docs/reference/optimizers.md:184-190  "When per-step iterate noise is approximately independent, `Var[x_n] ≈ Var[z]/n`"
docs/user-guide/optimizers.md:421-424  "$$\\text{Var}[x_n] \\approx \\frac{\\text{Var}[z]}{n}$$ ... The published checkpoint has $\\sqrt{n}\\times$ less noise than the final iterate"
_schedule_free.py:162  `new_z = tree_map(lambda z, du: z + du, state.z, inner_update)` — z is a cumulative sum of the per-step updates, so successive z's are not independent
Monte-Carlo (n=500, 4000 trials) of `z=cumsum(eta); x=cumsum(z)/arange(1,n+1)`: `Var[z_n] = 500.40  Var[x_n] = 167.81  ratio = 0.335` vs claimed `1/n = 0.002`
survivors.fix_sketch: Replace the claim with the correct asymptotic for Polyak-Ruppert averaging of a correlated iterate sequence (a constant-factor variance reduction, ≈1/3 for a driftless walk), or drop the quantitative statement entirely and keep only the qualitative "averaging reduces iterate noise".

verification.title: Schedule-free's claimed √n noise reduction is wrong by an order of magnitude: the averaged iterates are a cumulative sum, not independent
verification.reasoning: The code facts are right: _schedule_free.py:162 is `new_z = tree_map(lambda z, du: z + du, state.z, inner_update)` — z is a running sum — and lines 176-181 make x the uniform running average of those z's, so z_1..z_n are strongly correlated and 'the per-step iterate noise is approximately independent' is not a correct description of what is being averaged. Var[x_n] ≈ Var[z]/n does not follow from independence of the per-step gradient noise, and the reporter's random-walk arithmetic (ratio → 1/3) is right *for a driftless walk*. However, the conclusion the docs state is the classical Polyak–Ruppert asymptotic (Polyak & Juditsky 1992): for a mean-reverting iterate process — which SGD near a minimum is, an OU process with correlation time τ ≈ 1/(ηλ) — Var[x_n] ≈ 2τ·Var[z]/n, i.e. genuine 1/n scaling once n ≫ τ. A driftless random walk is precisely the regime in which averaging cannot help, and it is not the regime Polyak–Ruppert averaging is deployed in. So the docs' *derivation* is wrong and the constant is missing, but the headline scaling is the textbook result, not an order-of-magnitude error. I also could not reproduce the reporter's quote from reference/optimizers.md: lines 184-190 hedge with 'When per-step iterate noise is approximately independent' and say 'significantly lower noise', never '√n×'. Only user-guide/optimizers.md:415-425 states the unhedged √n claim.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A practitioner reads user-guide/optimizers.md:415-425 ('the per-step iterate noise is approximately independent (the gradient samples are independent), so Var[x_n] ≈ Var[z]/n ... √n× less noise') and expects a ~22× noise reduction on the published checkpoint at n=500 steps. The stated justification is invalid — `_schedule_free.py:162` makes z a cumulative sum, so the averaged sequence is autocorrelated — and the actual reduction depends on the iterate mixing time τ ≈ 1/(η·λ). In the pre-asymptotic regime n ≲ τ (small LR, flat curvature — common in DP fine-tuning) the reduction collapses toward the random-walk bound of ≈1.7× in standard deviation rather than 22×. The docs give no condition under which the √n figure applies, so the reader has no way to tell which regime they are in.
verification.refutation: Downgraded medium→low and CONFIRMED→PLAUSIBLE. The reporter's proposed correction ('a constant-factor variance reduction, ≈1/3, independent of n') is itself wrong as a general statement — it holds only for the driftless random walk they simulated, and asserting it as the fix would replace one over-claim with another. The defect that survives is doc imprecision: a wrong justification and a quantitative figure stated without its mixing-time condition. No code, no privacy accounting, and no default depends on it (`affects_epsilon: false` is correct; nothing in the repo derives ε or a step count from this sentence), and the reference-page wording is already hedged.

survivors.title: `_schedule_free.py` documents a `get_eval_params` accessor that does not exist anywhere in the repo

survivors.title: `update_rms_clip` is a global cross-leaf RMS in the chain but a per-tensor RMS inside Adafactor, so the same knob name means two different algorithms and one large tensor rescales the whole model
survivors.claim: `_rms_clip_transform` concatenates every tensor leaf, computes one parameter-count-weighted RMS, and divides *all* leaves by `max(1, rms/threshold)`. Adafactor's built-in clip under the identically named `update_rms_clip` argument computes `rms = update.pow(2).mean().sqrt()` per leaf inside the flat loop and scales each leaf independently (_adafactor.py:241-243). Both are described to the user with the same sentence ("divides the moment-scaled update by ``max(1, rms / threshold)``") and _adam.py:11-15 attributes the global variant to Wortsman et al., whose StableAdamW rule is defined and universally implemented per parameter tensor. Because the global RMS is parameter-count weighted, it is effectively the RMS of the largest tensor.
survivors.failure_scenario: `adamw(lr=1e-3, update_rms_clip=1.0)` on a model with a 50M-element embedding whose moment-scaled update RMS is 3.0 and a 1k-element LayerNorm bias whose update RMS is 0.4. The global RMS is ≈3.0 (dominated by the embedding), so the LayerNorm bias is divided by 3 even though it was already inside the threshold — StableAdamW would have left it untouched. Combined with finding #1, a single blown-up BC coordinate (|u| = 2243 among 2e5) pushes the global RMS to 5.0 and rescales every parameter in the model by 1/5.
evidence: _chain.py:61-73  `sq_sum = torch.zeros((), dtype=torch.float64); count = 0; for leaf in _iter_leaves(updates): sq_sum = sq_sum + leaf...pow(2).sum(); count += leaf.numel()` ... `scale = torch.clamp(rms / threshold, min=1.0)` ... `clipped = tree_map(lambda u: u / scale_f, updates)`
_adafactor.py:241-243  `rms = update.pow(2).mean().sqrt(); scale = torch.clamp(rms / update_rms_clip, min=1.0); new_grads.append(update / scale)` — inside the per-leaf loop
_adam.py:11-15  "**StableAdamW RMS clip** — constructor knob ``update_rms_clip`` ... See Wortsman et al., \"Stable and low-precision training for large-scale vision-language models\" (2023)."
_adam.py:321-323  "``rms`` is the global root-mean-square over all tensor leaves."
survivors.fix_sketch: Make `_rms_clip_transform` per-leaf to match Adafactor and the cited paper (or expose `update_rms_clip_scope="global"|"per_tensor"` defaulting to per-tensor), and add a test with two leaves of very different RMS asserting the small-RMS leaf is untouched.

verification.title: `update_rms_clip` is a global cross-leaf RMS in the chain but a per-tensor RMS inside Adafactor, so the same knob name means two different algorithms and one large tensor rescales the whole model
verification.reasoning: The code difference is real and I confirmed both halves. `_rms_clip_transform` (_chain.py:61-73) accumulates `sq_sum` over every leaf, divides by the total `count` of elements, and applies one scalar `scale_f` to the whole pytree via `tree_map` — a parameter-count-weighted global RMS, exactly as claimed. `_adafactor.py:241-243` computes `rms = update.pow(2).mean().sqrt()` per leaf inside the flat loop. Wortsman et al.'s StableAdamW rule is indeed per parameter tensor, so the chain deviates from the paper it cites at _adam.py:11-15. BUT the reporter's central complaint — that the user cannot tell the two apart — is contradicted by the code they themselves quote: _adam.py:322-323 states "``rms`` is the global root-mean-square over all tensor leaves", so the primary entry point documents the global scope explicitly. And _adafactor.py:336-344 carries a deliberate comment ("NB: do not stack the chain-level ``update_rms_clip`` on top of Adafactor's built-in RMS clip") and passes `update_rms_clip=None` into `make_optimizer_chain` — the divergence is a considered design decision, not an accident. What survives is a genuine paper-fidelity gap plus a doc gap on the secondary factories (_rmsprop.py:214-215 and _adadelta.py:341 say "StableAdamW-style RMS clip" with no scope note; _radam.py:319-320 likewise omits "global"). Marked PLAUSIBLE rather than CONFIRMED because whether the global scope is a defect or an intended choice is a judgement call the maintainer has arguably already made; severity dropped to low because the effect is a conservative down-scaling that never inflates any update, is off by default (`update_rms_clip: float | None = None` at _adam.py:279/306), and touches no privacy accounting.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: `adamw(lr=1e-3, update_rms_clip=1.0)` on a model with a 50M-element embedding whose moment-scaled update RMS is 3.0 and a 1k-element LayerNorm bias whose update RMS is 0.4: the count-weighted global RMS is ~3.0, so `scale_f` ~3.0 is applied to every leaf and the LayerNorm bias — already well under threshold — is shrunk 3x. Reference StableAdamW would leave it untouched. This behaviour is documented at _adam.py:322-323 but not at _radam.py:319, _rmsprop.py:214, or _adadelta.py:341, and no test pins it: TestStableAdamW::test_clip_bounds_update_rms (test_adam.py:509-524) only asserts the clipped update has smaller total norm than the unclipped one, and test_no_clip_below_threshold (line 526-535) uses a below-threshold case — both pass unchanged under a per-tensor implementation.
verification.refutation: Partly refuted: the claim that the global scope is undisclosed is false for the flagship factory — _adam.py:322-323 says "``rms`` is the global root-mean-square over all tensor leaves" — and the Adafactor divergence is explicit and deliberate (_adafactor.py:336-344 comment plus `update_rms_clip=None` passed to the chain). Also note the clip can only shrink updates (`torch.clamp(rms/threshold, min=1.0)`), so no instability or blow-up follows from it; and the knob defaults to None, so no default configuration is affected.

verification.title: The tests that name the BC floor, the BC checkpoint round-trip, and the Adagrad runaway fix are all vacuous — they pass identically with the feature removed
verification.reasoning: I checked all four tests plus the code they exercise. Two of the three sub-claims hold outright, one is materially overstated. (a) OVERSTATED: test_adam.py:269-280 (and test_rmsprop.py:144-154, test_adagrad.py:140-153) do use sigma=1e6/1e3 so `corrected < 0` on every coordinate, but the floor is `denom = torch.where(corrected > 0, corrected, v_hat).sqrt() + eps` (_adam.py:238 and :253-254). Delete the `torch.where` guard alone and `corrected.sqrt()` on a negative tensor yields NaN, so `assert torch.isfinite(...)` FAILS — the test does defend the exact guard its docstring names. It is only 'vacuous' if you delete the subtraction and the floor together, which is tautological. What is fair: the intermediate regime 0 < v_hat - phi_hat << phi_hat is untested. (b) CONFIRMED: test_state_dict.py:91-105 and :58-65 both build `adamw(lr=1e-3)`; `noise_bias_correction` defaults to False (_adam.py:308), and test_adam.py:281-289 proves phi stays 0.0 in that mode, so `assert restored[0].phi == pytest.approx(state[0].phi)` is 0.0 == 0.0. `grep -n noise_bias_correction packages/opaque-optimizers/tests/test_state_dict.py` returns nothing — no BC state, scalar or PerGroup, is ever round-tripped in the whole package. (c) CONFIRMED: test_adagrad.py:115-138 feeds all-zero gradients and adagrad's `weight_decay` defaults to 0.0 (_adagrad.py:175), so the update is identically 0 and `assert torch.all(updates[k].abs() < 1e-3)` holds with or without the Phi_acc correction. (d) CONFIRMED: no test in any package constructs an Opaque optimizer with a callable LR — the only non-numeric `lr=` hits repo-wide are torch's own `SGD([p], lr=BASE_LR)` in two scheduler tests — so the `scale_by_neg_lr(schedule)` branch of `make_optimizer_chain` is exercised only by torchopt's upstream suite. Severity lowered from medium to low: these are coverage gaps, not user-visible defects; nothing here misbehaves at runtime.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A maintainer refactors the DP bias-correction path and silently breaks (i) serialization of `AdamState.phi` / `AdagradState.phi_acc`, or (ii) the Adagrad `v_acc - Phi_acc` subtraction, and the suite stays green: test_state_dict.py:91-105 and :58-65 compare phi=0.0 to phi=0.0 because they construct `adamw(lr=1e-3)` with BC defaulted off, and test_adagrad.py:115-138 asserts |update| < 1e-3 on inputs where the update is exactly zero by construction (zero grads, weight_decay=0.0). Likewise a checkpoint saved mid-run with a callable LR schedule has no test anywhere. The one claim that does NOT hold: deleting the `torch.where(corrected > 0, corrected, v_hat)` floor from _adam.py:238/253 DOES turn test_bc_floor_keeps_denom_positive red (NaN fails the isfinite assertion).
verification.refutation: Sub-claim (1) is refuted in part: the sigma=1e6 floor tests are not vacuous with respect to the floor — removing only the `torch.where` fallback at _adam.py:238 / :253-254 (or the equivalent in rmsprop/adagrad) produces sqrt of a negative tensor, NaN updates, and a failing `assert torch.isfinite(...)`. They are correctly named and do their stated job; the legitimate criticism is narrower (the 0 < v_hat - phi_hat << phi_hat regime is untested). Sub-claims (2), (3) and (4) stand as written.

survivors.title: TR-DPO writes per-example private reference logprobs to the shared temp dir on every run under a nonce key that guarantees the file is never read again
survivors.claim: `_setup_tr_dpo` states "The seed is therefore not cached (a per-run nonce in the cache key)", but `compute_ref_logprobs_for_dataset` has no write-suppression path: on a MISS it *always* calls `_save_cache` (line 242-246), and the nonce only guarantees the resulting file can never be re-read. So every TR-DPO run persists two `.safetensors` files (train + eval) containing one float per example per column — a per-record function of the private training data — into `tempfile.gettempdir()/opaque_ref_cache` with the process umask, and each is dead on arrival. There is no eviction, so the directory accumulates one such pair per TR-DPO run indefinitely.
survivors.failure_scenario: A user runs DPO with `sync_ref_model=True` on a 50k-pair private preference dataset, on a shared multi-user GPU box. Each invocation writes `/tmp/opaque_ref_cache/<random-sha>.safetensors` holding 50k `ref_chosen_logps` + 50k `ref_rejected_logps` — per-record statistics of the private corpus — readable by every other user on the machine, and never reused by anything because the fingerprint embeds `uuid.uuid4().hex`. Ten runs leave 20 such files behind. The trainer's own docstring tells a reviewer no file was written.

_dpo_trainer.py:592 — `nonce = ("trdpo-seed", uuid.uuid4().hex)`; line 603 — `cache_key=nonce + suffix`; no `cache_dir` argument
_precompute.py:242-246 — `if is_main_process(): ... _save_cache(path, cpu_columns)` — unconditional on every MISS, with no opt-out parameter
_precompute.py:99-101 — default `cache_dir` is `tempfile.gettempdir()/opaque_ref_cache`
_precompute.py:148 — `os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(path), exist_ok=True)` — no mode restriction on the directory
survivors.fix_sketch: Add a `write_cache: bool = True` (or `cache_key=None` ⇒ no persistence) parameter to `compute_ref_logprobs_for_dataset` and have `_setup_tr_dpo` pass the no-persist form, which is what its docstring already claims. Independently, create the cache directory with mode 0o700 and write files 0o600 so the non-TR-DPO cache is not world-readable either.

verification.title: TR-DPO writes per-example private reference logprobs to the shared temp dir on every run under a nonce key that guarantees the file is never read again
verification.reasoning: The mechanism is exactly as described. `_setup_tr_dpo` (packages/opaque-transformers/src/opaque/api/transformers/trl/_dpo_trainer.py:566-606) builds `nonce = ("trdpo-seed", uuid.uuid4().hex)` at line 592 and passes `cache_key=nonce + suffix` into `compute_ref_logprobs_for_dataset` with no `cache_dir` override, once for train and once for eval. In packages/opaque-alignment/src/opaque/api/alignment/dpo/reference/_precompute.py the fingerprint folds `repr(cache_key)` into the SHA-256 (line 87), so the uuid guarantees a permanent MISS; the MISS path ends at `if is_main_process(): ... _save_cache(path, cpu_columns)` (lines 241-246) with no opt-out parameter in the signature (lines 159-168 — `cache_key` and `cache_dir` only, no `write_cache`). `_cache_path` defaults to `os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "opaque_ref_cache")` (lines 97-100) and `_save_cache` does a bare `os.makedirs(..., exist_ok=True)` with no mode (line 148). There is no eviction anywhere in the module. Reachability is via the public `args.sync_ref_model` (line 243, gated to non-PEFT at 272-274). Severity dropped from medium to low: `affects_epsilon: false` is correct — nothing here touches the accountant or the released model — the artefacts are two small files per run (2 x len(dataset) float32 = ~400 KB for 50k pairs), and the world-readable-tmp concern is a property of the intended cache path shared by every non-TR-DPO DPO run, not something TR-DPO introduces. The docstring is imprecise rather than false: "The seed is therefore not cached (a per-run nonce in the cache key)" is accurate about reuse and the parenthetical names the exact mechanism, so a reader who follows it lands on the truth.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A user runs `DPOTrainer` with `sync_ref_model=True` (TR-DPO) on a private 50k-pair preference dataset. Because `_dpo_trainer.py:592` mints a fresh `uuid.uuid4().hex` per process, `compute_ref_logprobs_for_dataset` always misses and `_precompute.py:241-246` unconditionally writes `<tmpdir>/opaque_ref_cache/<sha256>.safetensors` for the train split and another for eval, each containing one float per example per column (ref_chosen_logps, ref_rejected_logps) — a per-record statistic of the private corpus. The directory is created with the process umask (typically 0755) and the files at 0644, so on a shared multi-user box other local users can read them; the files can never be re-read by Opaque itself and are never evicted, so N TR-DPO runs leave 2N dead files (~400 KB each at 50k pairs) behind.

Impact is narrower than stated: no privacy-accounting effect, files are small, and the shared-tmp / permissive-mode exposure is inherited from the deliberate cache design used by every DPO precompute run, so it is not TR-DPO-specific. The docstring's "not cached (a per-run nonce in the cache key)" describes the reuse semantics correctly and discloses the nonce mechanism, so the claim that it 'tells a reviewer no file was written' is the reporter's reading, not the text's assertion.

survivors.title: Alignment metric modules document their outputs as "not for release" while both shipped trainers publish their un-noised batch means every step
survivors.claim: Four separate docstrings in the metric surface assert that these tensors are "private internal state", "intended for logging/accumulation, not for release", and that being `detach()`-ed is what makes them safe. Detaching only blocks the autograd path; it says nothing about disclosure. Every one of these quantities is in fact released: `DPTrainer._training_step` means each per-example aux tensor into `metrics["loss_aux"]`, and `logs.update(step_result.get("loss_aux", {}))` forwards them into `self.log(...)` — i.e. stdout, TensorBoard, W&B — with no noise and no accounting. `rewards/accuracies` in particular is the batch mean of `1[chosen_logratio > rejected_logratio]`, a direct per-record indicator whose batch mean is released every step alongside `loss`, `grad_norm` and `clip_rate`. The engine's own comment (_dp_trainer.py:2014) is honest about this — "Same un-noised diagnostic posture as the logged `loss` mean above" — so the alignment-side docstrings are the ones that mislead.
survivors.failure_scenario: A reviewer reads `opaque.alignment.metric`'s "not for release" and `reward_metrics`' "private internal state" and concludes the telemetry stays inside the process. In reality, training a DP-DPO model with the default `log_completion_metrics=True` and `report_to=["wandb"]` streams `rewards/chosen`, `rewards/rejected`, `rewards/accuracies`, `rewards/margins`, `logps/chosen`, `logps/rejected`, `entropy` and `mean_token_accuracy` — all exact, un-noised functions of the private batch — to a third-party service once per step, outside the epsilon that the accountant reports.

It does: with the default `log_completion_metrics=True` and any `report_to` backend, `DPTrainer._training_step` means each per-example aux tensor (`_dp_trainer.py:2016-2018`) and `_maybe_log_save_evaluate` merges the dict into the log row (`_dp_trainer.py:3730`), so `rewards/chosen|rejected|accuracies|margins`, `logps/*`, `entropy` and `mean_token_accuracy` — exact, un-noised functions of the private batch — are emitted once per logging step alongside `loss`. The consequence is a misleading docstring, not a broken mechanism: the same un-noised posture already applies to the logged `loss`, and the accountant's epsilon is unaffected.
verification.refutation: Not refuted, but downgraded from medium to low: the claim is purely about docstring wording. No code path is wrong, the behaviour is an explicitly commented deliberate choice (_dp_trainer.py:2014), `detach()` is truthfully described with respect to gradients, and epsilon accounting is untouched. The fix is a four-line docstring edit.

survivors.title: README claims every public loss is NaN-injection verified; the family-wide sweep only checks gradient finiteness and 11 of 14 DPO heads have no locality test
survivors.claim: The README's headline DP invariant reads "Every public per-example loss is Tier 1 — strict per-example, NaN-injection verified (a single-record swap moves only that row's gradient)." The only family-wide test, `tests/dpo/loss/test_vmap_safety.py`, does not inject NaN at all — it draws `torch.randn(4)` and asserts `torch.isfinite(g_chosen).all()`, which is a smoke test for vmap composition, not a locality proof. Grepping the package's tests, actual NaN-injection locality assertions exist in exactly five files: `test_hinge.py:110`, `test_discopop.py:93`, `test_squarechipo.py:99`, `test_nll.py:205`, `test_dft.py:267`. The remaining 11 shipped DPO heads (`sigmoid`, `robust`, `ipo`, `simpo`, `chosen_nll`, `apo_zero`, `apo_down`, `exo`, `nca`, `bco`, `sppo`) plus `odds_ratio_loss` and all five log-ratio combinators (`f_divergence_remap`/`_logits`, `mpo_combine`, `wpo_weights`, `ld_dpo_split`) have none. `test_sweep_covers_full_family` guards only that new variants join the *finiteness* sweep, so a future head with a cross-example aggregate would pass CI.
survivors.failure_scenario: A contributor adds a head that normalises by a batch statistic (e.g. `chosen - chosen.mean()`), registers it in `dpo/loss/__init__.__all__`, and adds it to `_VARIANTS`. `test_dpo_loss_vmap_grad_finite` passes (the gradients are finite) and `test_sweep_covers_full_family` passes (the name is in the list). Nothing in the suite notices that one record's data now moves every other record's gradient, and the README continues to advertise the invariant as verified.
