verification.title: All 33 TRL-compatibility tests are gated behind an extra that CI never installs
verification.reasoning: The mechanics check out exactly. test_compat_trl_dpo.py:8 and test_compat_trl_sft.py:10 both `pytest.importorskip("trl")`; `grep -c 'def test'` gives 16 and 17. trl is declared only at packages/opaque-transformers/pyproject.toml:36 under `[project.optional-dependencies]`, and uv.lock:2503 pins it with `marker = "extra == 'trl'"`. The root `all` extra (pyproject.toml:50-54) expands to opaque[auditing,dpftrl,alignment,transformers] and `transformers` is `["opaque-transformers", "opaque-patches[transformers]"]` — no `[trl]`. The dev group (pyproject.toml:117-128) has pytest/ruff/scipy/dp-accounting/riskcal, no trl. ci.yml:99 and pr.yml:148,200 all run `uv sync --group dev --all-packages --extra all`; `--all-packages` selects workspace members, it does not enable members' optional extras. No workflow mentions trl. The local .venv has no trl either (`import trl` -> ModuleNotFoundError). So both modules skip everywhere and from_trl (only implementation users: _dpo_config.py / _sft_config.py) has zero executed coverage. What kills the severity is the reporter's chosen failure scenario: from_trl builds a kwargs dict and returns `cls(**converted)`, so every converted config passes through TrainingArguments.__post_init__, whose line 843-851 raises 'Set either privacy_noise_multiplier ... or privacy_target_epsilon; neither was provided' — and that raise IS covered by a test that runs, packages/opaque-transformers/tests/validation/test_dp_trainer.py:138-140 (`test_neither_set_raises`, no trl import). A silent noise=0 config is therefore not reachable by dropping a check in _dpo_convert.py; __post_init__ also rejects nm<0 (l.875-880) and nm=0 with a finite clip disabled (l.896-901).
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A refactor of packages/opaque-transformers/src/opaque/api/transformers/trl/_dpo_convert.py or _sft_convert.py mistranslates a *non-DP* TRL field — e.g. stops mapping TRL's `sft` head to opaque's `chosen_nll`, drops `beta`/`label_smoothing`/`ld_alpha` passthrough, or stops raising on the rejected `padding_free` / `truncation_mode='keep_end'` / `aot` cases. All 33 assertions that would catch it live in the two importorskip'd modules, so every CI lane reports them as skipped and the regression merges. A user migrating an existing TRL pipeline silently trains against a different objective than their TRL config specified. The DP knobs themselves are not at risk: TrainingArguments.__post_init__ (_training_arguments.py:843-851) rejects a config with neither noise multiplier nor target epsilon, and that raise is exercised by tests/validation/test_dp_trainer.py:138.
verification.refutation: The 'non-private trainer that reports a valid-looking epsilon' half of the failure scenario is refuted: from_trl returns `cls(**converted)`, and TrainingArguments.__post_init__:843-851 unconditionally raises when both privacy_noise_multiplier and privacy_target_epsilon are None — a shared guard covered by a test that does run (tests/validation/test_dp_trainer.py:138 test_neither_set_raises). Severity medium -> low: the gap is real but its blast radius is TRL field-translation fidelity on an optional migration helper, not privacy loss.

survivors.title: The alignment DPO/SFT loss test suite is self-referential — 'hand-computed reference cases' recompute the implementation's own formula
survivors.line: 25-56 (and see evidence for the pattern across the suite)
survivors.claim: The 19 loss test modules under packages/opaque-alignment/tests/dpo/loss/ assert (a) output shape, (b) vmap(grad) finiteness, (c) NaN row-locality, and (d) 'hand-computed reference cases' that are literally the implementation's formula re-typed into the test. test_squarechipo.py's four numeric cases all evaluate `0.5*(sigmoid(beta*delta)-1)**2` — the non-private baseline the module actually ships — under a class docstring citing arXiv:2505.21395. test_chosen_nll.py:37 asserts `allclose(out, -chosen_logp)`, i.e. exactly the un-normalised implementation. test_f_divergence.py:99-101 computes `expected = torch.exp((alpha-1)*x)/(alpha-1)` and compares to `f_divergence_remap(...)`, which is that same expression. No alignment test compares any loss to TRL or to an independently derived value.
survivors.failure_scenario: The five already-identified loss defects (missing phi(u)=u+log u link and randomized-response term in SquareChiPO; missing 1/|y_c| normalisation in chosen_nll; inverted alpha in f_divergence; absolute vs completion-relative position axis in ld_dpo; wrong fp16 clamp in discopop) all ship with a green suite, because the suite's numeric oracles were derived from the code rather than from the papers. Worse, the suite now actively resists repair: fixing `_squarechipo.py` to the paper breaks test_squarechipo_delta_zero_beta_one / _large_negative_delta / _delta_one_beta_one, so a maintainer working the backlog sees 'my fix broke 4 tests' and is pushed to revert.
evidence: test_squarechipo.py:24-25 `class TestDpoSquarechipo: """Hand-computed reference cases for the SquareChiPO loss (arXiv:2505.21395)."""` followed by l.28 `"""Δ = 0, β = 1: 0.5 · (σ(0) − 1)² = 0.5 · (0.5 − 1)² = 0.125."""`
test_squarechipo.py:55-56 `sig = torch.sigmoid(torch.tensor(1.0)).item(); expected = 0.5 * (sig - 1.0) ** 2`
test_chosen_nll.py:37-38 `out = ...; assert torch.allclose(out, -chosen_logp, atol=1e-7)`
test_f_divergence.py:99-101 `out = f_divergence_remap(x, f_divergence_type="alpha_divergence", alpha=alpha); expected = torch.exp((alpha - 1) * x) / (alpha - 1)`
`grep -rn 'import trl|from trl' packages/opaque-alignment` -> no matches; no alignment test imports any external reference implementation
survivors.fix_sketch: For each loss with a TRL counterpart, add a parity test against `trl.trainer.dpo_trainer` at sigma=0 / C=inf on a fixed synthetic (chosen_logps, rejected_logps, ref_*) tuple (this is also the §19.4 gate the plan declares). For losses with no TRL counterpart, put the paper's equation in a module-level docstring with the exact constants and derive the expected values by hand from that equation, not from the code.

verification.title: The alignment DPO/SFT loss test suite is self-referential — 'hand-computed reference cases' recompute the implementation's own formula
verification.reasoning: The three cited examples are accurate. test_squarechipo.py:24-25 does carry the 'Hand-computed reference cases ... (arXiv:2505.21395)' docstring while every numeric case evaluates 0.5*(sigmoid(beta*delta)-1)**2, which is verbatim _squarechipo.py:57-58 (and its own module docstring). test_chosen_nll.py asserts allclose(out, -chosen_logp) against an implementation that is `return -chosen_logp`. test_f_divergence.py:99-101 computes exp((alpha-1)*x)/(alpha-1), which is _f_divergence.py:116 modulo the _cap_exp clamp (so the test does not even exercise the clamp). `grep -rn 'import trl|from trl' packages/opaque-alignment` is empty — no external parity oracle anywhere in the alignment suite. But the sweeping form of the claim ('the 19 loss test modules', 'the suite's numeric oracles were derived from the code') does not survive reading the rest: test_sigmoid.py:41-59 derives expectations independently as `math.log(2.0)` and `-math.log(1/(1+exp(-1)))` for the canonical Rafailov objective — hand arithmetic from the published equation, not a re-typing of the tensor code. So the real, narrower defect is 'the losses whose *formula itself* is disputed (squarechipo, chosen_nll normalisation, alpha-divergence convention, ld_dpo axis, discopop clamp) have no oracle independent of the code'. Also, 'the suite actively resists repair' overstates: pinned tests failing when you change behaviour is what pinned tests are for; the fix is to update the test with the paper equation in the same commit, which is normal practice, not a trap. Marked PLAUSIBLE rather than CONFIRMED because the claim's weight rests entirely on sibling findings that the cited papers specify different formulas — I cannot verify arXiv:2505.21395's equation from this repo, and if the shipped formula is correct the tests are simply ordinary regression pins.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: For the subset of heads whose formula is in dispute, the test oracle is the code: e.g. if squarechipo_loss is missing the paper's phi(u)=u+log u link, fixing packages/opaque-alignment/src/opaque/api/alignment/dpo/loss/_squarechipo.py breaks test_squarechipo_delta_zero_beta_one / _large_negative_delta / _delta_one_beta_one, all of which encode the current formula, so nothing in CI ever signalled the divergence in the first place. Same for chosen_nll (test asserts exactly `-chosen_logp`) and alpha-divergence (test asserts exactly `exp((alpha-1)x)/(alpha-1)`, and never crosses the _cap_exp(20.0) clamp so the clamp is untested). This is invisible-by-construction only for those heads; canonical heads such as sigmoid are pinned against independently hand-derived values (math.log(2.0) etc.) and would catch a formula change.
verification.refutation: Partly overstated. Not all 19 modules recompute the implementation: packages/opaque-alignment/tests/dpo/loss/test_sigmoid.py:41-59 derives its expectations from the published DPO equation using math.log, independent of the tensor code path. And a test failing when the implementation is deliberately changed is the intended behaviour of a regression pin, not evidence that the suite 'resists repair'. Severity medium -> low: this is a test-methodology improvement request, not a defect; it becomes material only if the sibling loss-formula findings are themselves confirmed.

survivors.title: Auditing has exactly two negative controls, both single-seed with order-of-magnitude-loose bounds; no Type-I / coverage test anywhere
survivors.claim: `test_no_privacy_leakage` draws 100 iid N(3,1) scores, calls the first 50 'in' and the last 50 'out', and asserts `eps < 0.5` at a single fixed `np.random.seed(42)`. `test_no_separation` (test_audit.py:97-101) feeds in_scores == out_scores == range(100) and asserts `eps < 1.0`. Those are the only two tests in the 1764-line auditing suite that exercise the null hypothesis. There is no test that repeats the null many times and checks that the fraction of runs reporting eps > 0 is at most the nominal `significance`. Additionally, every audit test builds its `CoinFlip` from the deterministic fixture `mask = [True]*n_in + [False]*n_out` (test_integration.py:18, test_audit.py:36, test_gdp.py:33, test_eps_delta.py:30), so no test ever runs the estimator against the random Bernoulli(1/2) membership the Steinke et al. one-run analysis assumes.
survivors.failure_scenario: The known post-hoc-threshold defect (`_estimate.py:130,137-139` selecting the default threshold using the secret membership labels) inflates the measured Type-I error to 4-5x nominal. Under this suite that is invisible: a single null draw at significance=0.05 that reports eps=0.3 satisfies `eps < 0.5`, and a run reporting eps=0.9 satisfies `eps < 1.0`. A correct auditor should report eps == 0 on the null with probability >= 1 - significance; nothing asserts that. The same blindness covers the rank-truncation defect (`_gdp.py:_MAX_EXACT_RANKS = 2000`, truncated ranks filled with v_k=0.5): the largest audit anywhere in the tests is m = 2000 canaries (test_audit.py:205, test_eps_delta.py:128), exactly at the boundary, so the truncation branch is never entered.
evidence: test_integration.py:66-75 `def test_no_privacy_leakage(): np.random.seed(42); scores = np.random.normal(loc=3.0, scale=1.0, size=100); ... assert eps < 0.5, "Should detect minimal leakage"`
test_audit.py:97-101 `def test_no_separation(self): scores = list(range(100)); estimate = _make_estimate(scores, scores); ... assert eps < 1.0`
test_integration.py:18 `mask = np.array([True] * n_in + [False] * n_out)` — identical helper duplicated in test_audit.py:36, test_gdp.py:33, test_eps_delta.py:30
packages/opaque-auditing/src/opaque/api/auditing/one_run/_gdp.py:37 `_MAX_EXACT_RANKS = 2000`; largest test m is `np.arange(1000,2000)` vs `np.arange(0,1000)` = 2000 canaries (test_audit.py:205)

survivors.fix_sketch: Add a Type-I calibration test: 200 independent null runs (scores iid, membership from the real `auditing.coin_flip`), assert that the empirical fraction with `eps_delta().epsilon_at(significance=0.05, delta=1e-5) > 0` is <= 0.05 plus binomial slack. verification.title: Auditing has exactly two negative controls, both single-seed with order-of-magnitude-loose bounds; no Type-I / coverage test anywhere
verification.reasoning: The headline claim holds. `grep -rn 'for _ in range|for seed in|for trial' packages/opaque-auditing/tests/auditing/*.py` returns nothing — there is no repeated-trial loop anywhere in the 1764-line suite, so no test checks that the fraction of null runs reporting eps>0 respects the nominal significance. The two cited controls exist verbatim (test_integration.py:66-75 asserts eps<0.5 at np.random.seed(42); test_audit.py:97-101 asserts eps<1.0 on identical score arrays). The truncation claim is confirmed and in fact stronger than stated: _MAX_EXACT_RANKS=2000 is used only in _gdp.py:306, `r` is always m (_estimate.py:_best_r_u returns `m` unconditionally), and the largest audit in test_gdp.py is 100 canaries (np.arange(50,100) vs np.arange(0,50), and the 100/100 null cases) — the m=2000 tests the reporter cites (test_audit.py:205, test_eps_delta.py:128) go through _eps_delta.py, which never touches the truncation code. So `n_trunc > 0` is never executed. Two sub-claims are wrong. (a) 'exactly two negative controls' undercounts: test_eps_delta.py:102 (eps<1.0 on arange(100) vs arange(100)), test_gdp.py:264-267 (beta_at(0.3) within 0.1 of 0.7) and test_gdp.py:281-284 (advantage<0.1) are also null-hypothesis controls — still all single-seed and loose, so the thrust survives. (b) 'no test ever runs the estimator against the random Bernoulli(1/2) membership' is false: test_audit.py:13-26 defines `_flip` with `in_mask = rng.random(n) < 0.5` and it is used at lines 337-352 and 353-361, and test_gradient_scores.py:295 runs the real `auditing.coin_flip(dataset, num_canaries=50, key=key(42))` end-to-end into one_run + epsilon_at. Also worth noting for prioritisation: the untested truncation branch fills v_k=0.5 for truncated ranks, and since v_k in [0,0.5] by construction (_gdp.py:317) that substitution inflates the expected correct-by-chance count, i.e. it is conservative (lower reported epsilon), so the missing coverage there is a soundness-of-tightness gap, not an over-reporting risk.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: Because _estimate.py:137-139 picks the default threshold by maximising (n_in - fn_counts) + tn_counts — a maximisation over the *true* membership labels — the order-statistics test's u is optimistically biased, so on a genuinely null run (in-scores and out-scores from the same distribution) the auditor can report eps>0 far more often than the nominal significance allows. survivors.title: Monte-Carlo amplification PLDs (balls-in-bins, b-min-sep) are validated only by smoke tests and an MC-vs-MC comparison at 10x the production sample budget
survivors.claim: `bnb_mc_pld` and `bandmf_b_min_sep_warm_mc_pld` produce the epsilon reported for the flagship DP-FTRL amplification mechanisms. Their Rust tests assert only `eps > 0.0 && eps.is_finite()`, monotonicity in noise, parameter rejection, and (for b-min-sep) that two internal code paths agree within 0.05. The only quantitative Python check, `test_pld_agrees_with_generic_bnb_mc`, compares one MC implementation to another MC implementation at `num_mc_samples=1_000_000` with a 10% relative tolerance. The production default is `num_mc_samples: 100_000` (discretization/config.rs:125,160) — 10x fewer samples, so ~3x larger MC standard error — and the only test at that budget, `test_factory_path_finite`, asserts `math.isfinite(eps) and eps > 0`. No test compares any MC epsilon to a closed-form or external reference, and none asserts the MC estimate is conservative (an upper bound), which a privacy accountant must be.
survivors.failure_scenario: A user calls `ftrl_acc.balls_in_bins(ftrl_acc.mf_gaussian(1.5, identity_strategy()), num_bins=32, n_steps=128).epsilon_at(1e-5)` at defaults. The returned value is a seed-dependent MC point estimate with no confidence correction; the two MC estimators of the same quantity are known (by the repo's own test) to disagree by up to 10% at 10x the sample budget, so at the default budget the reported epsilon can plausibly sit several percent *below* the true value. The accountant reports it as an exact number with no uncertainty. Nothing in CI would catch an MC estimator whose mean is biased low.

verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A user calls `ftrl_acc.balls_in_bins(ftrl_acc.mf_gaussian(1.5, identity_strategy()), num_bins=32, n_steps=128).epsilon_at(1e-5)` at package defaults (num_mc_samples=100_000, seed=42). survivors.title: Poisson sampler statistical tests admit a ~9% biased sample rate, and the q=1 test tolerates dropping 10% of the dataset
survivors.claim: `test_statistical_properties_mean` runs 100 steps over a 1000-example dataset at q=0.1 and asserts `abs(actual_mean - 100) < 10`. The standard error of that mean is sqrt(1000*0.1*0.9)/sqrt(100) = 0.95, so the tolerance is ~10.5 sigma and accepts any effective sample rate in roughly [0.091, 0.109]. `test_sample_rate_one` sets sample_rate=1.0 — every example must be included with probability 1, so every batch size must be exactly 100 — but asserts only `all(90 <= size <= 100)`.
survivors.failure_scenario: An off-by-one or dtype bug in the inclusion mask (for example `rand() <= q` vs `rand() < q` combined with a rounding path, or a rate rescaled by (n+1)/n) that shifts the realised inclusion probability from 0.100 to 0.108 passes both statistical tests and the variance test (expected var 90, tolerance +/-20). Accounting is then done at q=0.1 while the mechanism samples at q=0.108, so every reported epsilon under Poisson amplification is understated — the single most load-bearing parameter in DP-SGD accounting after sigma. Separately, if the q=1.0 path silently dropped ~5% of indices, `test_sample_rate_one` still passes while the mechanism no longer matches the unamplified Gaussian it is accounted as.

test_poisson.py:73-75 `expected_var = 1000 * 0.1 * (1 - 0.1); actual_var = np.var(batch_sizes); assert abs(actual_var - expected_var) < 20`
test_poisson.py:231-236 `sampler = PoissonSampler(dataset, sample_rate=1.0, n_steps=5, key=key(42)); batch_sizes = [...]; assert all(90 <= size <= 100 for size in batch_sizes)`
No test measures the per-example inclusion frequency across steps.
survivors.fix_sketch: Replace the mean check with a per-example inclusion-rate check: over N steps, count how often each index appears and assert the pooled inclusion frequency is within a binomial 5-sigma band of q (with n_steps large enough that the band is <1% wide). Change `test_sample_rate_one` to `assert all(size == 100 ...)`.

verification.title: Poisson sampler statistical tests admit a ~9% biased sample rate, and the q=1 test tolerates dropping 10% of the dataset
verification.reasoning: The arithmetic is right. test_poisson.py:47-60 asserts `abs(mean(batch_sizes) - 100) < 10` over 100 steps of a 1000-example dataset at q=0.1; the standard error of that mean is sqrt(1000*0.1*0.9)/sqrt(100) = 0.95, so the band is ~10.5 sigma and an effective rate of 0.108 (mean 108) passes. The variance test (:62-75, expected 90, tolerance +/-20) also passes at q=0.108 (var 96.3). test_poisson.py:231-236 does assert only `all(90 <= size <= 100)` at sample_rate=1.0. So the assertions are as loose as claimed. I downgraded severity because the blast radius depends on a bug that the implementation leaves almost no room for: _helpers.py:_plain_poisson_step_indices is three lines — `included = rng.random(num_examples) < sample_rate; indices = np.where(included)[0]` — with `sample_rate` passed through unmodified from the constructor (validated `0 < sample_rate <= 1`). The reporter's concrete hypotheses do not hold: `rand() <= q` vs `rand() < q` differs only on the probability-zero event u == q exactly, so it cannot shift the realised rate; and there is no rescaling code anywhere in the path to produce an (n+1)/n factor. The q=1.0 case is not a separate branch — numpy's `random()` returns values in [0, 1), so `< 1.0` is unconditionally true and every batch is exactly the full dataset; nothing 'silently drops 5% of indices'. This is therefore a genuine but low-value assertion-tightness gap, not a latent epsilon bug.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A future refactor of `_plain_poisson_step_indices` (e.g. adding a per-rank or truncation-aware rescaling of `sample_rate`, or switching to a Binomial draw of the batch count with a rounding step) that shifts the realised per-example inclusion probability from 0.100 to ~0.108 would pass test_statistical_properties_mean (mean 108, tolerance +/-10), test_statistical_properties_variance (var 96, tolerance +/-20) and every other test in the module, because none of them measures the per-example inclusion frequency. Accounting would still be done at the configured q=0.1 while the sampler realises q=0.108, understating reported epsilon. Today no such bug exists — the current implementation is a direct numpy Bernoulli mask on the configured rate — so this is regression-coverage risk only.
verification.refutation: The specific bug shapes the reporter offers are not reachable: `rng.random()` yields [0,1) so `<` vs `<=` is a measure-zero difference, and sample_rate=1.0 goes through the same `rand() < 1.0` mask, which is always True — batch size is deterministically the full dataset, so the loose `90 <= size <= 100` bound cannot be masking a dropped-index path.

survivors.title: Bounded Gaussian reports the nominal noise_stddev while its realised variance is strictly smaller, and DP-Adam/Adafactor bias correction subtracts the nominal value
survivors.claim: The same test module asserts both `output.noise_stddev == pytest.approx(1.0)` (the nominal nm*C) and `output.pytree.var().item() < 1.0` (the realised truncated-normal variance). `NoisedPytree.noise_stddev` is consumed by the optimizers' `noise_bias_correction` path, which maintains `phi = b2*phi + (1-b2)*noise_variance` and subtracts it from the second moment (`_adam.py:196` `effective_stddev = noise_stddev ...`, `:225-235` `nv = resolve_noise_variance(effective_stddev, path)`). No test in the repo feeds real `gaussian_noise(bound=...)` output into an optimizer; every optimizer bias-correction test constructs a synthetic `noised(grads, max_norm=1.0, noise_stddev=sigma)` with a hand-chosen sigma.
survivors.failure_scenario: `gaussian_noise(noise_multiplier=1.0, bound=2.0)` with C=1 produces noise whose true variance is ~0.77, not 1.0 (truncation at +/-2 sigma). Passing that `NoisedPytree` to `adam(noise_bias_correction=True)` makes phi converge to 1.0 while the actual noise contribution to E[g^2] is 0.77, so the debias over-subtracts by 0.23 on every leaf. `v_hat` is driven toward or below zero and the `torch.where(v_hat > 0, v_hat, m_hat*m_hat).clamp(min=bc_floor)` fallback at _adam.py:185 fires, silently replacing the second moment with `m_hat^2` — i.e. the optimizer degenerates to signSGD-like steps with no test detecting it.

verification.title: Bounded Gaussian reports the nominal noise_stddev while its realised variance is strictly smaller, and DP-Adam/Adafactor bias correction subtracts the nominal value
verification.reasoning: The factual core holds. _gaussian.py:_clipped_stddev returns `noise_multiplier * clipped.max_norm` regardless of `bound`, and `_sample` truncates/clamps to the interval, so the reported `noise_stddev` is the pre-truncation nominal sigma while the realised variance is smaller — I measured 0.7750 for nm=1.0, bound=2.0, C=1 (matching the reporter's 0.77), against a reported `noise_stddev` of 1.0. `bound` is reachable end-to-end: _training_arguments.py:457 documents `privacy_noise_mechanism_kwargs` and _dp_trainer.py:1355-1366 forwards `bound` into `gaussian_noise`, and the resulting NoisedPytree's `noise_stddev` is what optimizers consume. No optimizer test uses a real bounded noise_fn (`grep -rn 'bound=' packages/opaque-optimizers/tests` returns nothing). BUT the escalation is wrong. The `torch.where(v_hat > 0, v_hat, m_hat*m_hat).clamp(min=bc_floor)` at _adam.py:185 lives in the `noisy_squared_grads` (external second-moment stream) branch, which is mutually exclusive with `noise_stddev` (the constructor raises if both are passed, _adam.py:153-158). The actual noise_bias_correction branch is _adam.py:225-240 / :245-262 and guards over-subtraction with `corrected = v_hat - phi_hat; torch.where(corrected > 0, corrected, v_hat)` — when phi over-subtracts, it falls back to the *uncorrected* second moment, never to m_hat^2 and never to bc_floor. _adafactor.py:218-238 has the identical guard. I ran 200 Adam steps with noise_bias_correction=True on a 2000-element parameter at nm=1.0, C=1, true grad 0.3: unbounded gives mean|update| 0.105 with max 7.07, while bound=2.0 gives mean|update| 0.029 with max 1.15. The mismatch makes the correction *less* aggressive, not explosive — in the noise-dominated regime v_hat (~0.775 sigma^2 + signal) falls below phi_hat (~sigma^2), so the correction silently becomes a no-op.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A user sets `privacy_noise_mechanism_kwargs={'bound': 2.0}` with noise_multiplier=1.0 and clipping_norm=1.0 and an optimizer built with `adam(noise_bias_correction=True)`. The NoisedPytree reports noise_stddev=1.0 while the realised per-coordinate noise variance is ~0.775, so phi converges to 1.0 and over-subtracts by ~0.23 sigma^2. Because the BC branch falls back to the uncorrected second moment whenever `v_hat - phi_hat <= 0`, the practical outcome is that DP bias correction is silently disabled for most coordinates (measured: mean|update| 0.029 with bound=2.0 versus 0.105 unbounded over 200 steps), i.e. the feature the user enabled quietly does nothing rather than producing wrong-signed or exploding updates. No DP guarantee is affected; the cost is degraded convergence and a misleading `noise_std` training metric (_dp_trainer.py:1971 logs the nominal value). Note also that under `bound`, the truncation is applied around each coordinate's own value, so there is no single 'realised stddev' to report — it is data- and coordinate-dependent, which weakens the proposed fix of storing a closed-form truncated-normal std in the field.
verification.refutation: Downgraded from medium to low: the claimed collapse path is in the wrong code branch. _adam.py:185 (`m_hat*m_hat` fallback, bc_floor clamp) belongs to the `noisy_squared_grads` branch, which _adam.py:153-158 makes mutually exclusive with `noise_stddev`; the noise_bias_correction branch guards with `torch.where(corrected > 0, corrected, v_hat)` (and _adafactor.py:220-237 identically), falling back to the uncorrected second moment. Empirically, bounded noise under BC produces *smaller* updates than unbounded (mean 0.029 vs 0.105, max 1.15 vs 7.07 over 200 steps), so there is no signSGD degeneration and no v_hat -> 0 collapse.

survivors.title: `adaptive_clipped_grad` docstring claims it "automatically detects if distributed"; it does not, and the example labelled 'single-device or distributed' crashes under DDP
survivors.claim: The first worked example is headed 'Example (single-device or distributed):' and carries the inline comment '# (automatically detects if distributed!)'. The implementation contains no distributed detection whatsoever: `_grad_fn_impl` computes `num_clipped` and `clipping_rate` from purely local `grad_norms`, samples the fraction noise from `fold_in(state._rng_key, state._step)` and updates `_next_clipping_norm` locally. survivors.title: clip_pytree's stated formal guarantee ||output|| <= clipping_norm is violated by up to 0.32% in bfloat16 because the scale factor is downcast to the leaf dtype
survivors.line: 294-297 (and 157-160 for AUTO-S); guarantee stated at 127-132 and 232-233
survivors.claim: The clip scale `s = min(1, C/||g||)` is correctly computed in the promoted accumulation dtype (fp32 for bf16/fp16 inputs), but `scale_leaf` then applies it as `scale.to(dtype=t.dtype) * t`. For a bf16 leaf that rounds `s` to 8 mantissa bits (relative error up to 2^-9) and rounds every product again (another 2^-9), so the realized clipped norm can exceed `clipping_norm` by roughly (1 + 2^-9)^2 − 1 ≈ 0.39%. The docstring at 127-132 states 'Formal guarantee: For every input, the output has L2 norm at most R', and line 233 states 'DP-safe (the clipped output has norm <= clipping_norm)'. Neither holds at reduced precision. The accountant is calibrated to σ = nm·C, so the realized noise multiplier is nm/1.0032 — the mechanism is under-noised relative to its true sensitivity. docs/user-guide/precision.md:17-22 asserts the exact opposite invariant without noting this residual.
survivors.failure_scenario: bf16 training (the recipe recommended at docs/user-guide/precision.md:41-58, where `compute_dtype` is left at its safe default) with `clipping_norm=1.0` and `noise_multiplier=1.0`. Measured over 3000 random 1024-dim bf16 gradients, the worst-case post-clip L2 norm is 1.00320 — the true per-record sensitivity is 1.0032C, not C, so the effective noise multiplier is 0.9968 instead of the 1.0 the accountant is charged for. In fp16 the overshoot is 1.00042. Every reported ε is understated by the corresponding amount, silently and on every step.
evidence: _pytree.py:294-297 — `def scale_leaf(t): ... return scale.to(dtype=t.dtype) * t` (`scale` is fp32, `t.dtype` is bf16)
_pytree.py:127-132 — 'Formal guarantee: For every input, the output has L2 norm at most ``R``'
_pytree.py:232-233 — 'This is vmap-compatible and DP-safe (the clipped output has norm <= clipping_norm).'

Executed: 3000 trials of `clip_pytree({'w': randn(1024, dtype)*3}, 1.0)` then `global_norm(..., compute_dtype=float64)` → worst-case norm 1.0031985564786525 (bfloat16), 1.0004179916132927 (float16), 1.0 (float32)
packages/opaque-engine/tests/clipping/test_compute_dtype.py exercises the accumulation dtype but never asserts the post-clip norm bound at reduced precision
survivors.fix_sketch: Multiply by a scale guaranteed to round *down*: compute `s` in the accumulation dtype, then apply `torch.nextafter(s.to(t.dtype), zeros)` (or subtract 2 ulp) before the multiply; or perform the multiply in the accumulation dtype and round the *product* down to the leaf dtype. Alternatively divide the accountant's C by (1 + 2*eps(leaf_dtype)). Whichever is chosen, add a test asserting `global_norm(clipped, compute_dtype=float64) <= clipping_norm` for bf16/fp16 across randomized inputs, since the docstring states this as a formal guarantee.

survivors.title: _tensor_mf_noise redraws the full Gaussian vector every step, producing zero cross-step correlation — the defining property of matrix-factorization noise
survivors.claim: The MF mechanism requires a single i.i.d. vector sequence Z fixed across the whole run, with the noise at step t being `(C^-1 Z)_t = Σ_i (C^-1)_{t,i} z_i` reusing the *same* z_i at every step — that reuse is what makes the correlations cancel in the prefix sums. `_tensor_mf_noise` instead derives a fresh generator per step (`step_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, st._step_counter)`, line 242) and `_gaussian_linear_combination` draws a brand-new `torch.randn` for every non-zero coefficient in row t (line 168). The z_i at step t are therefore statistically independent of the z_i at step t−1. The per-step marginal variance `σ²·||row_t(C^-1)||²` is preserved, which is why the existing tests pass, but the mechanism degenerates to independent per-step Gaussian noise with a step-varying scale. This is the module's own documented 'engine that all strategy modules call' (docstring lines 9-10) and is the reference implementation exercised by ~20 tests, none of which assert any cross-step property.
survivors.failure_scenario: Call `_matrix_factorization_noise(grad_template, Cinv_dense, key=...)` with a dense lower-triangular `C^-1` and run n steps. Measured over 4000 independent runs with `C^-1 = tril(ones(3,3))` and σ=1: per-step std = [0.992, 1.427, 1.745] (matching the correct sqrt(1), sqrt(2), sqrt(3)), but corr(step 0, step 1) = 0.014 and corr(step 0, step 2) = 0.037, where the true MF mechanism requires 0.707 and 0.577. The prefix-sum error therefore grows as the DP-SGD random walk rather than being suppressed by the factorization, so all of DP-FTRL's utility advantage is silently lost on this path and the accountant's MF sensitivity no longer describes the released stream. The public `mf_gaussian_noise` path is unaffected (it always constructs a `StreamingMatrix`; verified corr(step 0, step 1) = −0.333 for `band_mf_strategy(bands=3)`), so the blast radius is the internal/reference path plus the missing test coverage.
evidence: _engine.py:242 — `step_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, st._step_counter)` — a *different* seed on every call

_engine.py:164-176 (`_gaussian_linear_combination`) — `for idx in range(first, last): ... noise = torch.randn(shape, ..., generator=generator); result = result + coef * noise` — z_i is regenerated from scratch inside the per-step generator
Contrast _lambda_cgd.py:220-227, which explicitly replays the *previous* step's key (`prev_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, step - 1)`) to reuse z_{t-1}; the dense path has no such replay
Executed (4000 runs, public path, band_mf_strategy(bands=3), n_steps=3): corr(0,1) = −0.3327 — the streaming path does carry genuine correlation

No test asserts cross-step correlation: packages/opaque-dpftrl/tests/matrix_factorization/test_noise_addition.py and tests/test_dp_ftrl.py check shapes, determinism, state advancement, and marginal scale only
survivors.fix_sketch: Derive the per-index keys from the *base* key rather than the step key — `generator_from_key(rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, idx))` inside `_gaussian_linear_combination` — so z_i is reproducible across steps, matching the λ-CGD replay convention. Then add a correlation test (empirical covariance of the noise sequence vs `σ² C^-1 (C^-1)^T`) that runs against both the dense and streaming engines; that test is what is missing today and is what would keep the streaming path honest under future refactors.

verification.title: _tensor_mf_noise redraws the full Gaussian vector every step, producing zero cross-step correlation — the defining property of matrix-factorization noise
verification.reasoning: The code claim is exactly right and I reproduced the measurement. _engine.py:242 derives `step_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, st._step_counter)` per call, and _gaussian_linear_combination (_engine.py:144-177) draws a fresh `torch.randn` per non-zero coefficient inside that per-step generator, so z_i at step t is independent of z_i at step t-1. Running _matrix_factorization_noise with a dense C^-1 = tril(ones(3,3)), sigma=1, 4000 runs gives per-step std [0.9925, 1.4273, 1.7453] (correct marginals sqrt(1),sqrt(2),sqrt(3)) but corr(0,1)=0.014, corr(0,2)=0.037 where true MF requires 0.707 and 0.577. However the blast radius is essentially nil: `_tensor_mf_noise` is only entered when `noising` is a dense torch.Tensor, and every public entry point passes a StreamingMatrix. mf_gaussian_noise -> _make_raw_mf_noise (_mf_gaussian_noise.py:229-248) either takes the LambdaCgd branch or calls `strategy.streaming_matrix(...)` and hands that to _matrix_factorization_noise; the second-moment path (_second_moment.py:78-90) also goes through _make_raw_mf_noise. Grepping the whole repo, the only other callers of _matrix_factorization_noise are tests, and the only tests that pass a dense tensor use torch.eye (test_dp_ftrl.py:139, test_noise_addition.py:18,26) - diagonal matrices, for which the missing cross-step reuse is a no-op. There is no documented extension point that reaches it either: MfStrategy.streaming_matrix is typed to return StreamingMatrix, MfStrategy is not mentioned anywhere in docs/, and docs/tutorials/extending_opaque.ipynb (referenced by .github/workflows/pr.yml:232) does not exist. So this is a latent bug in an internal, test-only path plus a genuine gap in test coverage (no test asserts any cross-step covariance on either engine), not a defect any user can hit. One nuance the report gets wrong in the safe direction: if the dense path ever were reached, `affects_epsilon: false` is not obviously right - the released stream would no longer be a post-processing of Cx+z, so the MF sensitivity analysis would not describe it and the epsilon could move in either direction.

survivors.title: AdaClip accounting assumes σ_b = expected_batch_size × fraction_noise_std, but the implementation noises a rate computed with the realized batch size
survivors.claim: `_sample_noisy_clipping_rate` adds `N(0, fraction_noise_std²)` to `clipping_rate = num_clipped / batch_size`, where `batch_size = norms.numel()` is the *realized* Poisson batch size (_clipped_fun.py:569,586). The released quantity therefore carries noise `fraction_noise_std × B_realized` on the sensitivity-1 clipped count. The accountant hard-codes the *expected* batch size instead: `sigma_b = self.expected_batch_size * self.fraction_noise_std` (_adaclip.py:54 and 90), and `adaclip()` documents `expected_batch_size` as 'Data-independent batch size (sample_rate × dataset_size under Poisson sampling)'. On every step where the Poisson draw comes in below the mean, the realized noise on the quantile query is smaller than the accountant assumes, so the composed ε is understated. The effect is negligible at large batch sizes and severe at the small batch sizes typical of DP LLM fine-tuning.
survivors.failure_scenario: DP fine-tuning with `sample_rate` giving `expected_batch_size = 8` (a realistic LoRA/PEFT setting), `fraction_noise_std=0.05` (the default), `noise_multiplier=1.0`. The accountant is built as `adaclip(gaussian(1.0), expected_batch_size=8)` and computes `effective_noise_multiplier = 0.6247`. On a step where the Poisson draw yields B = 4 (P(B ≤ 4) ≈ 10% for Binomial with mean 8), the realized σ_b is 0.05×4 = 0.2 instead of 0.4, and the true effective noise multiplier for that step is 0.3714 — 41% below what was charged. At expected_batch_size=32 with a realized batch of 16 the gap is 0.848 vs 0.9545 (11%); at 256 it is under 0.3% and immaterial.
evidence: _adaptive.py:103-114 — `def _sample_noisy_clipping_rate(clipping_rate, *, key, step, fraction_noise_std): ... noise = torch.randn(1, generator=generator).item() * fraction_noise_std; return clipping_rate + noise`
_clipped_fun.py:569,586 — `batch_size = norms.numel()` ; `rate = num_clipped / max(1.0, float(batch_size))` — realized, not expected
_adaclip.py:52-56 — `sigma_b = self.expected_batch_size * self.fraction_noise_std; s = _native.adaclip_sensitivity(nm, sigma_b, self.num_groups); return 1.0 / s`
_adaclip.py:110-112 — 'expected_batch_size: Data-independent batch size (sample_rate × dataset_size under Poisson sampling).'
The same mismatch applies to the per-group path (_adaptive.py:454-463), which likewise divides by the realized `batch_size`
survivors.fix_sketch: Make the released statistic match the accountant: pass the data-independent `expected_batch_size` into `adaptive_clipped_grad` and release `num_clipped / expected_batch_size + N(0, fraction_noise_std²)` (this is what Andrew et al. 2021 specify — the denominator is the constant m, not the realized draw). Alternatively scale the per-step noise as `fraction_noise_std * expected_batch_size / batch_size` so the absolute noise on the count is constant. Add a test pinning the realized absolute count-noise std against `AdaClip.effective_noise_multiplier` across a range of realized batch sizes.

verification.title: AdaClip accounting assumes σ_b = expected_batch_size × fraction_noise_std, but the implementation noises a rate computed with the realized batch size
verification.reasoning: Every link in the chain checks out in the code. (1) Release path: `_clipped_fun.py:568-586` sets `batch_size = norms.numel()` (the realized Poisson draw) and `rate = num_clipped / max(1.0, float(batch_size))`; `_adaptive.py:530` reads that `aux.clipping_rate` and `_sample_noisy_clipping_rate` (lines 103-114) adds `torch.randn(1)*fraction_noise_std` to it — a constant-std noise on the *ratio*, so the absolute noise on the count is `fraction_noise_std × B_realized`. The per-group path (`_adaptive.py:454-472`) and the distributed path (`_distributed.py:47,60,96`, which divides by the summed *realized* global batch) do the same. (2) Accounting path: `_adaclip.py:52-55` and `88-91` both use `sigma_b = self.expected_batch_size * self.fraction_noise_std`, fed to `adaclip_sensitivity` (adaclip.rs:30-35, z̃ = sqrt(1/z² + K/(4σ_b²))). (3) Reachability through the shipped trainer: `_dp_trainer.py:3925-3934` wraps the mechanism in `dpsgd_acc.adaclip(..., expected_batch_size=expected_batch_size)` whenever `clipping_mode == "adaptive"`, and `expected_batch_size = a.train_batch_size` with `sample_rate = expected_batch_size / dataset_size` (lines 1171, 1201) under Poisson sampling — so B fluctuates around the constant the accountant was given. No guard, no documentation of the discrepancy anywhere (docs/user-guide/clipping.md:229 and docs/user-guide/accounting.md:154 both just say `expected_batch_size = sample_rate * dataset_size`). I reproduced the reporter's numbers from the formula: nm=1.0, fns=0.05, m=8 → σ_b=0.4 → z̃=1.6008 → eff_nm=0.6247; B=4 → σ_b=0.2 → z̃=2.6926 → eff_nm=0.3714. Andrew et al. 2021 and tf-privacy's QuantileEstimatorQuery both normalize the noised count by a data-independent `expected_num_records`, which is exactly the fix sketched. Keeping medium: it is a genuine (if bounded) ε understatement on the quantile term only, immaterial at the batch sizes most DP-SGD runs use (<0.3% at m=256) and only material at small batches; the gradient term (1/z²) is untouched.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: `DPTrainer` with `clipping_mode="adaptive"` and Poisson sampling (the default sampler), `train_batch_size=8`, `noise_multiplier=1.0`. `_build_mechanism` constructs `adaclip(gaussian(1.0), expected_batch_size=8, num_groups=1)`, whose `effective_noise_multiplier` is 0.6247, and every step is charged at that rate. At runtime, `adaptive_clipped_grad` releases `num_clipped / B + N(0, 0.05²)` where B is the realized Poisson draw. On a step where B=4 (roughly 10% of steps at mean 8), the absolute noise on the sensitivity-≤1 clipped count is 0.05×4 = 0.2 rather than the charged 0.4, and the true per-step effective noise multiplier is 0.3714 — 41% below what was accounted. The composed ε over such steps is therefore an understatement rather than an upper bound. At train_batch_size=32 a realized B=16 gives 0.8480 vs the charged 0.9545 (11%); at 256 the gap is under 0.3%.

survivors.title: Accountant serialization crashes for any Budget that is not a dataclass, although Budget is a public Protocol that permits it
survivors.claim: `Budget` is exported as a structural Protocol (`_budgets.py:35-61`, re-exported in `opaque.api.accounting.core.types.__all__`) requiring only `value`, `name`, `decreasing`, `evaluate`. `Accountant.__init__` accepts any such object. But `_accountant_state_dict` serializes the budget via `dataclasses.fields(b)`, which raises `TypeError` for a non-dataclass, and `_deserialize_budget` looks the class name up in a closed `_BUDGET_REGISTRY` with no extension point, so even a custom dataclass budget serializes fine and then fails to load.
survivors.failure_scenario: A user defines `class TokenBudget: value=...; name=...; decreasing=True; def evaluate(self, p): ...` (satisfies the Protocol, not a dataclass) and passes it as `Accountant(budget=TokenBudget())`. Training runs; the first `save_model`/`_save_checkpoint` calls `_save_accountant` -> `state_dict(accountant)` -> `_accountant_state_dict` -> `dataclasses.fields(b)` -> `TypeError: fields() should be called on dataclass instances`, aborting the checkpoint mid-training. If instead the budget IS a custom dataclass, save succeeds and the later resume raises `ValueError: Unknown budget type: TokenBudget`, silently making the checkpoint unloadable.
evidence: _accountant.py:221-224 — `out["budget"] = {"type": type(b).__name__} | {f.name: getattr(b, f.name) for f in dataclasses.fields(b)}`
_accountant.py:235-250 — `_BUDGET_REGISTRY` is a hardcoded five-entry dict with no registration hook; `raise ValueError(f"Unknown budget type: {type_name}")`
_budgets.py:35-61 — `class Budget(Protocol)` with only four members; nothing requires a dataclass
opaque-accounting/.../core/types.py:29-36, 50-61 — `Budget` is re-exported in the public `types` surface
survivors.fix_sketch: Either narrow `Accountant.__init__` to reject budgets not in `_BUDGET_REGISTRY` at construction time (fail fast, not at checkpoint time), or add a `register_budget(cls, to_dict, from_dict)` hook and fall back to it when `dataclasses.is_dataclass(b)` is False.

verification.title: Accountant serialization crashes for any Budget that is not a dataclass, although Budget is a public Protocol that permits it
verification.reasoning: Both failure modes reproduce exactly as described. I ran them: `Accountant(budget=TokenBudget())` (plain class satisfying the four Protocol members) → `state_dict(acct)` → `TypeError: must be called with a dataclass type or instance` from `dataclasses.fields(b)` at `_accountant.py:221-224`; and a custom *dataclass* budget serializes to `{'budget': {'type': 'MyB', 'thr': 1.0}}` and then fails to load with `ValueError: Unknown budget type: MyB` from `_deserialize_budget` (`_accountant.py:235-250`), whose `_BUDGET_REGISTRY` is a closed five-entry dict with no registration hook. `Budget` is indeed a bare four-member Protocol (`_budgets.py:35-61`) re-exported from the public `types` surface, and `Accountant.__init__` (line 83) performs no validation. Where the reporter overstates: the failure is NOT reachable from the trainer. `DPTrainer` builds its accountant as bare `Accountant()` with no budget at all (`_dp_trainer.py:1347`), so `_save_accountant` → `state_dict` never emits a `budget` key and no checkpoint can abort this way; the trainer's own budget object (`cal.epsilon_budget(...)`, line 4017) is a registered `EpsilonBudget` used only for calibration. Reachability is limited to a user hand-rolling an `Accountant(budget=custom)` and serializing it themselves, and `Accountant.__init__`'s docstring already says the budget 'Should be a Budget from the budgets module'. Low severity is right — arguably it is a fail-fast/extension-point gap rather than a defect.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A user working with the accounting API directly (not via DPTrainer) defines `class TokenBudget:` with `value`, `name`, `decreasing`, `evaluate` — satisfying the exported `Budget` Protocol — and does `acct = Accountant(budget=TokenBudget()); json.dump(state_dict(acct), f)` to persist privacy provenance. The dump raises `TypeError: must be called with a dataclass type or instance` from `dataclasses.fields(b)` in `_accountant_state_dict`. If the custom budget is instead a dataclass, `state_dict` succeeds and writes `{"budget": {"type": "MyB", ...}}`, but the later `from_state_dict(Accountant(), ...)` raises `ValueError: Unknown budget type: MyB`, making the saved file unloadable. DPTrainer checkpoints are unaffected: the trainer constructs `Accountant()` with no budget.
verification.refutation: The stated scenario ('first save_model/_save_checkpoint ... aborting the checkpoint mid-training') is wrong — `_dp_trainer.py:1347` builds `Accountant()` with no budget, so the trainer never serializes a budget at all. The bug is real but only reachable through hand-written Accountant usage.

survivors.title: calibrate()'s cleanup docstring overstates what is released: every probe's Rust-backed Pld handle survives in the per-class lru_caches
survivors.claim: The docstring says native caches are cleared in `finally` "so calibration probes do not retain Rust-backed memory after the search completes". `_clear_all_native_caches()` only clears objects in the `NativeCache` weak registry (the b-min-sep transcript corpora). The `Pld` objects returned by each probe are held by the class-level `functools.lru_cache` on each `pld` implementation (maxsize 8, 16 on CachedProcess), which is never cleared — and lru_cache also keeps a strong reference to each probe's `self`. For the `prefix=` path this is deliberate (the prefix PLD is meant to be reused) but it is also never released.
survivors.failure_scenario: `calibrate(epsilon_budget(3.0, 1e-5), lambda nm: dpsgd_acc.poisson(dpsgd_acc.gaussian(nm), 0.01) * 1000, 0.1, 5.0, prefix=big_process)` over a fine grid: after the call returns, `Repeated.pld`, `Poisson.pld`, `Gaussian.pld` and `CachedProcess.pld` each still hold up to 8 (16) live Rust `Pld` handles plus their owning process objects — for a 1e-4-discretization 1000-step composition each PLD grid is tens of MB, so ~hundreds of MB stay resident across a sequence of calibrations even though the docstring promises the opposite.
evidence: calibration.py:151-153 — "Native LRU caches registered via :mod:`opaque.api.accounting.core._native_cache` are cleared in ``finally`` so calibration probes do not retain Rust-backed memory after the search completes"
calibration.py:251-252 — `finally: _clear_all_native_caches()`
_native_cache.py:38-41 — `_clear_all_native_caches` iterates only `_registry` (the `NativeCache` WeakSet); Pld lru_caches are not registered
_repeated.py:28 / _composed.py:25 / _cached.py:42 — `@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=8|16)` on `pld`, no `cache_clear` reachable from `calibrate`
survivors.fix_sketch: Either narrow the docstring to "registered NativeCache handles" (dropping the blanket "calibration probes do not retain Rust-backed memory" claim), or additionally call `.cache_clear()` on the `pld` wrappers of the process classes touched during the search (which pairs naturally with the invalidation registry needed for the `set_discretization` finding).

verification.title: calibrate()'s cleanup docstring overstates what is released: every probe's Rust-backed Pld handle survives in the per-class lru_caches
verification.reasoning: Verified by reading and by running. `calibration.py:251-252` calls only `_clear_all_native_caches()`, and `_native_cache.py:38-41` iterates only the `NativeCache` WeakSet registry — the `pld` LRU caches are not registered there. `@functools.lru_cache` sits on `pld` for every process class (`_repeated.py:28`, `_composed.py:25`, `_cached.py:42` maxsize=16, `_poisson.py:59`, `_gaussian.py:21`, `_adaclip.py:58`, `_per_step.py:50`, …) and holds strong references to both the returned native `Pld` (`Pld` is a type alias for the PyO3 `_native.Pld`, `_base.py:44`) and to `self`. survivors.title: MAX_LINEAR_FFT_SIZE guard is inert exactly for the PMFs that need it (zero tail budget), so the documented circular fallback never fires and the huge buffer is allocated anyway
survivors.claim: The fallback picks `fft_len = truncated_len.max(a.len()).next_power_of_two()`. When Chernoff truncation is disabled — `Pmf::self_compose` line 307-316 sets `bounds = (0, probs.len()*count - count)` whenever both tail budgets are 0 — `truncated_len == full_result_len`, so the "smaller circular buffer" is bit-identical to `alias_free_fft_len`, the very allocation the cap was added to avoid. Every MC-built PLD has zero tail budgets: `bnb_mc_pld` (monte_carlo.rs:346), `bnb_mc_pld_identity` (identity.rs:328) and `bandmf_b_min_sep_*` (mc.rs:319, 423) all return `PrivacyLossDistribution::new_asymmetric(...)` without calling `.with_tail_budgets(...)`, unlike the analytic constructors (gaussian.rs:36, poisson.rs:54, truncated_poisson.rs:90, parallel_poisson.rs:90).
survivors.failure_scenario: A user calls `bnb_pld * 1000` on a native `Pld` handle returned by `dp.bnb_mc_pld(...)` (the `Pld.__mul__` operator is public). A typical MC grid spans roughly [-3, 3.5] at discretization 1e-4, i.e. ~65,000 bins; `full_result_len = 65_000 * 1000 = 6.5e7` exceeds MAX_LINEAR_FFT_SIZE (3.36e7), so the code takes the "fallback" branch — but computes `fft_len = 6.5e7.next_power_of_two() = 1.34e8`, allocating ~1 GB for the real buffer plus ~1 GB for the complex spectrum, and OOMs on a typical machine instead of degrading to the bounded circular convolution the comment promises.
evidence: fft.rs:222-228: `let fft_len = if alias_free_fft_len <= MAX_LINEAR_FFT_SIZE { alias_free_fft_len } else { truncated_len.max(a.len()).next_power_of_two() };`
fft.rs:160-163: "Beyond this limit, we fall back to the smaller (circular) FFT buffer" — the buffer is not smaller when `bounds` is the full range

pld/pmf/dense.rs:305-316: `let use_chernoff = effective_right_budget > 0.0 || effective_left_budget > 0.0; let (lower_bound, upper_bound) = if use_chernoff { ... } else { (0, self.probs.len() * count - count) };`
monte_carlo.rs:346, identity.rs:328, mc.rs:319 and mc.rs:423 all construct the PLD without `.with_tail_budgets(...)`, unlike gaussian.rs:36 / poisson.rs:54
survivors.fix_sketch: When `alias_free_fft_len > MAX_LINEAR_FFT_SIZE` and no Chernoff bounds were supplied, either derive bounds from a default tail budget first, or cap `fft_len` at MAX_LINEAR_FFT_SIZE and account the resulting aliasing explicitly into `infinity_mass`. Alternatively set tail budgets on the MC-built PLDs so the Chernoff path engages.

verification.title: MAX_LINEAR_FFT_SIZE guard is inert exactly for the PMFs that need it (zero tail budget), so the documented circular fallback never fires and the huge buffer is allocated anyway

(b) Zero-budget PMFs are exactly the ones documented as not composable: `BallsInBins` says 'The returned PLD covers all n_steps... Do NOT compose externally' (_balls_in_bins.py:74-76), and the sanctioned `per_step(proc) * K` path overrides `repeated_pld` to call `_pld_at_horizon(K)` instead of `self_compose` (_per_step.py:67). verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A user takes a whole-process MC PLD — e.g. `ftrl_acc.balls_in_bins(...)` (or `_native.bnb_mc_pld_identity(...)` directly) whose PMF has ~118k bins and zero tail budgets — and self-composes it, which the public `DpProcess.__mul__`/`Pld.__mul__` operators permit even though the class docstring says not to. survivors.title: self_convolve_with_bounds truncates the composition count to u32 (and to i32 on the single-bin path) with no guard
survivors.claim: `*c = c.powu(count as u32)` and `a[0].powi(count as i32)` are truncating casts from `usize`. `PyPld::self_compose(count: usize)` accepts any Python int up to usize::MAX, so a count >= 2^32 silently computes a different exponent while `result_lower_loss_index = self.lower_loss_index * count as i64` (dense.rs:322) still uses the full count — producing an internally inconsistent PLD rather than an error. On the `a.len() == 1` short-circuit (which is the path taken by `eps_delta_pld` and `identity_pld`, whose PMFs have a single bin) the multi-gigabyte allocation that would otherwise OOM first is skipped, so the truncation is actually reachable there.
survivors.failure_scenario: `acc.eps_delta(1.0, 1e-6).pld().self_compose(2**31)`: the PMF has `probs = [1 - 1e-6]` (len 1), so line 212 returns `(1-1e-6).powi(2**31 as i32)`; `2**31 as i32` is -2147483648, so `powi` computes `(1-1e-6)^-2147483648`, i.e. a value vastly greater than 1 placed in probs[0]. The resulting `delta_at`/`epsilon_at` are meaningless numbers rather than an error or an overflow.

fft.rs:245: `*c = c.powu(count as u32);`

pld/pmf/dense.rs:322: `let result_lower_loss_index = self.lower_loss_index * count as i64 + lower_bound as i64;` uses the untruncated count

survivors.title: `_momentum_workload_coef` applies the learning-rate schedule along the Toeplitz lag axis, not the step axis, and its docstring states a workload that is not Toeplitz
survivors.claim: The docstring says "For momentum β and per-step learning rates η_t, the workload matrix W has entries W[t,s] = η_t · β^{t-s} for s ≤ t. The Toeplitz coefficients are [η_0, η_1·β, η_2·β², ...]." The second sentence does not follow from the first: a matrix with W[t,s] = η_t·β^{t−s} is not Toeplitz (its lag-k diagonal holds η_t·β^k, which varies with t), so it has no first column that determines it. What the code builds — `lr * base` = [η_0, η_1·β, η_2·β², …] used as a Toeplitz first column — is W'[t,s] = η_{t−s}·β^{t−s}, i.e. the schedule is indexed by the *lag* rather than by the row. This is what both BandMF and BLT use for schedule-aware coefficient tuning, and the transformers DP-FTRL trainer auto-injects the optimizer's schedule into it.
survivors.failure_scenario: `band_mf_strategy(bands=32, momentum=0.9, lr_schedule=cosine_schedule(...))` with a schedule decaying 1.0 → 0.0 over 1000 steps: the workload column becomes [1.0, 0.9·η_1, 0.81·η_2, …], whose tail is driven to ~0 by the cosine tail, so L-BFGS is told the workload has an effectively tiny bandwidth and returns coefficients tuned for a workload no optimizer realises. Privacy is unaffected (sensitivity is recomputed from the produced C) but the advertised "tighter privacy at the realised workload" is not delivered and the coefficients can be worse than the unweighted ones. The Rust side already implements the correct per-row weighting, so the two halves of the codebase disagree on what LR weighting means.

survivors.fix_sketch: Either optimise against the true non-Toeplitz momentum+schedule workload (as the Rust `*_gram_matrix_lr` routines do), or state plainly in the docstring that `lr_schedule` weights the lag axis and is equivalent to per-step LR weighting only for a constant schedule.

verification.title: `_momentum_workload_coef` applies the learning-rate schedule along the Toeplitz lag axis, not the step axis, and its docstring states a workload that is not Toeplitz
verification.reasoning: The docstring text is quoted accurately (_band_mf.py:36-38) and its two sentences are mutually inconsistent: W[t,s]=η_t·β^{t−s} has lag-k diagonal entries η_t·β^k that vary with t, so it is not Toeplitz and has no defining first column. What the code builds (lines 57-63: `base=[β^i]`, `return lr * base`) is used as a Toeplitz first column by `optimize_toeplitz(n_steps, bands, workload_coef=...)` (line 94, and _toeplitz.py:409-442), i.e. the realised workload is W'[t,s]=η_{t−s}·β^{t−s} — schedule indexed by lag. The same helper is imported by BLT (_blt.py:68), and _dpftrl.py:90-108 auto-injects the optimizer's schedule for `mf_band`/`mf_blt`, so the path is reachable by default from the HF trainer. Privacy is genuinely unaffected: `BandMfStrategy.sensitivity` is `coefs.norm()` recomputed from the produced C (_band_mf.py:133-135), independent of the workload used for tuning. Two corrections to the reporter's framing: (a) docs/mechanisms/dp-ftrl/band-mf.md:156 already states this caveat explicitly, so this is a docstring-accuracy gap, not an undiscovered defect — the fix is confined to the docstring (and to the overstated "tighter privacy at the realised workload" phrasing in _dpftrl.py:90-96); (b) the Rust `*_gram_matrix_lr` routines (bisr.rs:452-479, v[i] = lr_t · sum_acc) do weight per row, but they serve BnB Gram matrices for BISR/λCGD, a different mechanism family, and are themselves unreachable from Python (see finding 3) — calling this "the two halves of the codebase disagree" overstates it, since a Toeplitz optimiser structurally cannot represent a non-Toeplitz workload.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: `band_mf_strategy(bands=32, lr_schedule=cosine_schedule(...))` (default momentum=1.0, i.e. prefix-sum) materialises the workload column as the schedule itself, [η_0, η_1, …, η_{n−1}], so L-BFGS optimises against a workload that downweights long *lags* rather than late *steps* — a different matrix from the W_{t,s}=η_t·β^{t−s} the docstring claims and from what the optimizer actually realises. The resulting banded coefficients are tuned for the wrong workload; ε is unchanged (sensitivity is recomputed from the produced C via `coefs.norm()`), the cost is utility only. Note that for β<1 the effect shrinks: with β=0.9 the momentum decay already truncates the column well before a cosine tail matters, so the schedule is close to a no-op there — the mismatch bites hardest at momentum near 1.0.
verification.refutation: The reporter's "L-BFGS is told the workload has an effectively tiny bandwidth" only holds for momentum≈1; at their stated β=0.9 the β^i factor already dominates the cosine tail. The claim that the Rust side proves the codebase contradicts itself is also weak — the LR-weighted Rust routines belong to BISR/λCGD BnB accounting and are dead code from Python. The behaviour is documented (band-mf.md:156); this is docs drift in the docstring, not a numerical-correctness bug.

survivors.title: sync_object's callable field_op retry swallows TypeErrors raised from inside the callable, re-executing any collectives it already issued
survivors.claim: The arity probe `try: field_op(value, device) except TypeError: field_op(value)` cannot distinguish "this callable takes one argument" from "this callable raised TypeError internally". A documented-supported `fn(value, device)` that issues an all-reduce and then raises TypeError (e.g. on a `None` field) has its collective executed, then is invoked a second time and issues it again — two collectives on that rank versus one on every other. The public docstring at :155-164 advertises callable field_ops as a supported extension point.
survivors.failure_scenario: A user registers `field_ops={'clip_norm': my_reducer}` where `my_reducer(value, device)` calls `reduce_scalar(...)` and then does `float(value)`; on a step where `clip_norm` is None the `float(None)` raises TypeError *after* the reduce. `sync_object` retries with `my_reducer(value)`, issuing a second reduce. That rank has now made two collectives where its peers made one, desyncing the group with no error message pointing at the cause.
evidence: _state.py:191-195 — `if callable(field_op): try: result = field_op(value, device) except TypeError: result = field_op(value)`
_state.py:155-164 docstring — "``field_ops`` maps field name to ... a callable ``fn(value[, device]) -> float | int | None``" and "**Callable semantics:** invoked on the raw field value (any type)"
No in-repo handler currently passes a callable field_op, so this is latent rather than active
survivors.fix_sketch: Resolve arity once with `inspect.signature` (or require a fixed two-argument signature) instead of catching TypeError, so an exception raised inside the callable propagates rather than triggering a re-invocation.

verification.title: sync_object's callable field_op retry swallows TypeErrors raised from inside the callable, re-executing any collectives it already issued
verification.reasoning: The code is exactly as quoted (_state.py:191-195): `try: result = field_op(value, device) except TypeError: result = field_op(value)`. A bare `except TypeError` around a call cannot separate an arity mismatch from a TypeError raised inside the body, so the pattern is real. Two facts shrink the blast radius below what the reporter implies. (1) The reporter's own example does not actually double-reduce: if the callable is `def my_reducer(value, device)` with two *required* parameters, the retry `field_op(value)` fails at argument binding before any body executes, so no second collective is issued — the user instead gets a confusing "missing 1 required positional argument" TypeError that masks the real `float(None)` error. The double-collective desync requires the callable to also accept a single-argument call, i.e. `def my_reducer(value, device=None)` or `*args` — which the docstring's `fn(value[, device])` signature does invite. (2) Reachability is narrower than "public API": `sync_object` is in `_state.__all__` but is NOT re-exported from `opaque.api.engine.distributed` or from `opaque.distributed` (whose `__all__` at packages/opaque-engine/src/opaque/distributed/__init__.py:31-48 omits it), so a user must import the private `_state` module to reach it — it appears in docs/user-guide/distributed.md:279 as a table entry only. No in-repo caller passes a callable field_op (dpsgd clipping `_distributed.py:85` and dpftrl `_distributed.py:92` pass only op strings), so this is latent.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A user imports the private `opaque.api.engine.distributed._state.sync_object` and passes `field_ops={'clip_norm': my_reducer}` where `my_reducer(value, device=None)` (device defaulted, as the documented `fn(value[, device])` signature invites) first calls `reduce_scalar(...)` and then does `float(value)`. On a step where the field is None, `float(None)` raises TypeError after the collective has been issued; the bare `except TypeError` retries with `my_reducer(value)`, which runs the body again and issues a second all-reduce — that rank makes two collectives where peers make one, hanging or desyncing the group with no error pointing at the cause. If instead `device` is a required positional parameter, no second collective happens; the retry raises an arity TypeError that masks the original error.
verification.refutation: The reporter's concrete example (`my_reducer(value, device)` with two required args) does not reproduce the desync — the retry raises TypeError at call binding before executing the body, so only one collective is issued. The bug needs a callable with a defaulted/variadic second parameter. Also, `sync_object` is not exported from `opaque.distributed`, so it is not the public extension point the finding describes, and no in-repo code passes a callable field_op.

survivors.title: Fused and eager loss twins disagree on the token-count divisor dtype under half precision
survivors.line: 70, 80 vs 115-116 (same pattern in _dft.py:81,103 vs 140-141 and logprob/_sequence.py:75,96 vs 154-155)
survivors.claim: `fused_nll_loss` is documented as "Mathematically `nll_loss(hidden_states @ lm_head_weight.T, labels)`" (and likewise for `fused_dft_loss` / `fused_sequence_logp`), but the two paths build the per-example divisor in different dtypes. Eager: `mask = (shifted_labels != -100).to(shifted_logits.dtype)` then `mask.sum(-1).clamp(min=1)` — a token count materialised in the *logits* dtype, i.e. bf16 or fp16 under autocast. Fused: `n_valid = (labels[..., 1:] != -100).sum(-1).clamp(min=1)` — an exact int64 count. bfloat16 carries 8 mantissa bits, so integers above 256 are quantised: near 3000 the representable spacing is 8, so a 2997-token example divides by 3000 on the eager path and by 2997 on the fused path.
survivors.failure_scenario: SFT on 4k-context data under `bf16=True`. An example with 2997 supervised tokens gets `loss_eager = sum / 3000.0` and `loss_fused = sum / 2997`, a 0.1% relative divergence that propagates identically into the per-example gradient. A parity test written to `atol=1e-10` between `nll_loss` and `fused_nll_loss` (the shape of tests/logprob/test_logprob.py:265-281, which only runs in fp64) will fail the moment it is extended to half precision, and any TRL-parity gate comparing the two paths will report a discrepancy whose cause is invisible from the docstrings.
evidence: _nll.py:70 — `mask = (shifted_labels != -100).to(shifted_logits.dtype)`; _nll.py:80 — `... / mask.sum(-1).clamp(min=1)`
_nll.py:115-116 — `n_valid = (labels[..., 1:] != -100).sum(-1).clamp(min=1); return ce_sum / n_valid`  (int64)
_dft.py:81 and :103 vs _dft.py:140-141 — identical split

logprob/_sequence.py:75 `target_mask = completion_mask[..., 1:].to(shifted_logits.dtype)` and :96 `logp / target_mask.sum(-1).clamp(min=1)` vs :154 `count = completion_mask[..., 1:].sum(-1).clamp(min=1)` (long, straight from the collator)
tests/logprob/test_logprob.py:250 — `_fused_logp_inputs(..., dtype=torch.float64)`; the CPU parity test never exercises half precision
survivors.fix_sketch: Compute the count in an exact integer dtype on the eager paths too: `denom = (shifted_labels != -100).sum(-1).clamp(min=1).to(shifted_logits.dtype)` — summing bools in int64 and casting the (small, exactly-representable) result, rather than casting first and summing in half. Then add a half-precision parity assertion between each fused/eager pair.

verification.title: Fused and eager loss twins disagree on the token-count divisor dtype under half precision
verification.reasoning: The dtype asymmetry is exactly as described and is reachable in the documented recipe. Eager: _nll.py:70 builds `mask = (shifted_labels != -100).to(shifted_logits.dtype)` and :80 divides by `mask.sum(-1).clamp(min=1)` — a token count whose *output* dtype is the logits dtype (PyTorch accumulates half reductions in fp32 but casts the result back), so under autocast it is bf16/fp16. Identical split in _dft.py:81 vs :103 and logprob/_sequence.py:75 vs :96. Fused: _nll.py:115-116 and _dft.py:139-141 compute `(labels[..., 1:] != -100).sum(-1)` on an int64 label tensor — an exact count; _sequence.py:154-155 counts on the raw `completion_mask`, which the collator emits as `torch.long` (sft/collator/_language_modeling.py:130 `torch.zeros((B, L), dtype=torch.long)`), so it is also exact in the real pipeline. Reachability: docs/user-guide/precision.md:41-49 documents bf16 autocast around the loss closure as the 'easiest path', and _fused_lce.py:52-56 shows the fused Triton path requires CUDA + fp16/bf16 — precisely the configuration where the eager divisor is quantised. The finding's arithmetic is off, though: bfloat16 has 8 bits of precision, so in [2048, 4096) the spacing is 16, not 8, and 3000 is not even representable — a 2997-token example divides by 2992 on the eager path (0.17% high-side error in the loss), not 3000. fp16 (11-bit precision) has spacing 2 there, so the error is ~0.03%. The blast radius is genuinely small: it is a per-example constant rescale of the loss and hence of the per-example gradient, and in the DP path those gradients are clipped to `max_norm` anyway; it does not touch epsilon. Also worth noting the eager numerator `(-logp * mask).sum(-1)` is itself accumulated to a half output, so the divisor is not the dominant precision term. Confirmed as a real inconsistency between two functions documented as mathematically equal, at low severity.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: SFT on 4k-context data inside `torch.autocast(device_type="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)` (the recipe in docs/user-guide/precision.md:41-49), with `opaque-alignment[patches]` installed so `lce_available()` is True. For an example with 2997 supervised tokens, `fused_nll_loss` divides the CE sum by the exact int 2997 while `nll_loss` divides by `mask.sum(-1)` rounded to the nearest bf16 value, 2992 — a ~0.17% relative divergence in the loss and in the resulting per-example gradient. The existing CPU parity test (tests/logprob/test_logprob.py:265-281, fp64) and the GPU one (:285-302, bf16 but only 9 tokens, well inside bf16's exactly-representable integer range) both stay green, so a fused/eager parity gate would only surface this once examples exceed 256 supervised tokens under half precision.

survivors.title: null_ref_context disables the policy's adapter when handed a PEFT ref_model, contradicting its own documented precondition
survivors.claim: The Row-1 guard is `if ref_model is not None and not _is_peft_model(ref_model)`, so it only short-circuits for a *non-PEFT* separate reference. When `ref_model` is itself a PEFT model and `model` is a PEFT policy without a `"ref"` adapter, control reaches Row 3 and enters `with_disabled_adapter(model)` — disabling the **policy**'s adapter for the block, even though the caller supplied an explicit separate reference. The inline comment at line 175 asserts the opposite precondition: "(ref_model is None here, established by the guard at Row 1.)" That is false; Row 1 establishes only `ref_model is None or _is_peft_model(ref_model)`. The documented dispatch table (lines 115-135) does not cover a PEFT `ref_model` at all.
survivors.failure_scenario: A user with a LoRA policy and a separately-trained LoRA reference writes `with null_ref_context(policy, ref_model=lora_ref): ref_logits = lora_ref(**batch)`. The context manager silently strips the *policy*'s adapter for the duration. If the same block also runs a policy forward (the natural reading of "turns model into its own reference"), that forward uses base weights instead of the adapted policy; on exit `_restore_adapters` re-enables it, so the corruption is confined to the block and leaves no trace. No in-repo caller hits this today — `_dpo_trainer.py:636` invokes `null_ref_context(ref_model)` with a single argument — so the defect is latent for external users of the public API.

survivors.title: `dropout=` and `batchify=` are silently ignored for any model family that is not in the registry
survivors.claim: `apply_transformers_model_patches` returns at line 126 when `detect_family` yields no `model_type` match and at line 134 when no apply function is registered — both *before* the `disable_dropout` block (147-154) and the PeftModel batchify block (156-170). survivors.failure_scenario: Train a model whose `config.model_type` is outside the 26 registered families (e.g. `qwen2_moe`, `starcoder2`, `stablelm`, or any locally-defined architecture registered with `AutoModel`). `apply_model_patches(model, compat=True)` returns having applied nothing model-level: `nn.Dropout` modules keep their configured `p`, and `PeftModel.forward` is never batchified. The run proceeds with dropout active under `vmap(..., randomness="same")`, i.e. one shared mask per microbatch, contradicting the documented "DP-SGD trains without dropout" contract, and the user sees no warning at default log level.

_router.py:129-134: `logger.debug(...)` ... `return`

verification.title: `dropout=` and `batchify=` are silently ignored for any model family that is not in the registry
verification.reasoning: The control flow is exactly as described. `apply_transformers_model_patches` (packages/opaque-patches/src/opaque/api/patches/transformers/_router.py:114-134) returns before the `disable_dropout` block (151-154) and the PeftModel batchify block (156-170) whenever `detect_family` yields a `model_type` with no registered apply fn. `disable_dropout` has exactly one call site (the router line 154), so nothing else zeroes dropout for an unregistered family — the TRL DPO trainer's `_disable_dropout_in_model` is a separate, DPO-only path. `_registry.detect_family` is a bare `config.model_type` lookup, so any architecture outside the 27 shipped families in patches/transformers/models/ hits this. Two corrections to the reporter's framing, both of which cap the severity at low: (1) The consequence is NOT silent training with a shared dropout mask. The engine vmaps with `randomness="same"` (packages/opaque-engine/src/opaque/api/engine/clipping/_clipped_fun.py:219 and :500), and functorch hard-errors on a random op with a batched tensor input under that mode — the repo's own docs say so: components/dropout.py:7-9 quotes the message, and tests/transformers/models/test_gpt2.py:26-30 says active dropout 'otherwise trips vmap's same randomness'. So the run fails loudly at the first training step rather than degrading quality or privacy. (2) The skip is a deliberate, tested behaviour at the dispatcher level: tests/transformers/test_public_factory.py:514 `test_unregistered_family_silently_skips`, and DPTrainer._apply_opaque_model_patches documents it (packages/opaque-transformers/src/opaque/api/transformers/trainer/_dp_trainer.py:658-661: 'When opaque doesn't recognise the model family it logs an info-level message'). What is genuinely wrong is the layering: `disable_dropout` and the PeftModel batchify are family-independent concerns sitting behind a family gate, so the info-level message under-states the consequence ('no model-level patches applied' does not tell the user their run is about to die on dropout).
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: Load a model whose `config.model_type` is outside the shipped family list (e.g. `starcoder2`, `stablelm`, `qwen2_moe`, or a locally-registered AutoModel architecture) whose config leaves any dropout non-zero, and train it with DPTrainer defaults (`use_compat_patches=True`). `apply_transformers_model_patches` returns at _router.py:126 after only a `logger.info` (invisible at the default WARNING level), so `disable_dropout` never runs and the `nn.Dropout` modules keep their configured `p`. The first optimizer step then dies inside `vmap(..., randomness="same")` with `RuntimeError: Vmap does not currently support same randomness with a batched tensor input`, a message that names neither the model, the dropout module, nor the `dropout=False` / `use_compat_patches` knobs. The same early return also skips the PeftModel batchify wrapper, so a PEFT-wrapped unregistered model additionally receives 1-D per-sample `input_ids` under vmap. Models whose dropout is already 0.0 (most modern LLM configs) are unaffected.
verification.refutation: Partially refuted on impact, not on existence: the claimed silent outcome ('one shared mask per microbatch', 'contradicting the DP-SGD trains without dropout contract') cannot happen — functorch's `check_randomness` rejects a batched random op under `randomness="same"`, which is precisely why components/dropout.py exists (its own docstring quotes that error). No epsilon or gradient-correctness consequence. The dispatcher-level skip is also deliberate and covered by test_public_factory.py:514 plus the DPTrainer docstring, so the only real defect is that two family-independent patches were placed behind the family gate and the log level under-sells the failure.

The fused kernel computes `F.linear(X, Wu)` with no bias term.
