verification.title: Fused LoRA MLP never checks `up_proj` for a bias, and checks the other two only after the fused kernel has already run
verification.reasoning: Code reading confirms both mechanical claims. packages/opaque-patches/src/opaque/api/patches/peft/components/mlp.py:68-91: `Opaque_LoRA_MLP.apply(...)` runs at line 68, and only afterwards do lines 86-89 check `gate_proj`/`down_proj` for a bias and bail to `original_forward(x)`; there is no `up_proj` branch. peft/_router.py:118-127 gates MLP fusion on `_has_lora` + `_no_lora_dropout` only, while the QKV gate at 84-95 additionally calls `_no_bias` on all three projections. kernels/lora.py:1103-1105 confirms the fused forward is `F.linear(X, Wu)` with no bias term. Two things materially shrink the blast radius the reporter claims. First, the silent-bias-loss path (up_proj biased while gate/down are not) is not reachable through any supported model: fusion only installs when the MLP class name (or an MRO ancestor) is one of the 17 entries in `_MLP_ACTIVATION_MAP`, and in every one of those HF implementations the bias flag is uniform across gate/up/down (Llama's single `config.mlp_bias` drives all three; Mistral/Qwen/Gemma/Olmo hardcode `bias=False`), so `gate_proj` always carries the bias too and line 86 catches it. Second, the reporter's suggested entry point is wrong: `register_activation_kind` (patches/transformers/_factory.py:111) feeds the transformers-side activation-kernel factory, not `_MLP_ACTIVATION_MAP`, which is private and has no registration API — a user cannot add a class to it without editing the module. What remains genuinely confirmed is the wasted work: on a legitimately biased MLP (e.g. a Llama-architecture checkpoint with `mlp_bias=True`) the fused kernel and its autograd node are built on every forward of every layer and then thrown away in favour of `original_forward`, doubling MLP forward FLOPs and transient activation memory.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: Fine-tune a Llama-architecture checkpoint that sets `config.mlp_bias=True` with LoRA on gate/up/down. `_auto_fuse_lora` installs the fused forward (it never checks for bias on the MLP path), so every MLP forward runs `Opaque_LoRA_MLP.apply` in full — three GEMMs plus the Triton activation, plus the autograd node and its saved gate/up/h tensors — then discards the result at mlp.py:86 and recomputes the whole MLP through PEFT's original forward. Result: ~2x MLP forward cost and a transient extra activation peak per layer, with correct numerics. The silent loss of the up-projection bias described in the finding requires a hand-built MLP whose class name matches `_MLP_ACTIVATION_MAP` but whose bias flags differ between up_proj and gate/down_proj; no HuggingFace model in the map can be configured that way.
verification.refutation: The numerical-correctness half is effectively unreachable: fusion is keyed on 17 hardcoded HF MLP class names, all of which set bias uniformly across gate/up/down, so the missing `up_proj` check is always shadowed by the `gate_proj` check at mlp.py:86. `register_activation_kind` (transformers/_factory.py:111) does not extend `_MLP_ACTIVATION_MAP` — that dict is private with no registration path — so the cited user-extension route does not exist. The finding survives only as a performance/dead-compute defect plus latent fragility, hence low.

verification.title: Lite LoRA backward vmap rules reshape dX to grad_out's shape, which only holds for square projections
verification.reasoning: The shape arithmetic checks out. `_lora_w_backward_lite` (kernels/lora.py:96-109) returns `dX.reshape(*batch_shape, W.shape[1])`, i.e. last dim = in_features; `_LoRAWBackwardLite.vmap` (194-200) then does `dX.reshape(grad_out.shape)` whose last dim is `W.shape[0]` = out_features, so the element counts differ whenever in_features != out_features. Identically, `_lora_qkv_backward_lite` returns last dim `Wq.shape[1]` (hidden) while `_LoRAQKVBackwardLite.vmap:546,569` reshapes to `grad_Q.shape` (last dim = Q output width). The non-lite siblings get this right — `_LoRAWBackward.vmap:148` reshapes to `X.shape` and `_LoRAQKVBackward.vmap:434` likewise — which is the tell that the lite rules are simply wrong rather than relying on some invariant. Why severity stays low: the lite rules only execute when `Opaque_LoRA_W/QKV.setup_context` sees `needs_weight_grads == False` (lora.py:249-252, 592-596), i.e. the LoRA A/B tensors do not require grad, AND the backward runs under vmap. In the canonical DP-SGD LoRA path that never happens: `torch.func.grad` marks the differentiated params (the LoRA weights) as requiring grad inside the transform level, so `.T`/`.to(dtype)`-derived A and B report `requires_grad=True` and the non-lite, correctly-reshaping path is taken. That is also why non-square projections (k_proj, v_proj, gate/up/down, all of which get `Opaque_LoRA_W` installed by peft/components/linear.py) do not blow up in normal use. The existing coverage misses it because tests/kernels/test_lora.py builds A/B without `requires_grad` (so it does hit the lite rule) but only with square HIDDEN x HIDDEN weights (`_kaiming_weight(HIDDEN, HIDDEN)`, `_make_qkv_weights`).
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: Take any configuration where the LoRA A/B tensors are NOT the differentiated parameters but per-sample gradients are still taken under vmap — e.g. calling the exported `opaque_lora_w` / `opaque_lora_qkv` (kernels/__init__.py:29-31) inside `vmap(grad(f))` over inputs with frozen adapters, or DP-training only a non-LoRA head on top of a frozen LoRA-adapted backbone. `Opaque_LoRA_W.setup_context` takes the `needs_weight_grads=False` branch, backward dispatches to `_LoRAWBackwardLite`, and its vmap rule computes dX of shape (vmap*batch, seq, in_features) then calls `dX.reshape(grad_out.shape)` with last dim out_features. For any non-square projection — k_proj (2048->512 on Llama-3.x GQA), gate/up (hidden->intermediate), down (intermediate->hidden), or a Gemma2-style q_proj (2304->2048) — this raises `RuntimeError: shape '[...]' is invalid for input of size N` from inside a vmap rule, with no mention of the layer or the real cause. It is a crash, not a silent wrong gradient.
verification.refutation: Not refuted — the reshape is unambiguously wrong. Severity held at low only because the lite backward is unreachable on the main DP-SGD LoRA path (functorch's `grad` sets requires_grad on the differentiated LoRA weights, so `setup_context` picks the non-lite rule at lora.py:249-252, which reshapes to `X.shape` correctly); if the lite rule were on the hot path, every GQA k_proj and every MLP projection would already be crashing. Also note the reporter under-states scope on one point: `Opaque_LoRA_W` is installed on every PEFT LoRA Linear (peft/components/linear.py:13-30), not just o_proj/q_proj, so the affected set is far wider than stated — but only within the frozen-adapter lite path.

survivors.title: Backward-side vmap rules assume batch dim 0 without validating `in_dims`, while their forward-side siblings explicitly raise
survivors.claim: `_LoRAWBackward.vmap`, `_LoRAQKVBackward.vmap` and `_LoRAMLPBackward.vmap` unpack `in_dims` into names that are then discarded (`_grad_Q_bdim`, `_X_bdim`) and unconditionally treat dim 0 as the vmap batch (`B_vmap = X.shape[0]`, `X.reshape(B_vmap, -1, hidden_dim)`). `Opaque_MoE.vmap`, `_MoEBackward.vmap`, `Opaque_FusedMoE.vmap` and `_FusedMoEBackward.vmap` do not read `in_dims` at all. The corresponding forward rules (`Opaque_LoRA_W.vmap` lora.py:265-272, `Opaque_RoPE.vmap`, `Opaque_RMSNorm.vmap` rms_norm.py:624-628, `_CrossEntropyBackward.vmap` cross_entropy.py:399-405) all raise on a non-zero or unexpected bdim, showing the authors consider the case reachable.
survivors.failure_scenario: If any of these rules is ever reached with a tensor whose batch dim is not 0 — functorch does not normalise bdims, they migrate as ops like `transpose`/`movedim` are applied — or with a mixture where one operand is unbatched (`bdim=None`) and another is batched, the per-sample reshape silently pairs sample i's activations with sample j's gradients and returns wrong per-example gradients with `out_dims=0`, which downstream clipping accepts without complaint. There is no assertion and no test that supplies a non-zero bdim.
evidence: kernels/lora.py:132-135: `grad_out_bdim, X_bdim, W_bdim, A_bdim, B_bdim, scaling_bdim = in_dims` then `B_vmap = X.shape[0]` — none of the unpacked dims is ever consulted
kernels/lora.py:401-404: `_grad_Q_bdim = in_dims[0]` / `_X_bdim = in_dims[3]` / `B_vmap = X.shape[0]`
kernels/moe.py:123-129: `def vmap(info, in_dims, grad_out, x, ...)` — `in_dims` unused
contrast kernels/lora.py:265-266: `if X_bdim != 0: raise ValueError(f"X should be batched at dim 0, got {X_bdim}")`
survivors.fix_sketch: Add the same `if bdim != 0: raise` / `if bdim is None: raise` validation to every backward-side and MoE vmap rule (or `movedim` the operands to 0 up front), and add a regression test that runs one of them under `vmap(..., in_dims=1)`.

verification.title: Backward-side vmap rules assume batch dim 0 without validating `in_dims`, while their forward-side siblings explicitly raise
verification.reasoning: The factual descriptions are accurate: `_LoRAWBackward.vmap` (lora.py:132-135), `_LoRAQKVBackward.vmap` (401-404) and `_LoRAMLPBackward.vmap` (873-876) unpack in_dims into discarded underscore-prefixed names and then hardcode `B_vmap = X.shape[0]` with `out_dims=0`; `Opaque_MoE.vmap` / `_MoEBackward.vmap` (moe.py:121-133, 154-158) and the fused_moe rules (fused_moe.py:322-341) never read in_dims at all. But reachability of a non-zero or None bdim is not established, and several things argue against it. (a) The library never constructs a non-zero in_dim: the only vmap call sites build `in_dims = tuple(0 if i in batch_argnums else None ...)` (_clipped_fun.py:405, used at :217/:498/:539). (b) functorch's batching rules overwhelmingly `moveBatchDimToFront`, so tensors flowing through transposes/reshapes arrive with bdim 0. (c) The strongest evidence is the reporter's own contrast: the forward-side rules (Opaque_LoRA_W.vmap:265-272, Opaque_RMSNorm, _CrossEntropyBackward) DO raise on bdim != 0 and they see the same tensors in the same call stacks in the CUDA test suite without firing — that is empirical evidence the invariant holds, not evidence the violation is reachable. (d) fused_moe.py:322 states the assumption as an explicit contract comment ('DP-SGD contract: grad_out/x/top_k batched at 0; shared weights unbatched'), so this is a documented precondition rather than an oversight. (e) Even if the precondition were violated, the claimed silent sample-mixing is unlikely: with a shifted or absent bdim the subsequent `X.reshape(B_vmap, -1, hidden)` / `grad_out.reshape(B_vmap, -1, out)` pair feeds `torch.bmm`, which would raise on mismatched batch/token counts except under exact size coincidences. So `affects_epsilon: true` is overstated. This is defensive-hardening debt, not a demonstrated defect.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: Reachable only outside the library's own driver: a caller who invokes the kernels directly under `torch.func.vmap(..., in_dims=1)` (or with a LoRA-layer input that is unbatched while its gradient is batched, e.g. a shared prefix/prompt tensor feeding a LoRA projection inside a per-sample grad). `_LoRAWBackward.vmap` then treats the wrong axis as the vmap batch, and because it returns `out_dims=0` unconditionally the mislabelled result is handed back to the clipper. In practice the mismatch surfaces first as a `RuntimeError` from the `torch.bmm` of `X_3d.transpose(-2,-1)` against `grad_out_Bt` (mismatched batch or token counts); silently wrong per-example gradients require the batch and token dimensions to coincide numerically. Through opaque's own API (DPTrainer / clipped_grad), in_dims are always 0 or None (_clipped_fun.py:405), so this cannot be triggered.
verification.refutation: Downgraded from an epsilon-affecting correctness bug to a hardening nit. The engine's only vmap call sites construct in_dims as 0/None (_clipped_fun.py:405); functorch normalises batch dims to the front for the ops on these paths; the sibling forward rules that assert bdim==0 run on the same tensors in the same tests and never fire, which is positive evidence the invariant holds; and fused_moe.py:322 documents the batched-at-0 contract explicitly. No code path through the public API reaches these rules with a non-zero bdim, and a violation would most likely raise from `torch.bmm` rather than silently corrupt per-sample gradients, so `affects_epsilon` should be false.

survivors.title: NEGATIVE: no canary construction or 'injection' exists -- coin_flip only subsets natural training rows, while the README advertises 'coin-flip canary injection'
survivors.claim: coin_flip() takes `dataset` solely for len(); it selects num_canaries existing row indices uniformly at random and flips a coin per index. Nothing is constructed, mislabelled, perturbed, or inserted. The package README describes the capability as 'coin-flip canary injection' in two places, and the package is otherwise faithful to Steinke et al. / Xiang et al., both of which rely on crafted canaries (mislabelled or out-of-distribution examples) to obtain the strong in/out separation their reported epsilon-hat values depend on. No canary-crafting utility exists anywhere in the repo (grep for 'canary' outside opaque-auditing returns only the two examples' --audit-canaries flags, which pass through to coin_flip).
survivors.failure_scenario: A maintainer reading 'coin-flip canary injection' expects the package to construct high-signal canaries. It does not: the canaries are ordinary in-distribution training rows, which for an LM fine-tune are nearly indistinguishable from held-out rows even without DP. The audit therefore reports eps-hat near 0 for every configuration, and a genuine under-noising bug -- e.g. an off-by-sqrt(W) noise scale -- produces no detectable separation, so the audit fails to falsify it. The result is a passing audit that carries no evidence.

_coin_flip.py:113-118  def coin_flip(dataset: Any, *, num_canaries: int, key: RngKey) -- dataset is used only at line 137 for len(dataset)
packages/opaque-auditing/README.md:4  'coin-flip canary injection'
packages/opaque-auditing/README.md:30  '- opaque.auditing.coin_flip() -- coin-flip canary injection'
docs/user-guide/auditing.md:16 does describe it accurately ('Randomly select m examples as canaries'), so only the README overstates
survivors.fix_sketch: Either ship a canary-crafting helper (random-token sequences, label flips, or gradient-space canaries as in Steinke et al. section 5) or correct the README to 'coin-flip canary partitioning' and document in the user guide that natural-example canaries yield a valid but very weak lower bound.

verification.title: NEGATIVE: no canary construction or 'injection' exists -- coin_flip only subsets natural training rows, while the README advertises 'coin-flip canary injection'
verification.reasoning: Verified _coin_flip.py:113-154. `dataset` is touched only at line 137 (`len(dataset)`); lines 143-146 do `rng.choice(dataset_size, size=num_canaries, replace=False)` and a per-index coin flip. Nothing is constructed, mislabelled, perturbed, or appended. `grep -rn canary` outside opaque-auditing returns only DataLoader/collate plumbing in docs and the three examples (train_dpsgd.py:1289-1307, train_sft.py:1582-1619, train_dpo.py:1968-2003) — all of which pass the natural HF training set straight into coin_flip. There is no canary-crafting helper anywhere in the repo. The README wording is confirmed at line 4 ('coin-flip canary injection') and line 30 ('opaque.auditing.coin_flip() — coin-flip canary injection'). The reporter is also right that the other docs are accurate: the coin_flip docstring (line 121, 'Randomly selects num_canaries examples from the dataset') and docs/user-guide/auditing.md:15 ('Randomly select m examples as canaries') both describe the real behaviour. So this is a README-only overstatement plus a genuinely absent capability, not a code bug. Two corrections to the reporter's framing: (a) loss_scores supports `reference_scores`, and examples/train_dpsgd.py:1317-1325 uses it, i.e. the implemented attack is exactly Steinke et al. Algorithm 3's loss-difference score — which the paper does evaluate with natural in-distribution canaries, so the setup is a legitimate (weak) variant, not a broken one; (b) a determined user can designate crafted canaries by constructing CoinFlip directly — it is exported via opaque.auditing.types and the tests build it by hand (test_integration.py:18-24) — but that requires setting the private `_in_mask` field and is undocumented, so 'no supported path' still holds.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A user reads packages/opaque-auditing/README.md:4 and :30 ('coin-flip canary injection') and expects coin_flip() to construct high-signal canaries (mislabelled, random-token, or gradient-space). It does not — it selects num_canaries ordinary training rows uniformly at random and flips a coin per row (_coin_flip.py:143-146). Natural in-distribution canaries give far weaker in/out separation than the crafted canaries the reported eps-hat values in Steinke et al. rely on, so the audit's power to falsify an under-noising bug is much lower than the README implies. It does not follow that eps-hat is 'near 0 for every configuration' — Algorithm 3 loss-difference scoring on natural canaries does produce non-trivial separation at high canary counts — but a user who takes a small eps-hat as evidence of correct noising is over-reading a low-power test, and there is no documented API for supplying stronger canaries (constructing CoinFlip by hand and setting the private _in_mask field is the only route).
verification.refutation: Not refuted, but scope-corrected: the code is faithful to its own docstring and to the user guide; only the README's two uses of the word 'injection' are wrong. The 'eps-hat near 0 for every configuration' and 'the audit carries no evidence' parts of the failure scenario are unsupported — the implemented score (loss(w0)-loss(wt), Algorithm 3) is the paper's own natural-canary variant, which the paper reports as valid though lower-power.

survivors.title: No key-domain separation between the auditing RNG namespace and the mechanism RNG namespace; the shipped example derives the coin flips and the step-1 DP noise from the identical folded key
survivors.claim: coin_flip derives canary selection from np.random.default_rng(key.seed) and the coin flips from np.random.default_rng(fold_in(key, 1).seed). Neither derivation carries a domain-separation tag. The DP-SGD noise stream uses rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, st._step_counter) with _step_counter starting at 0, so step 1 uses fold_in(key, 1) -- byte-identical key material to the coin flips. PoissonSampler uses np.random.default_rng(key.seed) -- byte-identical to the canary-selection stream, and both quick starts use key(42). The one-run theorem requires the coin vector S to be independent of the mechanism's internal randomness; deriving both from the same 64-bit value makes them deterministic functions of a single seed rather than independent.
survivors.failure_scenario: examples/train_dpsgd.py:1191 calls auditing.coin_flip(..., key=key(args.seed)) and lines 1689/1694 call gaussian_noise(..., key=key(args.seed)). The coin flips are numpy PCG64 seeded with fold_in(key(seed),1).seed; the step-1 Gaussian noise is a torch.Generator seeded with the same value mod 2**63-1. Likewise docs/user-guide/auditing.md uses coin_flip(..., key=key(42)) while the PoissonSampler docstring example uses PoissonSampler(dataset, sample_rate=0.01, key=key(42)) -- the same PCG64 stream. I measured no exploitable dependence (P(canary in batch 1) = 0.04988 under shared seed vs 0.04999 under independent seeds over 400 trials, i.e. within noise), because the two consumers draw from different generator families / consumption patterns. The defect is that nothing in the design guarantees this; a future change to either derivation (e.g. moving the coin flips to a torch generator) would silently correlate the audit's null hypothesis with the mechanism it is auditing.

survivors.fix_sketch: Derive both auditing streams through a string tag, e.g. fold_in(key, 'opaque.auditing.canary_select') and fold_in(key, 'opaque.auditing.coin_flip'), and document in the user guide that the audit key must be independent of the training key.

verification.title: No key-domain separation between the auditing RNG namespace and the mechanism RNG namespace; the shipped example derives the coin flips and the step-1 DP noise from the identical folded key
verification.reasoning: The central code fact checks out. _coin_flip.py:143 uses np.random.default_rng(key.seed) and :145 uses np.random.default_rng(fold_in(key, 1).seed) with no tag. _gaussian.py:236 initialises _step_counter=0 and :395 does step_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, st._step_counter), so the second noise step derives from fold_in(key, 1) — the same 64-bit blake2b output that seeds the coin flips. examples/train_dpsgd.py:1191 (coin_flip) and :1689/:1694 (gaussian_noise) both pass key(args.seed), so in the shipped example the key material really does coincide. fold_in does accept str tags (_engine.py:58-88) and the paired-stream path already uses constant folds (_gaussian.py:333-336), so domain separation is available and simply unused on the plain path. BUT the evidence is materially wrong on one point and the impact claim is unsupported: (a) the shipped example does NOT seed PoissonSampler with key(args.seed) — train_dpsgd.py:1739 uses `key=fold_in(key(args.seed), rank, epoch)`, so the canary-selection stream and the sampler stream are already separated in the real example; the collision only exists between two docstring quick-starts that both happen to use key(42). verification.corrected_failure_scenario: In examples/train_dpsgd.py the audit's coin vector is drawn from np.random.default_rng(fold_in(key(seed), 1).seed) while DP-SGD's second noise step (step_counter==1) draws from torch.Generator seeded fold_in(key(seed), 1).seed % (2**63-1) — the same key material, differing only in PRNG family. The exposure is forward-looking: because neither auditing stream carries a domain-separation tag, any future change that moves the coin flips onto a torch generator, or that makes gaussian_noise consume numpy, would silently make S a low-entropy deterministic image of the same value that drives the noise, invalidating the one-run theorem's independence premise with no test able to catch it. The docstring-level collision (coin_flip's canary selection and PoissonSampler both showing key(42)) is real but benign: it affects which rows are canaries, not the coin vector.

survivors.title: +inf membership scores corrupt the TPR/FPR denominators used by attack_auc and attack_beta_at
survivors.claim: thresholds is built as np.concatenate((union1d(in,out), [np.inf])) and counts use side='left', so a canary whose score is exactly +inf is never counted below any threshold, including the terminal +inf. Consequently fn_counts[-1] < n_in and tn_counts[-1] < n_out whenever any score is +inf, and _auc_from_counts / tp_counts / fp_counts normalise against those truncated totals instead of the true group sizes. (Unlike the NaN case this does not corrupt _best_r_u, which correctly treats a +inf in-score as a member guess at every threshold.)
survivors.failure_scenario: A bf16 model produces loss = +inf for 50 of 500 in-canaries, so loss_scores returns -inf for those; if the reference-score subtraction flips the sign convention (score = loss(w0) - loss(wt) with loss(w0) = +inf) the affected canaries end up at +inf. Measured on the real code: with 50 of 500 in-scores set to +inf, fn_counts[-1] = 450 instead of 500, and attack_auc returns 0.5379 where the true AUC including the 50 top-ranked canaries is ~0.585 -- the 50 strongest pieces of evidence are silently excluded from the AUC denominator. Symmetrically 50 +inf out-scores give tn_counts[-1] = 450 and AUC 0.5426.
evidence: _roc.py:46-47  unique_scores_sorted = np.union1d(in_scores, out_scores); thresholds = np.concatenate((unique_scores_sorted, [np.inf]))  -- +inf appears twice and nothing is strictly below it
_roc.py:52-53  fn_counts = np.searchsorted(in_sorted, thresholds, side='left'); tn_counts = np.searchsorted(out_sorted, thresholds, side='left')
_estimate.py:70-71  tp_counts = (fn_counts[-1] - fn_counts)[::-1]; fp_counts = (tn_counts[-1] - tn_counts)[::-1]
_estimate.py:307-308  tnr = tn_counts / tn_counts[-1]; fnr = fn_counts / fn_counts[-1]
Measured: 500/500 clean -> AUC 0.5393, fn[-1]=500. 50 +inf in-scores -> AUC 0.5379, fn[-1]=450. 50 +inf out-scores -> AUC 0.5426, tn[-1]=450.
survivors.fix_sketch: Use n_in / n_out (from the CoinFlip) as the TPR/FPR denominators instead of fn_counts[-1] / tn_counts[-1], and append np.nextafter(np.inf, 0) or use side='right' at the terminal threshold so +inf scores are counted.

verification.title: +inf membership scores corrupt the TPR/FPR denominators used by attack_auc and attack_beta_at
verification.reasoning: Reproduced against the real code. _roc.py:46-47 builds thresholds = concat(union1d(in,out), [inf]); when any score is +inf that value already appears in union1d, so inf is duplicated and no threshold is strictly greater than it. _roc.py:52-53 uses side='left', so searchsorted(sorted, inf, 'left') returns the count of values strictly below inf, i.e. fn_counts[-1] = n_in - (#+inf in-scores) and tn_counts[-1] = n_out - (#+inf out-scores). _estimate.py:70-71 and :307-308 then normalise against those truncated totals. I ran it in the repo venv (500 in ~ N(0.2,1), 500 out ~ N(0,1)): clean -> attack_auc 0.5843, fn[-1]=500, tn[-1]=500; 50 in-scores set to +inf -> 0.5794 with fn[-1]=450; 50 out-scores set to +inf -> 0.5902 with tn[-1]=450. The out-score direction is worse than the reporter stated: adding 50 maximally-false-positive out-scores makes the reported AUC go UP (0.5843 -> 0.5902) while the true concordance drops (0.5716 -> 0.5204). No guard exists: one_run only checks non-emptiness (_estimate.py:65-66) and split_scores only casts to float (_coin_flip.py:105-109), so nothing rejects non-finite scores. attack_beta_at is affected too, since tp_counts[-1]/fp_counts[-1] inherit the truncated totals via _estimate.py:70-71. The reporter's carve-out is also correct: _best_r_u (_estimate.py:137-139) uses self.n_in and self.n_out rather than the terminal counts, so epsilon is not affected — affects_epsilon: false stands. Severity stays low because reachability is narrow: -inf scores (the common overflow direction, since loss_scores returns -losses at _loss.py:113) are handled correctly; you need a +inf, which requires the reference-score path (_loss.py:124, scores = -loss(wt) - (-loss(w0)) = loss(w0) - loss(wt)) with an infinite loss at the *untrained* model w0 — e.g. bf16 overflow on the reference pass at examples/train_dpsgd.py:1319-1325.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A user follows the Algorithm 3 pattern (loss_scores with reference_scores, as in examples/train_dpsgd.py:1317-1325). The untrained model overflows in bf16 on some canaries, so loss(w0) = +inf and score = loss(w0) - loss(wt) = +inf for those rows. Those are the strongest possible pieces of evidence, but _roc.py:47/52-53 place them at or above the terminal threshold with side='left', so they are excluded from the terminal counts. Measured on the real code with 500/500 canaries: 50 +inf in-scores give fn_counts[-1]=450 and attack_auc 0.5794 vs 0.5843 clean, i.e. 50 perfect member detections push the reported AUC down. Worse, 50 +inf out-scores (50 perfect false positives) give tn_counts[-1]=450 and attack_auc 0.5902 vs 0.5843 clean — the metric moves in exactly the wrong direction while true concordance falls from 0.5716 to 0.5204. attack_beta_at is skewed the same way via tp_counts[-1]/fp_counts[-1] (_estimate.py:70-71). Epsilon is unaffected: _best_r_u normalises with n_in/n_out, not the terminal counts.

Severity stays low rather than medium because it requires a +inf score, which only the reference-score subtraction path can produce (plain loss_scores yields -inf on overflow, which is handled correctly), and because only diagnostic metrics — not the epsilon lower bound — are affected.

survivors.title: Dependabot never sees the ten sub-package manifests, Cargo.lock, or uv.lock
survivors.claim: The `pip` ecosystem entry has `directory: "/"` only. Dependabot's pip updater is directory-scoped, so it reads the root `pyproject.toml` (dependency-groups dev/examples/docs) and nothing else. All runtime pins — `torch>=2.9.0`, `transformers>=4.57.0,<6`, `peft>=0.18.0`, `scipy`, `torchopt`, `optree`, `safetensors`, `datasets` — live in `packages/*/pyproject.toml` and are never proposed for update. There is no `cargo` ecosystem entry (so `Cargo.lock`, including `pyo3 0.23`, `rand 0.8`, `statrs 0.18`, gets no security updates) and no `uv` entry (so `uv.lock`, which is what CI actually installs, is never refreshed).
survivors.failure_scenario: A CVE lands in a transitive Rust crate in Cargo.lock or in a pinned Python dep declared only in `packages/opaque-transformers/pyproject.toml`. Dependabot files no PR because neither location is configured, and the maintainers — who have the 'Dependabot updates for actions' checkbox in WORKFLOWS.md — reasonably assume coverage. The vulnerable version keeps shipping in every published wheel because uv.lock is what CI resolves.
evidence: .github/dependabot.yml:20-38 single pip entry with `directory: "/"`, no `directories:` list
`ls packages/*/pyproject.toml` -> 10 manifests, none referenced
No `package-ecosystem: "cargo"` and no `package-ecosystem: "uv"` entry in the file
Cargo.lock and uv.lock are both committed at repo root; CI installs from uv.lock via `uv sync`
survivors.fix_sketch: Replace `directory: "/"` with `directories: ["/", "/packages/*"]` on the pip entry (or switch to `package-ecosystem: "uv"` which understands the workspace + uv.lock), and add a `cargo` entry with `directory: "/"`.

survivors.title: opaque-accounting wheel embeds build-host `__pycache__/*.pyc`, making the wheel non-reproducible
survivors.claim: `[tool.maturin] python-source = "src"` with `python-packages = ["opaque.accounting", "opaque.api.accounting.core"]` copies those directories verbatim, with no `exclude` configured. If the build host has ever imported the package (e.g. a developer or a runner that ran `uv sync`/pytest before `uv build`), the resulting wheel contains stale bytecode.
survivors.failure_scenario: Reproduced: building on this checkout produced `opaque_accounting-0.0.0.dev0-cp311-abi3-linux_x86_64.whl` containing `opaque/accounting/__pycache__/__init__.cpython-311.pyc` and `opaque/api/accounting/core/__pycache__/__init__.cpython-311.pyc`. Two builds of the same commit on hosts with and without a warm `__pycache__` produce different wheel contents and different RECORD hashes, so the published artifact cannot be verified against a rebuild. A stale `.pyc` whose recorded source mtime/size happens to match the installed `.py` is also loaded in preference to the source.
evidence:
packages/opaque-accounting/pyproject.toml:34-38 `[tool.maturin]
features = ["python-extension"]
module-name = "opaque.api.accounting.core.opaque_accounting"
python-source = "src"
python-packages = ["opaque.accounting", "opaque.api.accounting.core"]` — no `exclude`
Built wheel namelist includes `opaque/accounting/__pycache__/__init__.cpython-311.pyc` and `opaque/api/accounting/core/__pycache__/__init__.cpython-311.pyc`
`find packages/opaque-accounting/src -name __pycache__ -type d` -> present in the working tree
Contrast: the setuptools-built wheels (opaque_engine, opaque_patches, opaque_transformers) contain no .pyc
survivors.fix_sketch: Add `exclude = ["**/__pycache__/**", "**/*.pyc"]` to `[tool.maturin]`, and/or `git clean -xdf packages/opaque-accounting/src` in the CI preflight before `uv build`.

verification.title: opaque-accounting wheel embeds build-host `__pycache__/*.pyc`, making the wheel non-reproducible
verification.reasoning:
Directly reproduced from the artifact already present in this checkout: /home/user/opaque/target/wheels/opaque_accounting-0.0.0.dev0-cp311-abi3-linux_x86_64.whl. Its namelist (53 entries) contains 17 `__pycache__/*.cpython-311.pyc` files, including opaque/accounting/__pycache__/__init__.cpython-311.pyc and opaque/api/accounting/core/{,composition/,mechanisms/,amplification/}__pycache__/*.pyc. So maturin's `python-source = "src"` + `python-packages` copy (pyproject.toml:34-38, no `exclude`) does NOT filter bytecode, despite `__pycache__/` being in the repo .gitignore, and the working tree does contain those directories. The factual core holds.

Two parts of the stated impact do not survive scrutiny, so the severity stays at the floor rather than rising:
(1) 'the published artifact cannot be verified against a rebuild' overstates it. Every wheel-building job builds from a clean `actions/checkout@v5` and runs only rust-toolchain / setup-uv / setup-python / `bash .github/scripts/set_build_versions.sh` before `uv build --wheel` — release.yml:125-144, ci.yml:206-224, pr.yml:399-416. None of those steps import the package, and `uv build` is isolated, so no `__pycache__` exists on the runner. Released/preview wheels are therefore bytecode-free; only a hand-built wheel from a warm dev tree (exactly the one in target/wheels) is affected.
(2) 'A stale .pyc ... is also loaded in preference to the source' is effectively unreachable. CPython's default (timestamp) pyc invalidation compares the recorded source mtime and size against the installed .py; installers write the .py with a fresh mtime, so the shipped .pyc is discarded and recompiled. It would take a deliberate mtime-preserving install plus an exact size match to shadow the source.
What remains: bloated wheels and byte-for-byte non-determinism between a clean and a dirty build host — a real hygiene defect, no runtime or privacy consequence. affects_epsilon: false is right.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A maintainer who has run pytest/`uv sync` in the checkout builds the accounting wheel locally (`cd packages/opaque-accounting && uv build --wheel`) and publishes or shares that wheel. Because `[tool.maturin]` sets no `exclude`, maturin copies `src/opaque/**/__pycache__/*.pyc` verbatim: the wheel in this checkout at /home/user/opaque/target/wheels/opaque_accounting-0.0.0.dev0-cp311-abi3-linux_x86_64.whl carries 17 such .pyc entries with corresponding RECORD hashes. A rebuild of the same commit on a clean tree produces a different file list and different RECORD, so the two artifacts do not compare equal. CI-produced wheels are unaffected — release.yml/ci.yml/pr.yml build from a fresh checkout with no import step — and the shipped .pyc files do not shadow the .py sources at runtime, since pyc timestamp validation invalidates them once the installer rewrites the source mtime.
verification.refutation: Partial refutation of the stated impact, not the fact: (a) the release/preview/CI wheel jobs (release.yml:125-144, ci.yml:206-224, pr.yml:399-416) all start from `actions/checkout@v5` and run no Python import before `uv build`, so published artifacts contain no __pycache__ — the 'published artifact cannot be verified against a rebuild' framing does not apply to anything the project actually ships; (b) the 'stale .pyc loaded in preference to the source' claim is wrong in practice, because CPython validates a timestamp-mode .pyc against the .py's mtime and size and installers write the .py fresh, so the embedded bytecode is invalidated and recompiled on first import.

survivors.title: dp-concepts.md states the per-step epsilon of the Gaussian mechanism as C/sigma while defining sigma as the noise multiplier
survivors.claim: The basic-composition paragraph says "For a mechanism with noise multiplier $\sigma$ and sensitivity $C$, a single step gives $\varepsilon_0 \approx C / \sigma$, so $T$ steps cost approximately $T \cdot C / \sigma$." The noise multiplier is by definition the noise standard deviation divided by the sensitivity (the repo uses this convention: `_gaussian.py:161-162`, "The realized standard deviation is `noise_multiplier * clipped.max_norm`"). With that definition the sensitivity cancels and eps_0 ~ 1/sigma, not C/sigma. Separately, the advanced-composition formula quoted at line 130 is the Dwork-Rothblum-Vadhan bound but is attributed to "Kairouz et al. 2015", whose contribution is the *optimal* composition theorem, a different (tighter) result.
survivors.failure_scenario: A user follows the stated scaling to sanity-check a calibration: they double the clip norm C from 1.0 to 2.0 while keeping `noise_multiplier` fixed, and expect epsilon to double per the doc's formula. It does not change at all, because doubling C doubles the absolute noise std in lockstep. The user concludes the accountant is wrong and lowers the noise multiplier to compensate, spending real privacy budget on a documentation error.
evidence: dp-concepts.md:122-124 — "For a mechanism with noise multiplier $\\sigma$ and sensitivity $C$, a single step gives $\\varepsilon_0 \\approx C / \\sigma$, so $T$ steps cost approximately $T \\cdot C / \\sigma$."
_gaussian.py:161-162 — "The realized standard deviation is ``noise_multiplier * clipped.max_norm``." (so noise_multiplier = std / sensitivity)
dp-concepts.md:126-130 — advanced composition eps = sqrt(2T ln(1/delta)) * eps_0 + T * eps_0 (e^{eps_0} - 1) attributed to Kairouz et al. 2015 (arXiv:1311.0776)
survivors.fix_sketch: Change to "eps_0 ~ 1/sigma for noise multiplier sigma (equivalently C/sigma_abs for absolute noise std sigma_abs)", and attribute the quoted advanced-composition bound to Dwork, Rothblum, Vadhan (2010), keeping Kairouz et al. for the optimal composition theorem.

verification.title: dp-concepts.md states the per-step epsilon of the Gaussian mechanism as C/sigma while defining sigma as the noise multiplier
verification.reasoning: Read docs/user-guide/dp-concepts.md:117-134 verbatim. The sentence is exactly as quoted: 'For a mechanism with noise multiplier $\sigma$ and sensitivity $C$, a single step gives $\varepsilon_0 \approx C/\sigma$'. The repo's convention is unambiguous: packages/opaque-dpsgd/src/opaque/api/dpsgd/noise/_gaussian.py:161-163 documents 'The realized standard deviation is ``noise_multiplier * clipped.max_norm``', i.e. noise_multiplier = std/sensitivity. Under that definition C cancels and eps_0 ~ 1/sigma (up to the delta-dependent factor). The accountant path corroborates it: packages/opaque-dpsgd/tests/accounting/test_cross_validation.py:404-414 calls _native.gaussian_pld(z_eff, ...) with only the noise multiplier -- no clip norm enters epsilon anywhere. So the formula as written is dimensionally inconsistent with the repo's own convention. The second sub-claim also holds: the quoted bound sqrt(2T ln(1/delta))*eps_0 + T*eps_0(e^{eps_0}-1) is the Dwork-Rothblum-Vadhan (2010) advanced composition; arXiv:1311.0776 (Kairouz-Oh-Viswanath) is the optimal composition theorem. This is a common loose citation rather than a fabrication, so it is the weaker half of the finding.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A reader of the conceptual overview concludes that at fixed `noise_multiplier`, raising `max_grad_norm` from 1.0 to 2.0 doubles the per-step epsilon. It does not: the realized noise std scales with the clip norm in lockstep (_gaussian.py:161-163) and the accountant's epsilon is a function of the noise multiplier alone (gaussian_pld(z_eff)). The reader either wastes time reconciling the doc with the accountant's output, or -- less likely -- treats the accountant as buggy. Actual privacy loss is unlikely: nothing in the library asks the user to hand-compute epsilon from this formula, the paragraph itself labels the bound 'correct but extremely loose', and calibration is performed by the PLD accountant. The impact is reader confusion in an explainer, not a miscalibrated run.
verification.refutation: Not refuted. The only correction is to the reporter's blast radius: their scenario ends with the user 'spending real privacy budget on a documentation error', which overstates it -- epsilon is computed by the PLD accountant from the noise multiplier, never from this formula, so a user acting on the confusion would have to override the calibrator by hand. Severity stays low (it was already low).

verification.title: `test_perfect_separation` in the auditing ROC suite executes zero assertions if the threshold leaves the Pareto frontier
verification.reasoning: The code is as quoted (test_roc.py:41-47): both assertions sit inside `if len(idx) > 0:` with no else and no assertion that idx is non-empty, so the test is structurally capable of passing while asserting nothing. I reproduced get_tn_fn_counts([5,6,7,8,9],[0,1,2,3,4]) against the real implementation (_roc.py:34-58) and today it returns thresholds=[0., 5., inf], tn=[0,5,5], fn=[0,0,5]; np.where(thresholds==5) yields index 1, so the assertions do currently execute and do currently pass. The defect is latent-vacuity, not a presently-silent test. One correction to the reporter's reachability story: their specific trigger is backwards. pareto_frontier drops points on cross_product <= 0, i.e. it already discards collinear/equal points; relaxing that to strictly-dominated-only (< 0) would keep *more* points, so 5.0 would survive. Threshold 5.0 is the corner of the frontier here and is robust to that particular change. Reachable triggers are different ones: changing the threshold grid (e.g. emitting midpoints or -inf instead of the raw union), a dtype/exact-float-equality change making `thresholds == 5` fail, or switching searchsorted side.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: Someone changes how get_tn_fn_counts builds its threshold grid -- e.g. emitting midpoints between adjacent scores, or prepending -inf, or returning float32 -- so that the exact value 5.0 is no longer present in `thresholds`. `np.where(thresholds == 5)[0]` becomes empty, the guard short-circuits, and the only test pinning TN/FN at the perfectly-separating threshold reports green while asserting nothing. Because get_tn_fn_counts feeds tpr_at_given_fpr and hence the one-run epsilon lower bound, a genuine regression in the separating-threshold counts would ship unnoticed by this test. Note this is a lost-safety-net issue only: the test passes and asserts correctly today.
verification.refutation: Not refuted -- the guard really can make the test vacuous. But two of the reporter's framings are overstated: the title's conditional reads as if the test is silent now (verified: it is not, thresholds=[0,5,inf] with 5.0 at index 1, tn=5, fn=0), and the proposed trigger (relaxing the Pareto tie-break from <=0 to <0) would retain more frontier points and so would not drop 5.0. Severity stays low; the one-line fix in the sketch (assert len(idx) == 1 before the two assertions) is still the right change.

verification.title: The "End-to-end loop" in the DP-SGD user guide iterates the batch sampler directly (yielding index lists, not data) and never composes the accountant
verification.reasoning: Both factual halves check out. (1) docs/user-guide/dp-sgd.md:147 literally reads `for step, batch in enumerate(sampler):`, and `sampler` is the PoissonSampler constructed at dp-sgd.md:108-112. packages/opaque-dpsgd/src/opaque/api/dpsgd/sampling/_poisson.py:118-134 defines `__iter__` returning `Iterator[list[int]]` via `_sample_step` -> `_plain_poisson_step_indices`, and the class docstring (line ~70) says 'Use with DataLoader's batch_sampler parameter' with an example that does exactly that. (2) The page contains no `Accountant`, no `epsilon_at`, no `| step_proc`; the DP-FTRL counterpart at dp-ftrl.md:120-129 does show the running-epsilon idiom (`acct |= step; eps_so_far = acct.epsilon_at(delta=1e-5)`), and accounting.md:181 documents `process = process | step_proc` as the DP-SGD-shaped form, so this is a genuine parity gap between the two end-to-end pages. First, the 'does not run' claim is true but weaker than presented: the block is already an obvious skeleton -- `model` is undefined, `torchopt.apply_updates` is called although the block imports only `torch`, `make_functional` and `state_dict`, and `fmodel` is bound then unused -- so a literal copy-paste dies on `NameError: torchopt` before it ever reaches the vmap/indexing error. Second, 'never tracks epsilon' overstates the harm: section 1 calibrates the noise multiplier against `acc.epsilon_budget(3.0, delta=1e-5)` with `num_steps=1000`, so epsilon is pinned up front by the standard calibrate-first workflow; the missing composition costs a per-step readout, not the budget itself. Separately, the reporter missed the sharper defect in the same block: section 4 builds the sampler with no `n_steps=`, and `__iter__` with `n_steps is None` runs `while True`, so the guide's only complete loop has no termination and no `num_steps` bound -- that one really can overrun the 1000 steps calibration priced. refuted.title: Bounded Gaussian noise is a data-dependent renormalized truncation, not post-processing — docs and module instruct users to account for it as the plain Gaussian mechanism
refuted.claim: `gaussian_noise(bound=...)` samples from a Gaussian *renormalized* over [low, high] where the renormalization interval is centred on the private value (`z_low = (low - center_c)/std`, `z_high = (high - center_c)/std`, `u = alpha + u*(beta-alpha)`). The output density is p(y|x) = phi((y-x)/sigma) / (sigma * Z(x)) with Z(x) = Phi((high-x)/sigma) - Phi((low-x)/sigma), i.e. the normalizer depends on the data. The module docstring (lines 25-28) says "the privacy accounting is the standard (eps, delta)-Gaussian — bounding only modifies the noise distribution", and docs/mechanisms/dp-sgd/gaussian.md:177-178 and docs/user-guide/noise.md:175-178 say to "treat the bound as bounded-support post-processing on the standard (eps, delta)-Gaussian mechanism" with "Accounting (unchanged from the unbounded mechanism)". This is false: post-processing must be a function of the released output alone, and here the *sampling distribution* is a function of the private input. The privacy loss picks up an extra additive term log(Z(x')/Z(x)) on every output that the Gaussian PLD does not contain. The docs are internally inconsistent too — noise.md:144 states "No probability mass sits at the boundaries", which is exactly what rules out the post-processing (clamp) interpretation. The module simultaneously claims the mechanism *is* Chen and Hale's bounded Gaussian mechanism (line 167-168, gaussian.md:172) and that Chen and Hale's analysis "does not apply" (line 25-27), and then supplies no analysis of its own.
refuted.failure_scenario: Documented configuration `gaussian_noise(noise_multiplier=1.0, bound=(0.0, 10.0), key=key(42))` (this exact asymmetric form is the third worked example in the docstring at lines 219-222 and is permitted by `_resolve_bound`, which only requires low <= 0 <= high). Take sigma = 1 (noise_multiplier 1.0, max_norm 1.0) and one coordinate whose clipped value is x = 0 on dataset D and x' = 1 on neighbouring D'. Z(0) = Phi(10) - Phi(0) = 0.5000; Z(1) = Phi(9) - Phi(-1) = 0.8413. Every released y in [0,10] therefore carries privacy loss log(Z(1)/Z(0)) = 0.520 nats *in addition to* the standard Gaussian privacy loss. Because this offset is deterministic, T-fold composition shifts the PLD by T * 0.520. Following docs/mechanisms/dp-sgd/gaussian.md:196-199 verbatim (`dpsgd_acc.poisson(dpsgd_acc.gaussian(1.0), sample_rate=0.01)` composed 1000 times) the accountant reports the unbounded-Gaussian epsilon while the realized epsilon is understated by up to ~520 nats. The user ships a model believing eps ~= 2 when the mechanism does not satisfy any eps in that range.

verification.title: Bounded Gaussian noise is a data-dependent renormalized truncation, not post-processing — docs and module instruct users to account for it as the plain Gaussian mechanism
verification.reasoning: The mathematical description of the code is right and I confirmed it line by line: _gaussian.py:276-283 computes z_low=(low-center_c)/std, z_high=(high-center_c)/std, alpha=Phi(z_low), beta=Phi(z_high), u=alpha+u*(beta-alpha), sample=center_c+std*Phi^-1(u) - textbook inverse-CDF sampling from N(center, sigma^2) conditioned on [low,high], with normalizer Z(x)=Phi((high-x)/sigma)-Phi((low-x)/sigma) that depends on the private center. So yes, calling this 'post-processing' in _gaussian.py:22-28, docs/mechanisms/dp-sgd/gaussian.md:176-178 and docs/user-guide/noise.md:171-177 (all quoted verbatim and verified) is technically wrong wording, and the privacy-loss expression does pick up +log(Z(x')/Z(x)). But the finding's conclusion - that epsilon is understated and the guarantee is void - does not follow, and I refuted it numerically. The reporter computed only the additive normalizer term and never computed the actual divergence, ignoring that the SAME truncation deletes the Gaussian tails, which is precisely where the large privacy loss lives. On the interval [low,high] the log-likelihood ratio is a bounded linear function of y, so the bounded mechanism is even pure-eps-DP. I computed the exact hockey-stick divergence H_{e^eps}(p_c || p_c') by numerical quadrature for the finding's own configuration (sigma=1, bound=(0,10), C=1, x=0 vs x'=1, both directions) and across a 2620-sample random sweep over sigma in [0.1,10], asymmetric bounds low in [-16,0], high in [0,16], eps in [0.03,10], and center pairs inside the sensitivity ball. In every single case delta_bounded(eps) <= delta_gaussian(eps); the maximum observed ratio was 1.0000009, which is trapezoid quadrature error at delta ~ 3.6e-9. For the cited config: at eps=0 (TV) gauss=0.3829 vs trunc=0.2039/0.2771; at eps=0.5 gauss=0.2384 vs trunc 0.0151/0.0862/0.0894/0.1465; at eps=1 gauss=0.1269 vs trunc <= 0.0650. Since the per-coordinate tradeoff function dominates the Gaussian's at every eps, f-DP composition monotonicity carries the domination through both the product over coordinates and the T-step composition, so dpsgd_acc.gaussian(nm) remains a valid (in fact conservative) upper bound. What survives is a documentation-accuracy defect - the justification given is wrong even though the conclusion is right - and the absence of any proof or test for it in the repo. That is low severity, not critical.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: There is no privacy failure. The residual defect is that _gaussian.py:22-28, docs/mechanisms/dp-sgd/gaussian.md:176-178, and docs/user-guide/noise.md:171-177 justify reusing dpsgd_acc.gaussian() by calling the bound 'bounded-support post-processing', which is the wrong justification: the sampler at _gaussian.py:276-283 renormalizes over an interval recentred on the private value, so the density carries a data-dependent Z(x). The right justification is that conditioning both neighbouring Gaussians on the same fixed interval caps the log-likelihood ratio and strictly shrinks the hockey-stick divergence, so the plain-Gaussian PLD remains a valid upper bound. A reviewer reading the current text could reasonably (and, per this finding, did) conclude the accounting is unsound. Fix is a docs/docstring correction plus a regression test that numerically bounds delta_bounded(eps) <= delta_gaussian(eps) over the reachable (sigma, bound, center) range - not a change to the sampler or the accountant.
verification.refutation: Direct numerical computation of the hockey-stick divergence refutes the claimed epsilon understatement. Using the finding's own example (sigma=1, bound=(0,10), neighbouring centers x=0 and x'=1, i.e. Z(0)=0.5 vs Z(1)=0.8413), the bounded mechanism's delta at eps=0.5 is 0.0894 (0->1) / 0.1465 (1->0) versus the plain Gaussian's 0.2384; at eps=1.0 it is 0.00016 / 0.0650 versus 0.1269; at eps=0 (total variation) it is 0.2771 versus 0.3829. The bounded mechanism is uniformly MORE private, not less. Same result for the finding's other cited configs and for a 2620-point random sweep over sigma, asymmetric bounds, eps, and center pairs within the clip ball: max delta_bounded/delta_gaussian = 1.0000009 (quadrature noise). The reason is visible in the code itself: because the sample is confined to [low,high] (_gaussian.py:284 clamps and the inverse-CDF at 281 guarantees support), log(p_c(y)/p_c'(y)) = (c-c')(y-(c+c')/2)/sigma^2 + log(Z(c')/Z(c)) is a BOUNDED linear function of y, so the mechanism satisfies pure eps-DP and its delta hits exactly 0 at moderate eps (e.g. 0 at eps=3.0 for sigma=1.1, bound=(-3,3), C=1, where the Gaussian still has delta=4.7e-4). The finding computed only the additive log(Z'/Z) offset and never the divergence, so its arithmetic ('+28.9 epsilon over 1000 steps', '~520 nats') measures a term that is more than cancelled by the tail removal it ignored. dpsgd_acc.gaussian(nm) is a conservative upper bound here, and examples/train_dpsgd.py:1474, train_sft.py:1799, train_dpo.py:2248 are not shipping an invalid guarantee.

refuted.title: Bounded Gaussian noise is a data-dependent truncation, not post-processing — accounted as plain Gaussian, and completely untested for privacy
refuted.claim: `gaussian_noise(bound=...)` samples from a normal truncated to [low,high] whose renormalising constant is computed from the *data-dependent* centre (`z_low=(low-center_c)/std`, `z_high=(high-center_c)/std`, `u = alpha + u*(beta-alpha)`). The output density is p_x(y) = phi((y-x)/sigma) / (sigma * Z(x)) with Z(x)=Phi((high-x)/sigma)-Phi((low-x)/sigma). The privacy loss between neighbouring aggregates x, x' is therefore the Gaussian term PLUS log(Z(x')/Z(x)), which is nonzero. Both the module docstring ('the privacy accounting is the standard (eps, delta)-Gaussian — bounding only modifies the noise distribution') and the user docs ('treat the bound as bounded-support post-processing on the standard (eps,delta)-Gaussian mechanism') assert this is post-processing. It is not: post-processing requires a map whose distribution is independent of the data given the mechanism output; here the noise distribution itself depends on the pre-noise value. No test in the repo asserts anything about the privacy of the bounded path — the tests only check support bounds, a KS fit to truncnorm, and that the *nominal* noise_stddev metadata is returned.
refuted.failure_scenario: User follows docs/user-guide/noise.md verbatim: `gaussian_noise(noise_multiplier=1.0, bound=(-1.0, 4.0), key=...)` with clipping_norm C=1.0 (so sigma = nm*C = 1.0), and accounts with `dpsgd_acc.poisson(dpsgd_acc.gaussian(1.0), q) * T`. For a coordinate whose clipped aggregate moves from x=-1 to x'=0 between neighbouring datasets, the extra privacy-loss term is log(Z(0)/Z(-1)) = log(0.8413/0.5000) = 0.520 nats — per step, per coordinate, on top of the Gaussian PLD. The reported epsilon is therefore a lower bound on the true epsilon, not an upper bound, and the whole DP guarantee for every bounded run is void. (Symmetric bounds are also affected: bound=(-2,2), sigma=1, x=1 -> x'=2 gives |extra| = 0.519.)

The BC branches use `torch.where(corrected > 0, corrected, v_raw)` with no clamp, which does differ from the `max(v̂ − φ̂, floor)` written in `_bias_correction.py:20-24` and `docs/user-guide/optimizers.md:156`. But the causal claim — that this missing floor is what produces unbounded updates — does not survive arithmetic. The denominator is `v_hat.sqrt() + eps` (eps OUTSIDE the sqrt, _adam.py:241/254), so the update is already hard-bounded by |m̂|/eps ≈ |m̂|·1e8; it is not unbounded. And applying the documented floor at its shipped value, bc_floor = eps² = 1e-16, gives sqrt(1e-16) = 1e-8 = eps exactly, i.e. a denominator of 2e-8 versus a worst case of 1e-8 today: the floor changes the worst-case update magnitude by at most a factor of 2, and only for coordinates where `corrected` has already fallen below 1e-16. It cannot turn the reporter's max|update| of 2243 into anything near O(1); if anything, on the branch that actually matters (`corrected <= 0`, where noise dominates), the shipped `torch.where(..., v_raw)` fallback is strictly safer than the documented floor — flooring at 1e-16 there would give |m̂|/2e-8 ≈ 1.5e4, i.e. LARGER than what the code does. So the code implements a different and better-behaved estimator than the doc describes; the reporter has inverted which one is dangerous. The reporter's own fix_sketch concedes this by proposing a relative floor `kappa*v_raw` rather than wiring `bc_floor` in — that is a new design, not a restoration of intended behaviour. Reachability is also gated: `noise_bias_correction` defaults to False on every factory (`_adam.py:317`), and docs/user-guide/optimizers.md:228-232,251-254 documents BC-on as the LR-sensitive choice ("BC actively amplifies the resulting schedule overshoot") and explicitly recommends leaving it off until LR is tuned. What survives is a documentation/dead-code cleanup: the doc formula and the `# see module docstring on the rationale` comment at _adam.py:346 both describe a floor the code does not apply (and the _adam.py module docstring, lines 1-48, never mentions a floor at all), and `bc_floor` should be deleted from `_adagrad`/`_adadelta`.

The worst case is a wrong pairwise comparison, not a deadlock. (2) The premise — two ranks holding the same key set in different insertion orders — is not produced by any code path in the repo. `per_group()` builds `values` by iterating `all_patterns.items()` (a dict) filtered by membership in `used_groups`; the `set` at _per_group.py:129 is used only for `in` tests, so insertion order is the caller's kwarg order and is deterministic and identical on every rank under SPMD. `sync_adaptive_clip_state` rebuilds `new_values` from `sorted(current_pg.values.keys())` (dpsgd/clipping/_distributed.py:59), so post-sync order is canonical on all ranks. `PerGroup.__mul__`/`__rmul__` preserve order. Serialization round-trips through a template built by the same code on each rank. The reporter's "one rank rebuilt it from a checkpoint dict" requires rank-conditional user code, which breaks the SPMD assumption the whole module is built on. (3) The companion claim about `state._num_clipped.items()` at dpsgd/clipping/_distributed.py:50-53 is the same story: `_num_clipped` is keyed off the same PerGroup, built identically on every rank. refuted.title: No detection of a stale or un-threaded noise state: reusing the same `GaussianNoiseState` reproduces identical noise on every step
refuted.claim: `noise_fn(grads, st)` derives its generator purely from `(st._rng_key, st._step_counter)` and returns a new state with the counter bumped. Nothing marks the input state as consumed and nothing records which `(key, step)` pairs have been used. A caller that drops the returned state — `noisy, _ = noise_fn(grads, noise_state)`, or a refactor that rebinds `noise_state` inside an inner scope — silently re-draws the *same* noise vector at every step. The same is true of `AdaptiveClipState`. The README leans on "a functional API with explicit state — no hooks, no subclassing, no hidden mutation" as the safety property, but explicitness here is unenforced: the failure is invisible in loss curves (the noise is zero-mean and the model still trains) and invisible to the accountant (which composes a per-step process regardless).
refuted.failure_scenario: A user writes `noisy_grads, _ = noise_fn(grads, noise_state)` inside the loop (a plausible slip when the returned state is not otherwise needed). Every step now adds the identical vector z drawn from `fold_in(key, 0)`. The released sequence is `{ĝ_1+z, ĝ_2+z, …}`; an adversary differencing consecutive releases obtains `ĝ_{t+1} − ĝ_t` with the noise cancelled exactly, i.e. noiseless access to gradient differences. `Accountant.epsilon_at` still reports the calibrated ε. No exception, no warning, no metric changes.
evidence: packages/opaque-dpsgd/src/opaque/api/dpsgd/noise/_gaussian.py:377-380 — `next_state = GaussianNoiseState(_step_counter=st._step_counter + 1, _rng_key=st._rng_key)` — derived from the *input* state, with no consumption marker

packages/opaque-dpsgd/src/opaque/api/dpsgd/noise/_gaussian.py:394-395 — `effective_stddev = _clipped_stddev(grads); step_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, st._step_counter)` — the only inputs to the draw
packages/opaque-dpsgd/src/opaque/api/dpsgd/clipping/_adaptive.py:505-517 — `AdaptiveClipState` has the same shape and the same absence of a guard
docs/user-guide/dp-sgd.md:145-150 — the documented "End-to-end loop" threads state correctly but says nothing about what happens if you don't
refuted.fix_sketch: Add a cheap consumption guard: keep a per-`noise_fn` closure-local set (or just a monotonic high-water mark) of the step counters already served, and raise on a repeat — `noise_fn saw step_counter=0 twice; you are not threading the returned state`. This costs one integer comparison per step and is a pure-function-preserving check (the guard lives in the closure, not the state). Apply the same to `adaptive_clipped_grad` and `mf_gaussian_noise`.

The proposed fix - a closure-local high-water mark that raises on a repeated counter - would break that test, break in-process resume-from-checkpoint, and break any legitimate replay; it would convert a supported operation into an exception. What remains is the generic property of every immutable-state functional API (JAX included): if you discard the returned state, you get the old state's behavior. That is exactly what 'explicit state, no hidden mutation' means, and it is visible in one line at the call site. The claimed invisibility is also overstated in one respect: with a constant noise vector the accountant is unaffected, but this is user-authored code that visibly writes `_` where every documented example writes `noise_state`.

Every step then re-derives fold_in(key, 0) and adds the identical vector z, so consecutive releases differ by a noiseless gradient difference while the accountant still reports the calibrated epsilon. This requires the user to explicitly discard a returned value that every documented loop (docs/user-guide/dp-sgd.md section 6, all tutorials, examples/train_dpsgd.py) binds; and the same-state-in-same-state-out behavior it depends on is a tested guarantee (test_saved_state_replay_is_deterministic) required for checkpoint restore and for cross-rank identical noise, so it cannot be turned into an error.

refuted.title: A `NoisedPytree` carrying `noise_stddev=None` silently disables bias correction while the φ-EMA decays, under-subtracting the noise variance with no error or warning
refuted.claim: `NoisedPytree.noise_stddev` has dataclass default `None` (engine/types.py:374) and `NoiseStddev` is typed `float | PerGroup | None`. `_route_noisy_pytree` forwards it unconditionally: `return updates.pytree, {"noise_stddev": updates.noise_stddev}`. Every scaler then coerces with `effective_stddev = noise_stddev if noise_stddev is not None else 0.0`, which is the same code path as "an un-noised update arrived". The result is not a no-op: with BC enabled, φ *decays* by β₂ each such step while `nu` keeps absorbing the real σ² of the noise that is actually present, so the correction is silently under-applied and stays wrong for ~1/(1−β₂) steps afterwards. There is no validation that a privatised update carries its realized σ when `noise_bias_correction=True`.

refuted.title: "Pillutla Score" is not a construct in the cited paper and the stated guarantee is not what Theorem 1 says

verification.title: "Pillutla Score" is not a construct in the cited paper and the stated guarantee is not what Theorem 1 says
verification.reasoning: I checked the math the docstring actually claims, and it holds. inverse() (_blt_math.py:343-356) computes the inverse's decay parameters as the eigenvalues of Theta2 = diag(buf_decay) - outer(output_scale, 1). det(Theta - w*1^T - mu*I) = prod(lambda_i - mu) * (1 + sum_i w_i/(mu - lambda_i)), so the inverse decay parameters are the roots of g(mu) = 1 + sum_i w_i/(mu - lambda_i). g(0) = 1 - sum_i(w_i/lambda_i) = 1 - pillutla_score(). With w_i > 0, g' = -sum w_i/(mu-lambda_i)^2 < 0, so g decreases from 1 (as mu -> -inf) to -inf (as mu -> lambda_min^-), giving exactly one root in that range. score < 1 puts g(0) > 0 and hence that root in (0, lambda_min) -- all inverse decay parameters strictly positive. score > 1 puts it at mu < 0 -- a negative decay parameter, an oscillating and genuinely ill-behaved inverse. So 'Score < 1 ensures well-behaved inverse' is exactly right, and the docstring never claims it is the invertibility condition. Both halves of the reporter's failure scenario collapse: (a) since lambda_i in (0,1) implies sum(alpha_i/lambda_i) > sum(alpha_i), score < 1 *implies* sum(alpha_i) < 1, so no BLT violating the theorem's hypothesis can slip through a score gate -- the gate is strictly conservative; (b) rejecting a BLT with score > 1 is not over-conservative pedantry, it is rejecting one whose inverse has a negative decay parameter. The sole caller (_blt_math.py:975-982, get_init_blt) uses max_pillutla_score=1-1e-6 as a shrink factor on output_scale during initialization, not as a gate on inverse(); inverse() gates on decay-parameter separation (line 335-341) instead. That leaves only the nickname 'Pillutla Score', which I cannot verify against the paper text; even if the paper never names it, an internal nickname for a correctly-described quantity is a nomenclature preference, not a defect.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: No failure is reachable. The quantity is used at exactly one call site (get_init_blt -> from_rational_approx_to_sqrt_x, _blt_math.py:234-237) to rescale output_scale so the score stays below 1-1e-6, which -- because buf_decay lies in (0,1) -- is strictly stronger than the sum(alpha_i) < 1 hypothesis the reporter says is being bypassed. The most that could be written up is a docstring sentence noting the quantity is not named in the source paper.
verification.refutation: _blt_math.py:343-356 shows the inverse's decay parameters are the eigenvalues of diag(buf_decay) - outer(output_scale, ones), whose characteristic equation is 1 + sum(w_i/(mu - lambda_i)) = 0; evaluating at mu = 0 gives 1 - pillutla_score(), so score < 1 is exactly the condition for all inverse decay parameters to be positive -- the docstring's 'well-behaved inverse' claim, verbatim. The doc comment (adaclip.rs:7-18, 24 and python/adaclip.rs:5-19) says 'combined L2 sensitivity' in the summary, the body and the Returns clause, and never says noise multiplier. The Python stub packages/opaque-accounting/src/opaque/api/accounting/core/opaque_accounting.pyi:865-879 says the same and additionally cites 'Andrew et al. 2021' -- so the reporter's parenthetical that 'the module currently cites nothing' is true of the .rs file only, not of the shipped Python-facing surface. The caller inverts correctly (_adaclip.py:54-56) and the round-trip is pinned by a cross-validation test (test_cross_validation.py:404-414) asserting proc.epsilon_at(1e-5) == gaussian_pld(1/s).epsilon_at(1e-5) to rel=1e-12.

Reproduced on torch 2.10.0+cu128 with `f(x)=(x**3).sum()`, `x=[1,2,3]`: before patching, `grad(grad-sum)`, `jacrev(grad)` and `vjp(grad)` all return `[6,12,18]`; after `apply_runtime_patches()`, all three return **`[0,0,0]` silently**, with first-order `grad` still correct. **Fix:** scope the `create_graph=False` override to opaque's own transform (a thread-local set around `clipped_grad`'s `vmap(grad(...))`) rather than rebinding the module global for the process, and re-install a guard that *raises* on nested first-order transforms instead of removing the check. **Notes:** this is a documented, opt-outable trade-off — `docs/user-guide/memory-optimizations.md:133-141` lists "Only safe for first-order differentiation… Not compatible with higher-order transforms" and documents `vmap_checkpointing=False`. The undocumented residue is that the failure is **silent zeros** rather than an error (a reader of "not compatible" would expect a raise), and that the docs' own example list names `torch.func.hessian`, which is `jacfwd(jacrev(...))` and still returns the correct `[6,12,18]` — so the doc's illustrative case is one that still works while the genuinely broken cases (reverse-over-reverse) are unlisted.

### Auditing

**OPQ-127 — No canary construction or "injection" exists: `coin_flip` only subsets natural training rows, while the README advertises "coin-flip canary injection".** `packages/opaque-auditing/src/opaque/api/auditing/_coin_flip.py:137-154`; `packages/opaque-auditing/README.md:4, 30` · not-implemented · ε:no · **CONFIRMED**. `coin_flip()` touches `dataset` only at `:137` for `len()`; `:143-146` selects `num_canaries` existing row indices uniformly and flips a coin per index. Nothing is constructed, mislabelled, perturbed or inserted, and no canary-crafting utility exists anywhere in the repo (grep for `canary` outside opaque-auditing hits only the three examples' `--audit-canaries` flags, all of which pass the natural HF training set straight through). **Fix:** ship a canary-crafting helper (random-token sequences, label flips, or gradient-space canaries as in Steinke et al. §5), or correct the README to "coin-flip canary **partitioning**" and document in the user guide that natural-example canaries yield a valid but very weak lower bound. **Notes:** the coin_flip docstring (`:121`) and `docs/user-guide/auditing.md:15` both describe the real behaviour accurately — only the README's two uses of "injection" are wrong. The implemented score *is* Steinke Alg. 3's loss-difference (`loss_scores` supports `reference_scores`, and `examples/train_dpsgd.py:1317-1325` uses it), which the paper does evaluate with natural canaries — so the setup is a legitimate low-power variant, not broken. But a user reading a small ε̂ as evidence of correct noising is over-reading a low-power test, and there is no documented API for supplying stronger canaries (constructing `CoinFlip` by hand and setting the private `_in_mask` is the only route). Directly limits **OPQ-033**.

**OPQ-128 — No key-domain separation between the auditing RNG namespace and the mechanism RNG namespace.** `_coin_flip.py:143-146` · privacy-correctness · ε:no (today) · **PLAUSIBLE**. `coin_flip` derives canary selection from `np.random.default_rng(key.seed)` and the coin flips from `np.random.default_rng(fold_in(key, 1).seed)` — neither carrying a domain-separation tag. The DP-SGD noise stream uses `rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, st._step_counter)` with the counter starting at 0, so **step 1 uses `fold_in(key, 1)` — byte-identical key material to the coin flips**, and `examples/train_dpsgd.py:1191` passes `key(args.seed)` to `coin_flip` while `:1689/:1694` pass `key(args.seed)` to `gaussian_noise`. The one-run theorem requires the coin vector S to be independent of the mechanism's internal randomness. **Fix:** derive both auditing streams through a string tag — `fold_in(key, 'opaque.auditing.canary_select')` and `fold_in(key, 'opaque.auditing.coin_flip')` — and document in the user guide that the audit key must be independent of the training key (`fold_in` already accepts `str` tags, so the mechanism exists and is simply unused). **Notes:** measured **no** exploitable dependence today (P(canary in batch 1) = 0.04988 under a shared seed vs 0.04999 under independent seeds over 400 trials), because the two consumers draw from different generator families (numpy PCG64 vs a torch Generator seeded `seed % (2**63-1)`). `affects_epsilon` should be **false** — no current estimate is biased. The exposure is forward-looking: any future change moving the coin flips onto a torch generator would silently make S a low-entropy image of the value driving the noise, with no test able to catch it. One evidence item is wrong: the shipped example seeds `PoissonSampler` with `fold_in(key(args.seed), rank, epoch)` (`train_dpsgd.py:1739`), not `key(args.seed)` — that collision exists only across two docstrings, and it affects *which rows are canaries*, not the coin vector, so it is not an independence violation.

**OPQ-129 — `+inf` membership scores corrupt the TPR/FPR denominators used by `attack_auc` and `attack_beta_at`.** `_roc.py:47, 52-53`; `_estimate.py:70-71, 307-308` · numerical-correctness · ε:no · **CONFIRMED**. `thresholds = concat(union1d(in,out), [inf])`, so a `+inf` score appears twice and `side='left'` never counts it below any threshold — `fn_counts[-1] = n_in − (#+inf in-scores)` and likewise for `tn_counts`. Reproduced (500 in ~ N(0.2,1), 500 out ~ N(0,1)): clean `attack_auc` 0.5843; 50 `+inf` **in**-scores → 0.5794 with `fn[-1]=450` (50 perfect member detections push the metric *down*); 50 `+inf` **out**-scores → **0.5902** with `tn[-1]=450` while true concordance *falls* from 0.5716 to 0.5204 (50 perfect false positives push the metric *up*). **Fix:** use `n_in`/`n_out` from the `CoinFlip` as the TPR/FPR denominators, and append `np.nextafter(np.inf, 0)` or use `side='right'` at the terminal threshold. **Notes:** ε is unaffected — `_best_r_u` normalises with `n_in`/`n_out`, and a `+inf` in-score is correctly treated as a member guess at every threshold (unlike the NaN case, **OPQ-025**). Reachability is narrow: `-inf` (the common overflow direction, since `loss_scores` returns `-losses`) is handled correctly; `+inf` requires the reference-score path (`_loss.py:124`) with an infinite loss at the **untrained** model w₀.

**OPQ-130 — Test comment asserts a "Bonferroni" default that does not exist.** `tests/auditing/test_integration.py:42-44` · test-quality · ε:no · **CONFIRMED**. `grep -rni bonferroni` over the repo returns exactly two hits, both in this file (the comment at `:42` and the assertion message at `:44`). No multiplicity correction exists anywhere: `_estimate.py:137-139` is an unadjusted argmax over every Pareto threshold using the true labels, and `_eps_delta.py:41-47, 73-79` tests it at the raw significance. **Fix:** delete or correct the comment. If a correction is later added it belongs in `_best_r_u`/`_p_value`, not a test label. **Notes:** a comment in a test file cannot change any computed ε — `affects_epsilon` should be **false**. Its real cost is triage: a maintainer investigating **OPQ-004** greps for the correction, lands here, and concludes the multiple-threshold selection is already handled.

**OPQ-131 — Public façade surface is inconsistent: `opaque.auditing.attacks` omits `gradient_scores`.** `src/opaque/auditing/attacks/__init__.py:3-5`; `src/opaque/auditing/types.py:3-8` · api-misuse · ε:no · **CONFIRMED**. `opaque.api.auditing.attacks` exports both `gradient_scores` and `loss_scores`, and the top-level `opaque.auditing` re-exports both, but the `opaque.auditing.attacks` façade exports only `loss_scores` — so `from opaque.auditing import gradient_scores` works and `from opaque.auditing.attacks import gradient_scores` raises ImportError. Neither the existing contract tests (`test_facade_discipline.py`, `test_no_internal_namespace_in_facades.py`) nor the "Import all public namespaces" CI step checks façade/impl `__all__` parity. `grep -rn gradient_scores docs/ examples/` returns **zero** hits — the white-box gradient scorer, the one attack most likely to detect an under-noising bug, is undocumented and undiscoverable. **Fix:** add `gradient_scores` to the façade, add a façade/impl `__all__` parity contract test, and document `gradient_scores` in `docs/reference/auditing.md`. **Notes:** the `types.py` half (omitting `EpsDeltaMethod`/`GdpMethod`) is weaker — both are non-constructible method wrappers holding a private `_estimate`, obtained only from `OneRunEstimate.gdp()`/`eps_delta()`, and `types.py`'s docstring scopes itself to "the auditing result data classes"; the DX cost is limited to explicit type annotations.

**OPQ-139 — `test_perfect_separation` executes zero assertions if the threshold leaves the Pareto frontier.** `tests/auditing/test_roc.py:41-47` · test-quality · ε:no · **CONFIRMED**. Both assertions sit inside `if len(idx) > 0:` with no else and no assertion that `idx` is non-empty. Today it does pass correctly (`get_tn_fn_counts([5,6,7,8,9],[0,1,2,3,4])` returns `thresholds=[0., 5., inf]`, so index 1 exists, `tn=5`, `fn=0`), so this is latent vacuity, not a currently-silent test. **Fix:** `assert len(idx) == 1, f"threshold 5.0 missing from frontier: {thresholds}"` before the two assertions. **Notes:** the reporter's proposed trigger is backwards — relaxing `pareto_frontier`'s tie-break from `<= 0` to `< 0` would keep *more* points and 5.0 (a frontier corner) would survive. Real triggers are a changed threshold grid (midpoints, a `-inf` prepend), a dtype change breaking exact float equality, or a `searchsorted` side change.
